articles.title: Pydantic vs Zod for Validating LLM Tool Call Arguments
articles.description:
Originally published on robatdasorvi.com
For validating LLM tool call arguments, Pydantic and Zod fail the same way out of the box. They quietly drop any key the model made up and accept the rest. Use Pydantic for Python agents and Zod for TypeScript ones, then close every object. The closing matters more than which library you pick.
Because nobody asked it to reject anything. Pydantic v2's BaseModel defaults to extra="ignore", and Zod's z.object strips unknown keys. So a call like {"order_id": 4411, "refund_amount_usd": 50, "reason_code": "damaged"}, checked against a schema that only declares order_id and refund_amount_usd, comes back as a success with reason_code removed. The check ran, the call passed, and the model's belief that it had given a reason vanishes without a trace in your logs.
What bothers me about this failure is how quiet it is. No exception, no stack trace. The handler runs on a payload shorter than what the model wrote, and everything downstream looks normal. That is exactly why it survives.
Yes, and the closest old case is an interface that accepted a number without saying what it meant. Mars Climate Orbiter, lost in September 1999, is the clearest example. The NASA Phase I Mishap Investigation Board report, dated 10 November 1999, found that ground software produced output in pound-force-seconds where newton-seconds were expected, a factor of about 4.45 (NASA Mishap Investigation Board via LLIS). Every value was a plain number. Both were impulse values, and nothing in the interface said which unit system they used.
An LLM tool schema is the same kind of interface. A field typed as number accepts whatever the model believes a number is. Closing the object catches keys you never declared. It does not catch this second gap, a declared field whose meaning is ambiguous. For that, put the unit in the field name or description (refund_amount_usd) and add range constraints (Field(gt=0, le=10_000) in Pydantic, .positive().max(10000) in Zod).
Pick the one that matches your agent's language, then configure both the same way. Both can export JSON Schema, which is what the model provider actually sees.



Concern
Pydantic (Python)
Zod 4 (TypeScript)




Default for unknown keys
Ignored (extra="ignore")
Stripped


Close one object
model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
z.strictObject({...})


Export to JSON Schema
Model.model_json_schema()
z.toJSONSchema(schema)


Coercion risk
Lax mode accepts "5" for int

Strict unless you use z.coerce



Nested objects
Only closed if the nested model is also closed
Same: close each level



The selection usually comes down to the agent SDK you already use, since that decides what you pass in. Python agent SDKs such as OpenAI's pydantic_function_tool, Instructor, and PydanticAI take Pydantic models directly. TypeScript SDKs such as the Vercel AI SDK's tool({ inputSchema }) (named parameters before AI SDK 5) and OpenAI's zodFunction and zodResponseFormat take Zod schemas directly. Both validate at runtime and both give you static types: Zod through z.infer, Pydantic through the model class itself.
A closed Pydantic model for the refund example looks like this:
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class RefundArgs(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)
    order_id: int
    refund_amount_usd: float

RefundArgs.model_validate({"order_id": 4411, "refund_amount_usd": 50, "reason_code": "damaged"})  # raises ValidationError: reason_code, Extra inputs are not permitted

The Zod equivalent is one function name away:
import { z } from "zod";

const RefundArgs = z.strictObject({
  order_id: z.number().int(),
  refund_amount_usd: z.number(),
});

const parsed = RefundArgs.safeParse({ order_id: 4411, refund_amount_usd: 50, reason_code: "damaged" });
// parsed.success === false

Two details matter more than the syntax. Closing the root object does not close a nested filters object, so every level needs the setting. And a closed schema only rejects after the fact. Providers now offer grammar-constrained decoding that stops the extra key from being generated at all. OpenAI's Structured Outputs, announced on 6 August 2024, requires strict: true on the schema. The company reported that gpt-4o-2024-08-06 scored 100% on its complex schema-following evaluations, against under 40% for gpt-4-0613 (OpenAI, 2024). Constrained decoding and a validator on your side do different jobs. Within the JSON Schema subset it supports, the provider guarantees the shape. Refusals, and responses cut off at the token limit, can still come back non-conforming, and your validator is what tells you when the guarantee did not hold. OpenAI strict mode also requires additionalProperties: false and every property listed as required. extra="forbid" emits the first in model_json_schema(), but optional fields need to be expressed as required-but-nullable to pass.
Sometimes, and this is the strongest objection. Tam and colleagues tested format restrictions on reasoning tasks. They found strict formats hurt performance, and tighter constraints hurt more. They also noted that JSON output could place the answer field before the reasoning (Tam et al., "Let Me Speak Freely?", arXiv 2408.02442, 2024). If you force a tool call to fill in a JSON object before the model has reasoned, you may get worse decisions.
But the objection lands on how most teams apply schemas, not on schemas themselves. The paper's own results suggest where the damage comes from. Their natural-language-first variant, which reasons freely and converts the answer afterward, stayed closest to unconstrained performance. So give the model a free-text reasoning field or a separate step, then validate only the final arguments against a closed schema. Closing the object changes what the validator accepts. It does not change how the model thinks.
The paper's methodology was disputed by the Outlines team at dottxt (“Say What You Mean”, 2024), who argued that the paper's prompts differed between conditions and its free-text answers were parsed leniently, and that structured generation done properly matched or beat unstructured output.
A broader benchmark points the same way. JSONSchemaBench (2025) gathered roughly 10,000 real-world JSON schemas and compared constrained-decoding frameworks on coverage and compliance, including Guidance, Outlines, XGrammar, and the OpenAI and Gemini APIs (Geng et al., arXiv 2501.10868, 2025). Real schemas vary a lot in what they can express. A closed schema your provider can't fully enforce still needs your validator as the backstop.
My bot's long-form article lane lost 8 of 20 generations to JSON parse errors, and each failure silently burned a 48-hour slot. That is the mirror image of the dropped-key problem. The dropped key is a validator accepting too much. The article lane was real failures that nothing surfaced when they happened. Both are silent.
Earlier, four hardcoded target accounts that no longer existed absorbed 88% of the same bot's daily comment attempts for about six weeks, and every run logged success without raising an error.
The lesson carries over to tool calls: an unreliable output rate is survivable, but a rejection that has no counter, no alert and no reason attached looks exactly like a quiet day.
The Replit database deletion in July 2025 is a different kind of failure. An agent acted destructively in production rather than sending a malformed argument. My reading is that it shares a root assumption: nothing between the agent and production treated a destructive action as exceptional (eWeek, 22 July 2025; the CEO's own response is in his public posts on X from July 2025, @amasad). Schema validation would not have caught it, because the commands were valid. The lesson that carries over is narrower: treat a destructive tool as its own tool with its own closed schema and a human approval step, rather than one more optional argument on a general-purpose tool. My X growth agent worked this way: every post, reply, follow and like went through a Telegram approval I pressed by hand.
When a call is rejected, return the validation error to the model as the tool result so it can retry with corrected arguments. Cap the retry count. Log each rejection with the field name, so you can see which keys the model keeps inventing. Alert on a repeat rejection of the same field, since that points to a schema the model is misreading rather than a one-off. For retry strategy in more depth, see the LLM structured output essay.
Close every object at every level, reject unknown keys, and count each rejection as a named failure. A tool call with an undeclared field fails quietly, the same way the article lane's parse errors did. The model believed it was sending something the handler understood, and it wasn't. In the hypothetical refund example above, extra="forbid" or z.strictObject turns the dropped reason_code into a validation error on the first call.
If you're building this now, two related posts go further. LLM Structured Output: Validation, Retry or Constrained Decoding? compares the retry and grammar approaches. Agent Rule Conflicts: Why AI Pipelines Fail Silently covers silent failure more broadly. The library you pick matters less than the defaults you never changed.

articles.title: # What Is an AI Sandbox? How AI Agents Safely Run Code
articles.description:
AI agents are becoming more powerful every day. They can write code, execute commands, work with files, browse websites, and automate tasks.
But there is one important question:
What happens when an AI agent runs code that could damage your computer or access sensitive data?
This is where an AI sandbox becomes important.
Let's understand what it is, why developers use it, and how it works.
An AI sandbox is an isolated environment where an AI agent can perform tasks without getting unrestricted access to the host system.
Think of it as a separate workspace.
An AI agent can use this environment to:
Execute Python or JavaScript code.
Install and test dependencies.
Create and modify files.
Run scripts and commands.
Test generated code.
Experiment without directly affecting your main system.
The key idea is isolation: limit what the agent can access and what it can change.
Imagine asking an AI coding agent:
"Create a Python script that organizes all files on my computer."
The agent generates code and executes it.
What if the script accidentally deletes important files?
What if the generated code tries to access environment variables or private credentials?
Without proper restrictions, these actions could create serious problems.
A sandbox helps reduce these risks by limiting the agent's permissions and access.
A simplified workflow looks like this:
A user gives a task to an AI agent.
The AI generates code or commands.
The sandbox provides an isolated execution environment.
The code runs within the permitted boundaries.
The results are returned to the AI agent.
The agent reviews the results and continues if necessary.
For example, an agent might create a Python file, execute it inside a sandbox, inspect the output, and fix errors without directly modifying your main operating system.
Developers can use different technologies to isolate AI-generated code.
Containers
Docker containers provide isolated environments with their own filesystem, processes, and dependencies. However, containers are not automatically a complete security boundary.
Virtual Machines
Virtual machines provide a separate operating-system environment. They generally offer stronger isolation than ordinary containers, although their security still depends on configuration.
WebAssembly (WASM)
WebAssembly can execute code in a restricted runtime with controlled access to system resources.
Cloud Sandboxes
Some platforms create temporary cloud environments where AI agents can execute code without running directly on a developer's computer.
Each approach has different security, performance, and resource requirements.
A sandbox is only useful when its permissions are configured properly.
Important restrictions include:
Filesystem access: Allow access only to required directories.
Network access: Block or restrict unnecessary external connections.
Environment variables: Never expose sensitive API keys or credentials unnecessarily.
Resource limits: Control CPU, memory, storage, and execution time.
Permissions: Avoid running everything with administrator or root privileges.
Cleanup: Remove temporary environments and files when tasks finish.
Remember, simply running an AI agent inside Docker does not automatically make it secure.
No.
A sandbox reduces risk, but it does not eliminate every security problem.
Misconfigured permissions, container vulnerabilities, exposed credentials, and unsafe network access can still create security issues.
Developers should combine sandboxing with:
Permission controls
Human approval for sensitive actions
Secure credential management
Logging and monitoring
Regular security updates
The goal is to give AI agents enough freedom to complete useful tasks without giving them unlimited access.
AI agents are moving beyond answering questions.
They are starting to interact with real development environments, execute code, manage files, and automate workflows.
As these capabilities grow, security becomes increasingly important.
A developer should not have to choose between using powerful AI automation and protecting their system.
Sandboxing helps make both possible.
AI sandboxes are an important part of building safer AI-powered applications.
They provide controlled environments where AI agents can experiment, execute code, and complete tasks with limited permissions.
If you're building AI agents or experimenting with coding assistants, understanding sandboxing is a valuable skill.
What do you think? Should AI coding agents be allowed to execute commands automatically, or should every sensitive action require human approval?
Share your thoughts in the comments.

articles.title: 【アジャイルFAQ 番外編】正論が通らないとき…発注側や上層部が聞く耳を持たない場合の生存戦略
articles.description:
この記事を読んでいただきありがとうございます。アジャイルグループに所属する、藤井智弘です。今回も、予告なしの番外編をお届けします。
 と言いつつも、「上が理解しないからアジャイルができない？ごちゃごちゃ言ってないでやれよ」という、みもふたもない話ではあるのですが。
質問
#
 この連載の処方は参考になるのですが、その多くが最後は「発注側と交渉する」「組織に提起する」に行き着きます。うちの発注側・経営層は、はっきり言って聞く耳を持ちません。「現行通りやれ」「で、何人日？」「アジャイル？　流行りものはいい」で会話が終わります。正論（全てとは言いませんが、私には多くが正論のように思えます）が通らない環境では、結局アジャイルは無理なのでしょうか？
回答
#
 無理ではありません。ただし、順序を変える必要があります。この連載の処方を「交渉に勝ってから実践する」と読んだなら、それは逆です。実践できるところを先にやり、実績を作り、実績を持って交渉する。交渉とは最初の関門ではなく、最後の仕上げです。
誰の許可も要らないものが思いのほか多いということです。

まず、相手の「聞く耳のなさ」を分解する
#
 腹立たしい話から入る前に、一度冷静に相手を観察します。聞く耳を持たない側にも、たいてい構造的な理由があります。
実績のない提案はリスクにしか見えない: あなたにとってアジャイルは合理的な提案でも、相手にとっては「よく知らないやり方に、自分の責任を賭けろ」という要求です。断るのは、その人の立場ではむしろ誠実な判断です。
変えないことが最適解になる評価構造: 現状維持で誰も罰されない組織では、変更の提案は「うまくいって当然、失敗すれば提案者の責任」という非対称な賭けになります。
過去に「カタカナの流行りもの」で失敗している: 何年か前の別の三文字略語で痛い目を見た組織は、看板を見ただけで身構えます。
 つまり相手は、あなたの論理に反対しているのではなく、あなたの提案に含まれる不確実性に反対していることが多いのです。だとすれば、打ち手は「もっと正しく説明する」ではありません。不確実性を下げること——つまり、小さな実績です。第5回で、正論で押すと相手には「べき論の押し付け」と映り、かえってブレーキになると書きました。「正しく説明したのに通らない」で止まっているなら、それは同じ罠に囚われているのです。

生存戦略
#
 今回はいつもの「処方」ではありません。原則です。
第一原則: 許可の要らない領域から始める
第二原則: 実績を先に、交渉を後に
思想の議論になり、後者は事実の議論になります。思想は好みで却下できますが、事実は却下しにくい。この連載が繰り返し「まず測れ」と言ってきたのは、計測が改善の道具であると同時に、権限のない者の交渉力の源泉だからです。
第三原則: 看板を下ろして、中身を通す
直属の上司には「呼び名を変えて運用している」と伝えておくこと
提案書や契約書に開発方法論が明記されているなら、その文言との整合を先に確認すること
開発標準の成果物名で報告が求められるなら、チームの呼び名との対応表を1枚作っておくこと
 この3つを外すと、迂回と区別がつかなくなります。むしろ、名前を使わずに説明できるかどうかは、自分が中身を理解しているかのテストにもなります。
第四原則: 負けた交渉は、記録して再挑戦の弾にする
第五原則: それでも動かないなら、持ち出せる資産に投資する
組織が動くかどうかはコントロールできませんが、自分が何を学ぶかはコントロールできます。
なぜこの状況は30年繰り返されるのか
#
 権限のない者が現場から組織を変えようとする、という構図自体が、ソフトウェア開発の歴史そのものだからです。思い出してほしいのですが、アジャイルは経営層のトップダウンで生まれた方法論ではありません。重量プロセスに苦しむ現場の実践者たちが、権限のないところから小さく実践し、実績を持ち寄り、言葉を与え、やがて業界を動かした——草の根の運動でした。
 つまり「聞く耳を持たない相手の前で、それでも小さく始める」のは、アジャイルにとって例外状況ではなく、出生時の姿です。あなたが今いる場所は、30年前（あるいはもっと前）に先人たちがいた場所と同じです。そして彼らの武器も、今のあなたと同じでした。

次回: 「POが多忙でチームに来ません」／本編の連載一覧は第1回をご覧ください。

articles.title: 【アジャイルFAQだけど大きく途を踏み外した編】私が「私設・日本式アジャイルを撲滅する会」の会長である理由
articles.description:
この記事を読んでいただきありがとうございます。アジャイルグループに所属する、藤井智弘です。
質問
#
 取引先から「日本式アジャイル（ハイブリッドアジャイル）」という進め方を提案されました。要件定義まではしっかり固めて予算を確定し、開発は2週間ごとの反復で進め、最後にまとめて総合テストをするそうです。予算が確定するので社内の稟議も通しやすく、うちの会社に合っていると思うのですが、何か問題はあるでしょうか？
回答
#
 進め方そのものは、過渡期の形としてはありえます。問題は名前です。要件と予算を先に確定するなら、その後に変更できる量は、ウォーターフォールの変更管理とほとんど変わりません。それを「アジャイル」と呼ぶと、発注側は手に入らない柔軟性を期待してしまいます。アジャイルの自由度が得られないなら、「ハイブリッドウォーターフォール」と呼ぶほうが誠実です。

撲滅したいのは「やり方」ではなく「売り方」
#
 まず、何を撲滅したいのかをはっきりさせておきます。
なぜ「日本式」は売れるのか
#
 この売り方が一定の訴求力を持つ理由は、よく分かります。
変更できる量は、変わらない
#
 要件を確定して予算を確定するということは、その後の変更は「予算の枠の中での変更」になる、ということです。枠を超える変更は、変更依頼を出し、影響を見積り、承認を取る。これはウォーターフォールの変更管理プロセスそのものです。反復の単位が2週間になっても、総量で見ると変更できる量はほとんど変わりません。
親しみを込めて看板詐欺と呼んでいます。
信じています。ただ結果として、発注者は手に入らない柔軟性を期待させられている。
看板と中身がずれると、何を失うか
#
 名前の問題だけなら、目くじらを立てるほどではないかもしれません。しかし、このずれは実害を生みます。連載で扱ってきた問題の多くが、この形では構造として組み込まれてしまうからです。
学習が成果物に届かない: 要件が確定しているので、スプリントレビューで「こうではなかった」と分かっても、作るものは変えられません。第8回で見た、誰の意思決定にも影響しないレビューが、例外ではなく標準になります。
間違いに気づくのが最後になる: テストを最後にまとめるので、スプリントで「完成」したものは、実際には未検証です。第11回のテスト先送り型が、公式の工程になります。早く間違いに気づくというアジャイルの最大の効能が、そこで消えます。
手間は両方の合計になる: ウォーターフォールの文書と承認はそのまま残り、そこにスクラムのイベントが加わります。現場には「アジャイルにしたら会議が増えた」という記憶だけが残ります。
足腰を鍛える理由がなくなる: 最後に人手でまとめてテストするなら、テスト自動化もCIも要りません。業務系の現場で長年見送られてきたこの投資は、この形では永久に正当化されません。
POが検収係に戻る: 要件が先に確定しているので、POは方向を決める人ではなく、仕様どおりかを確かめる人になります。第8回で見た「社内外注」の構図が、そのまま温存されます。
 そして、いちばん大きい害は、これらの結果として組織に残る結論です。コストは増え、品質も納期も変わらず、学習も起きない。それが「アジャイル」の名前で行われるので、組織には「アジャイルを試したが、うちには合わなかった」という経験則が残ります。次に本物を試そうとする人の前に立ちはだかるのは、前例主義が多い中でこの失敗の記憶です。番外編「正論」で、過去にカタカナの流行りもので痛い目を見た組織は看板を見ただけで身構える、と書きました。その種を撒いているのが、この売り方なのです。
総額は、先に出せる
#
 では、発注側の「総予算を早く知りたい」にどう応えればいいのか。実は、アジャイルはこの要望と矛盾しません。
契約で確定しているのは、要件の一覧か。それとも、予算と目的か。
 要件の一覧が確定しているなら、反復をしていても、中身はウォーターフォールです。予算と目的が確定していて、中身が優先順位付きの候補一覧として扱われているなら、アジャイルの自由度は実際に手に入っています。変更依頼の書類を出さずに、項目の入れ替えができるかどうか。実地の判定は、それで十分です。
ハイブリッドウォーターフォール。この名前なら、発注者は正しい期待値を持てますし、受注側も約束していない柔軟性で責められずに済みます。
中身がないなら、看板を掲げるなです。
AI時代の、新しい看板
#
 ついでに、これから現れそうな新しい看板にも、会長として注意報を出しておきます。
 しかし、論理は逆を向いています。SDDの肝は、仕様が先にあることではありません。仕様を直して作り直すコストが、ほとんどゼロになることです。仕様は機能や増分の単位で小さく書き、動くものを見て学んだら、仕様を直して作り直す。仕様は契約書の付属書ではなく、リポジトリの中のファイルとして生き続けます。
後で変えるのが安く済むなら、前で全部を確定しておく理由は、むしろ弱くなるのです。
 危ないのは、SDDの形だけを借りて、システム全体の仕様を前工程で確定し、契約で凍結する組み合わせです。それは「AIで速く打鍵するウォーターフォール」であり、間違った仕様から、間違ったものを、今までより速く大量に作る仕組みです（そして人はおそらくそれをレビューしきれない）。
AIいいなり開発の組織ぐるみ版の完成と言ってもいいでしょう。
 公平のために付け加えると、AIによって「意図を先に、はっきり言葉にする」ことの価値が上がったのは事実です。先に書くこと自体は、アジャイルと矛盾しません。アジャイル宣言が言っているのは「よりも」であって、「書くな」ではありません。アジャイルに反するのは、先に書くことではなく、大きな単位で書いて凍結することです。
その仕様書は、契約の付属書か。それとも、リポジトリの中のファイルか。
 直すたびに変更依頼書が要るなら、AIが何を生成しようと、それはハイブリッドウォーターフォールです。
「日本式」という名前の皮肉
#
 最後に、会長として、どうしても言っておきたいことがあります。「日本式」という名前のことです。
会則
#
 というわけで、当会の会則を参考までに載せておきます。入会も退会も自由です（←冗談だからね。募集してないよ）。
第一条: 看板に偽りなし
中身がないなら看板を掲げるな
第二条: 過渡期は歓迎、到達点にはしない
第三条: 契約を確かめる
第四条: 変更は、入れ替えで
なぜこんな会があるのか
#
 会長を名乗るようになったのは、同じ看板の下で、正反対の二つの混乱を何度も見てきたからです。
 一つ目は、柔軟性がまったくない現場です。要件定義で決めた機能リストを、スプリントごとに順番に消化していく。私はこれを、分割払いと呼んでいます。買うものも総額も、契約の時点で決まっている。スプリントは、その支払いを何回に分けるかを決めているだけです。途中で「やっぱりこれは要らなかった」と分かっても、残債は払い続けるしかない。スプリントレビューで利用者の反応を見ても、次のスプリントで作るものは、もう決まっています。反復はしているのに、学習が入り込む隙間がないのです。
 二つ目は、その逆です。発注側が「アジャイルだから変更は自由」という看板を真に受けて、変更をどんどん出してくる。ところが予算と要件は確定済みなので、受注側には、その変更を吸収する枠がありません。最初は無理をして受け入れ、残業と品質の低下で吸収し、限界が来たところで変更管理が復活する。発注側からは「アジャイルと言ったじゃないか」、受注側からは「予算の中でと言ったじゃないか」。どちらも、嘘はついていません。
 この二つは、同じ看板の表と裏です。一つ目は、受注側が中身をウォーターフォールのまま守った結果。二つ目は、発注側が看板のほうを信じた結果。そして、どちらの現場にも欠けていたものは同じでした。本来のアジャイルで変更が歓迎されるのは、予算と期間という枠の中で、新しく入れるものの代わりに、優先順位の低いものを外すからです。変更とは追加ではなく、入れ替えのことです。この入れ替えのルールを、誰も契約にも合意にも書いていなかった。分割払いの現場では入れ替えが許されず、変更が殺到した現場では入れ替えが求められなかった。

 撲滅と言いながら、当会の目標は会の解散です。「日本式アジャイル」という言葉が使われなくなり、過渡期が過渡期として、正直な名前で呼ばれるようになったら、その時晴れがましい心持ちで当会は解散する事ができるでしょう。

articles.title: Scaling Socket.io Rooms in NestJS With the Redis Adapter
How I Got a WordPress News Site to a 96 Mobile PageSpeed Score Without Delaying JavaScript
articles.description:
News sites are some of the hardest WordPress sites to make fast. Every article page carries a featured image, ads, share buttons, related posts, and a pile of plugin CSS and JavaScript — and readers on slow mobile connections in Pakistan bounce the moment the page feels heavy. When I rebuilt a small news site's performance setup, I set one rule for myself: no JavaScript delay tricks. Delaying scripts until user interaction inflates lab scores while breaking real functionality, and on a news site that means broken share buttons, dead comment forms, and menus that only wake up after a tap. The goal was a genuinely fast page, not a fast-looking lab report.
The first real win was unused CSS. WordPress themes and plugins ship stylesheets written for every possible layout, and a single article page typically uses a fraction of them. I turned on Perfmatters' "Remove Unused CSS" feature in its local mode — no external processing service, no cloud queue. It generates a small used-CSS file per page type and drops the rest. The important detail: this only works if you verify every template afterward. A homepage, an article page, a category archive, and a tool page all use different components, so I checked each one visually after enabling it. One missed selector and a layout breaks silently for readers who never report it.
The second win was the hero image. On article pages the featured image is the largest contentful paint element, so it has to be discovered early. Perfmatters already preloads the first image and serves it as WebP, so I did not add a second preload — duplicate preloads are a classic self-inflicted wound that shows up as wasted bytes in every audit. What mattered more was making sure the image dimensions were set, so the browser reserves the space and the page does not jump while loading. Layout shift is the metric readers feel even when they cannot name it.
The third decision was what NOT to enable. Perfmatters offers a JavaScript delay feature that would have pushed the score higher on paper. I left it off deliberately. On this site the interactive elements — search, menus, comment forms, tool widgets — need to work on first tap, not after a delay script decides the user has interacted enough. The same reasoning applied to other aggressive options: I enabled exactly one CSS optimization and verified it, rather than stacking five features and debugging the interaction between them.
The result, measured on mobile: a PageSpeed score of 96, largest contentful paint around 2.5 seconds, zero milliseconds of render-blocking time, and zero kilobytes of unused CSS reported. No script delay, no deferred interactivity, no broken widgets. The lesson generalizes beyond news sites: pick one optimization at a time, verify it on every template, and resist features that trade real functionality for lab points. A fast site that works is worth more than a faster-looking site that does not.

articles.title: Running the Mock in Docker Compose for CI vs a Local Spec Server
articles.description:
Quick answer


Running a mock inside Docker Compose gives every developer and the CI pipeline the same mock on a predictable address, with no local install or version drift. A local spec server is faster to start for a single developer and easier to debug, but it depends on that machine's runtime and does not reproduce the networked environment. The reliable default is to put the mock in Compose as part of the service stack, and keep the local spec server for quick ad-hoc work. Whichever you choose, the mock definition should be a versioned spec file, not state built by hand inside a running GUI.

Manual start per developer


Consistency
Identical image and config everywhere
Depends on local runtime version


Network
Real service-to-service DNS and ports
localhost only


Debug speed
Slightly heavier
Fastest inner loop


CI parity
Same Compose file runs in CI
Needs separate setup



Mount the mock definition into a lightweight image and expose it on the internal network, so the application refers to it by service name rather than a host-specific address.
The application reads the base URL from configuration, so the same code talks to the mock locally and the real API in production with no code change. The volume is read-only, which keeps the running container from mutating the spec.
The biggest win is not convenience; it is eliminating the class of bugs that appear only because a developer's local mock behaved differently from what CI or staging used. When the same Compose file and the same versioned spec run in CI, a passing test means the integrated stack works, including DNS resolution, restart behavior, and the order services come up. A locally started server that a developer configured by hand cannot give that guarantee, and it makes failures hard to reproduce.
The Compose mock is the default for integration work, but a single developer editing the spec wants a fast feedback loop. Start the same spec directly on localhost while editing, then run the full Compose stack to verify before pushing. The key is that both modes read the identical spec file, so they cannot drift; only the wrapper changes.
Store the mock spec in version control and review it like code.
Pin the mock image version so pulls do not silently change behavior.
Give the mock a health check and make the app wait for it to be ready.
Add tests that reset the mock state between runs so cases do not interfere.
A depends_on relationship alone only controls start order, not readiness, so the application can attempt calls before the mock is accepting requests and fail intermittently. Give the mock service a health check that confirms the port responds, and make the application wait for that healthy state rather than a fixed sleep. This matters most in CI, where container startup timing varies and a flaky first request is otherwise hard to reproduce. Build the same readiness probe into the application's local development flow so behavior does not differ between machines. When the mock includes several stubs, add a startup log that lists the loaded spec and any seed data, which makes a misconfigured mount immediately obvious; an empty mock that returns defaults is a silent failure that can look like a passing but meaningless test. Treating the mock as a real service with health and readiness, rather than a background process assumed to be up, removes a whole class of timing-related failures.
Some mocks hold state across calls, such as a created resource that later gets fetched. In Compose, define an explicit reset endpoint and call it between test cases, or recreate the container for a clean start. Do not rely on the order of tests to leave state where the next expects it, because parallel or reordered runs will then fail unpredictably. The mock should start from a known baseline every time, which is far easier to guarantee when the spec and any seed data are mounted and the container is treated as ephemeral.
It adds some overhead, but you can keep the local spec server for fast editing and use Compose to verify the integrated stack. The point is that both read the same versioned spec, so there is no behavior drift.
Mount the directory read-only and keep any runtime state inside the ephemeral container. Persistent changes belong in the spec in version control, never written back into the mounted files.
You lose the parity that makes the approach valuable. If CI cannot run Compose, pin the same mock image and spec in the pipeline so the behavior matches, even if the orchestration differs.
Use synthetic seed data only. Real customer data should never be mounted into a mock, and keeping fixtures synthetic avoids both data leakage and accidental coupling to production records.
This is part of the Powerduck vs Mockoon: Mock Server and Local API Workflows — start there for the full mock-server comparison.

articles.title: Braintree's Vault Knows More Than the Retry Uses
articles.description:
Braintree merchants sit on an asset many of them never inspect: the vault. Cards get replaced by issuers, account updater services refresh credentials, and the vault quietly holds newer payment data than the subscription's last successful charge used. When a renewal fails on a stale credential while the vault holds a live one, the failure is not a customer problem. It is a plumbing oversight.
The oversight compounds because renewal failures look uniform in a report. Expired, superseded, and genuinely dead credentials arrive wearing similar decline codes, and a retry schedule that cannot tell them apart spends its attempts evenly across the living and the dead. Reading the failure against the vault's current state is the sort that turns a pile into a queue.
Good dunning discipline already insists on one habit: before every attempt, re-read the invoice fresh, because the world moves between failure and retry — a payment settles, an amount changes, a native attempt runs first. On Braintree, that same habit extends naturally to the credential attached to the invoice. What does the vault hold for this customer right now, today, before this attempt fires — the same card that just failed, a replacement issued since, a credential refreshed by the account updater, or nothing usable at all? Each answer dictates a different action, and none of them is "retry the stale card and hope." If newer payment data is sitting in the vault, the attempt belongs on that data, once, cleanly recorded. If the vault holds only the credential that already failed hard, the correct move is not another attempt at all. The fresh read is cheap. The attempts it prevents, and the attempts it redirects onto live data, are where its value sits.
Once failures are read against current vault state, the familiar sorting can do its work with better information. Hard declines stop immediately and route to a single clean card-update request, because a dead credential in the vault confirms what the decline already said: there is nothing here to retry. Soft declines are re-read and re-spaced, treated as timing rather than refusal, with the next attempt placed patiently instead of fired in a burst. Insufficient funds, which says nothing about the credential and everything about the calendar, rides a payday ladder out toward day 25 rather than consuming its attempts in the first week, when the account it draws on is in the same state that just failed. The vault does not replace that sorting; it sharpens it. A decline code tells you what the issuer said. The vault tells you what you actually hold. A queue built from both answers spends its attempts where a live credential and a plausible moment coincide, and closes the rest without ceremony.
Braintree's own native retry behaviour is already running underneath all of this, and a recovery layer that ignores it creates two rhythms on one card. The disciplined pattern is to weave outside attempts into the gaps of the platform's native schedule, under a combined cap of 15 attempts in total, with Swipe Again's own ceiling at 8. The customer, meanwhile, should never see any of this plumbing. What they see, when they need to see anything, is a short sequence in the merchant's own brand: email on day 1, day 3, and day 7 pointing to a card-update page, with SMS where the merchant's program allows it. If they later choose to cancel, that is a separate moment with its own honest shape: one branded save offer at the cancel click, with exit one click away. Behind the scenes, recovery attribution is stamped at a single choke point — retry first, then card update, then save offer, then honest external — so a renewal recovered because the vault held a live credential is credited once, to the step that did it, and never double-counted by the email that happened to precede it.
A field guide to Braintree dunning, the account updater's role, the decline codes that mean "look in the vault first," and the ones that mean stop, is the difference between retrying a subscription and actually recovering it. Braintree's route to market runs through the PayPal partner program, which is its own lesson in how this platform expects to be extended: deliberately.
Published by Swipe Again - failed-payment recovery for subscription businesses.

articles.title: How to deploy an AI assistant: Pattern 2, the control/data split (customer cloud)
articles.description:
A reference architecture for running the data plane of an AI assistant in the customer's own cloud account, with the provider keeping only a control plane
This document describes the second of three deployment patterns for an AI assistant platform. It is written for architects and platform engineers whose customer, or whose own organisation, has said: "our documents, our search index and our encryption key stay in our cloud account, under a key we can revoke without asking anyone."
The structure is the same as Pattern 1: a one-picture architecture, the request flow, the components, use cases, design considerations, what crosses the boundary, and when to choose it. The design is independent of any product; the technologies named can be replaced.
Terms used throughout. The provider is whoever builds and operates the platform software: a vendor, or an internal platform team. The customer is the organisation whose users and data the platform serves. In this pattern the customer also operates most of the system.
Prerequisites. On the customer's side: a cloud account, a Kubernetes service, managed Postgres and object storage, a key management service, and access to a cloud model provider in the chosen region. On the provider's side: a build pipeline that can sign artifacts and an OCI registry. The customer needs a team that can run Kubernetes and its supporting services in production.



Pattern
Data lives in
Operated by
Crosses the boundary




1. Shared service
the provider's account, inside a residency boundary
the provider
every user's traffic, inside the boundary


2. Control/data split (this document)
the customer's cloud account
the customer runs the data plane; the provider runs a control plane
signed software in, optional health metadata out


3. Isolated site
the customer's building
the customer, everything
two signed files in, one optional file out



The three questions still decide: where does the data live, who operates it, what crosses the boundary. For this pattern the third question is the one to get right, and the next section shows why.
The obvious way to meet the customer's rule is to split by component: move the pieces that store customer content into the customer's account and keep the rest.

The customer runs retrieval over their own vector store, a connector module that reaches their systems from inside their network, a cache, their documents bucket, Vault and a KMS key they can revoke. The provider reaches these over one private link with mutual TLS. Software is pull-only. Stored data never leaves the customer's account.
Now trace one chat message and mark every arrow where customer content crosses an account boundary with ◆.



#
Crossing
Why it exists




①
The user's question travels through the provider's edge, gateway and Chat Gateway
The entry point is the provider's


②
Retrieved passages come back over the link
The Orchestrator is the provider's


③
Results from the customer's systems come back over the link
Same reason


④
The full prompt goes to the model in the provider's account
The model is the provider's


⑤
The streamed answer sits in the provider's Redis for about five minutes
The Chat Gateway is the provider's



Five crossings per question. None of them is a breach: each is encrypted, disclosed, inside the residency boundary and gone within minutes. But the design cannot support the sentence the customer wants: "your data never reaches our account." Stored data does not; data in flight does, five times.
Two rules follow, and they apply to any architecture:
Mark every arrow where content crosses a boundary. If you cannot draw it, you do not know it.
"Defensible" is the floor. The useful question is whether the customer can verify the promise without trusting the provider.
The fix is to split by plane, not by component.
The control plane is everything that is the same for every customer and carries no content: building and signing software, publishing it, issuing licences, collecting health metadata, taking support requests. The provider keeps this.
The data plane is everything that touches a user, a document, a system or a prompt: entry point, gateway, sign-in, chat, Orchestrator, tools and actions, retrieval, connectors, data, keys, and the model call. The customer runs all of it, in their account.

Three things change. There is no connectivity link, because there is nothing for the provider to reach, and the provider has no inbound path at all. The model call stays home: the Orchestrator calls the customer's own cloud model providers in the customer's account, under the customer's contract. There is nothing to crypto-shred at exit, because the provider holds no configuration, sessions or buffer. The ◆ marker appears nowhere.

②

⑧

Every hop stays inside the customer's boundary. The provider's column in the detailed topology has no live-request arrows at all.

The defining case. Documents, index and keys in the customer's account, encrypted under a key the customer can revoke, with no content in the provider's infrastructure. The customer can operate Kubernetes and its supporting services, or has a managed-service team that can.
Because the customer runs the data plane, the provider's software has to run on whichever cloud the customer uses. The design keeps every cloud-specific dependency behind an interface: the model router, the identity binding for the registry pull, and the key management.
An internal platform team is the provider; a business unit with its own cloud account and its own compliance regime is the customer. The pull-only delivery and the egress proxy log give the business unit's auditors proof without trusting the platform team.
Delivery without access. The provider never pushes anything. Its pipeline signs every chart and image, attaches an SBOM and a vulnerability-scan attestation, and publishes to an OCI registry. In the customer's cluster, Argo CD polls the registry over the customer's own outbound HTTPS and applies new versions; a release gate lets the customer review the SBOM and attestation first; Kyverno verifies the signature with a bundled, offline trust root before any pod starts. The customer holds every admin credential.
For cross-cloud registry access, two methods work: federate the cluster's workload identity into a pull-only role at the provider, or issue a per-customer pull-only robot token the customer keeps in their own Vault. Both are scoped to that customer's repositories and can only pull.
Identity inside the boundary. The customer runs the identity broker, and the identity provider sits inside their boundary. The IdP token is verified once at login; after that the browser holds an opaque, hash-stored session. CLI tokens and API keys resolve the same way. No sign-in assertion crosses to the provider.
Tools and actions in the customer's account. The sandbox is self-hosted in the customer's account with no platform credentials and default-deny egress; a managed sandbox service would be a third party that sees content. The action gateway applies the customer's policy and approval steps. Tool connectors run against an allowlist the customer sets. Per-user tokens are sealed in a credential vault with a key id. Metering writes to a local store with limits per organisation and workspace.
The model router points at the customer's own providers. Several providers behind one interface, each in the customer's account, pinned to a region the customer chooses, reached over private endpoints, with invocation logging as the customer's own setting. The prompt never touches the provider's account. The nuance to state plainly: the model provider still sees prompts, under the customer's contract rather than the vendor's.
Data and authorization. Postgres with pgvector, the documents bucket, Redis and Vault live in the customer's account. Authorization is one decision point: policy compiled into every query, with row-level security beneath it. Encryption uses a customer-owned KMS key. Revoke it and everything stops and becomes unreadable, including to provider support.
High availability and disaster recovery are the customer's: multi-zone, a second region per their policy, immutable backups. The provider states no recovery targets here because there is no provider data plane to fail over. The provider commits only to registry availability, and an optional local registry mirror removes even that runtime dependency.
Telemetry is local by default: Fluent Bit, OpenTelemetry, Loki, Jaeger, VictoriaMetrics, a local Grafana. Cloud and cluster audit logs stay in the account. The egress proxy log is the customer's proof: it shows exactly two external names ever reached for the provider (the registry and, if opted in, the heartbeat), plus the customer's own model, identity and system endpoints.
Support works two ways, both optional: a redacted support bundle the customer reads before sending, or a break-glass session the customer opens, approves, time-boxes and records in their own audit log. The break-glass session is the one path that could ever show content to the provider, and the diagram says so.
The customer pays for the whole data plane: cluster, databases, model consumption under their own contract, a second region if they want one. Managed cloud services soften the operating cost but do not remove it. The provider's cost is small and fixed: a pipeline, a registry, a dashboard.
Model capacity, quota and regional placement are the customer's. The provider cannot add quota or fix an outage at the customer's model provider. Everything else scales as in Pattern 1, inside the customer's cluster.
Split by component (the first design above). Fewer things for the customer to run, but five content crossings per question.
A managed sandbox service. Less to operate, but a third party that sees content.
Push-based delivery with a provider credential into the customer's cluster. Simpler for the provider, but gives it an inbound path, which this pattern exists to remove.
Automatic heartbeat. Useful for support, but it must stay opt-in and payload-free, or the egress proxy log stops being proof.



Crossing
Direction
What travels
Who opens it
Can the customer switch it off?




Software pull
customer → provider registry; software flows in
signed charts, images, licence
the customer's Argo CD and nodes
yes; the running version keeps working, and a mirror removes the runtime dependency


Heartbeat
customer → provider
versions, health, error counts; fixed schema, no payloads
the customer's agent
yes; opt-in


Support bundle
customer → provider, manual
redacted diagnostics the customer read first
the customer
yes; never required


Break-glass session
customer opens; provider joins
whatever the customer shows; nothing retained
the customer
yes; per incident, time-boxed, recorded


Model call
customer → their own model provider
prompt with retrieved passages
the customer's Orchestrator
it is the product; but it stays under the customer's account, contract and region



Compare this with the first design's five content crossings per question. That comparison is the whole argument for splitting by plane.
The customer runs the whole data plane. This is close to the operating burden of an on-premises deployment, eased by managed cloud services.
Support works half-blind: heartbeat and redacted bundles by default.
Several model providers to support, with differences in models, limits and behaviour.
No provider recovery targets. The provider commits only to registry availability.
Version skew: N and N-1 are supported; a customer who stalls their release gate drifts out of the window.
Not zero third parties. The customer's model provider still processes prompts.
Choose the control/data split when the customer's rule is "our documents, index and keys in our account, under a key we can revoke, and no content in your infrastructure", and they can operate Kubernetes and its supporting services. If they want the provider to run everything, Pattern 1. If not even a prompt may leave their building, Pattern 3.
The provider prepares; the customer deploys.
Provider: release pipeline. Build, sign every chart and image, attach the SBOM and scan attestation, publish to the OCI registry, issue the signed licence and a pull-only credential per customer.
Customer: foundation. Cloud account, network, Kubernetes cluster, managed Postgres with pgvector, object storage, Vault, a customer-owned KMS key, the model accounts with private endpoints.
Customer: delivery path. Argo CD pointed at the provider's registry over outbound HTTPS, the release gate, Kyverno with the bundled trust root, the optional registry mirror. Verify that the egress proxy log shows only the registry.
Customer: identity and edge. The identity broker inside the boundary, federated to the customer's identity provider; the customer's domain, certificate, WAF and load balancer; the API gateway.
Customer: application and tools. Argo CD applies the signed charts: Chat Gateway, Orchestrator, retrieval, connectors, mesh, the tools-and-actions layer, the model router configured for the customer's providers.
Customer: observability and support. Local telemetry, audit logs to the customer's SIEM, the opt-in heartbeat if wanted, the break-glass procedure written into the customer's runbook.
Customer: resilience. High availability, a second region if policy requires it, immutable backups, and a test that revoking the KMS key stops everything as intended.
The full design in ten customer bands plus the provider's two control-plane bands. The hop numbers match the request flow table above. Open the figure at full size to read the component notes.

This is part 2 of a three-part series. The other parts are also linked in the series box at the top of this article.
Pattern 1, the shared service (SaaS): the provider runs everything inside a residency boundary.
Pattern 3, the isolated site (on-premises and air-gapped): everything runs in the customer's building, with models on local GPUs.

articles.title: One Image for Every OnePassApps Link: What the Open Graph and Twitter Card Tags Say
articles.description:
I work on OnePassApps, so this is our own site, and everything below is a measurement of our own public pages - fetched and decoded, not a guess.
When you paste a link to app.onepassapps.com into a chat app, a document, or a social post, what a reader sees before they click is not the page. It is a preview: a title, a line of description, and one image. That preview is built from tags in the page's <head>, and it is a layer of the site that almost nobody looks at.
So I looked at it. Sixteen public URLs, fetched one by one, and the preview image itself decoded pixel by pixel.
How this was measured: plain HTTPS GETs with a browser User-Agent - no JavaScript, no browser tab, no sign-in - one request per URL in the sitemap. For each page I read the Open Graph and Twitter card tags out of the <head>. The preview image was then downloaded and its PNG chunks decoded locally (IHDR for the header, then zlib-inflate and un-filter the scanlines), so the colours below are the file's own bytes rather than a browser's rendering of it.
All sixteen pages point at the same preview file:
https://app.onepassapps.com/og-image.png

It answers 200 with image/png, 42,818 bytes, 1200 by 630 pixels, 8-bit truecolour with no alpha channel, not interlaced.
Decode it and it is a single composition: a near-black background at #0B0D0F, a teal circle at #00E5D0 holding the robot mark, the wordmark "OnePassApps" in off-white #F8F5EF, and the line "Useful apps, one membership" underneath in grey #A3A3A3.
The same file backs every one of the sixteen URLs. The title and the description change from page to page; the picture never does. So a reader scrolling a chat thread sees the OnePassApps card over and over, and the only thing that tells two links apart is the line of text under it.
Per page, on all sixteen:
og:title matches the page's <title>, and twitter:title matches it too.
og:description and twitter:description are both the page's meta description, word for word.
og:url is the page's own URL, matching its canonical exactly.
og:type is website, og:locale is en_GB, og:site_name is OnePassApps.
og:image and og:image:secure_url are the same absolute URL, og:image:type is image/png, og:image:width is 1200, og:image:height is 630.
twitter:card is summary_large_image, twitter:url is the page's own URL, twitter:image is the same PNG.
Two things in that list are worth pulling out.
The alt text is the same on every page. og:image:alt reads "OnePassApps — Useful apps, one membership" on all sixteen pages, and twitter:image:alt repeats it. The alt describes the card, not the page it stands in for. That is a deliberate-looking choice - the card is the brand, so the brand's name and line is the honest description - but it does mean a screen reader hears the same sentence whatever it is announcing.
No account is attached to the card. There is no twitter:site and no twitter:creator on any of the sixteen pages. The card renders and it is unattributed: no handle, no account name, nothing for a reader to follow back to. If you are building a preview and want the card to name the account, that tag is where it goes.
og:type is website on all sixteen pages - including the seven studios and the two hosted apps. The structured data on those same pages calls them WebApplication nodes, with applicationCategory values of UtilitiesApplication, ReferenceApplication and EntertainmentApplication, and a featureList naming each studio's tools.
So the JSON-LD says "this is an app" and the Open Graph says "this is a website", on the same URL, on the same request. Both are defensible in their own vocabulary, but if you are deciding how to render a preview, the JSON-LD is the richer description.
/privacy is a 301 whose Location header is /terms#privacy. The privacy notice is a section of the terms document, not a page of its own, and a fragment is never sent to the server - so /terms is served identically either way.
/support answers 200 and is linked from the home page, and it is the one page on the site that asks crawlers to stay away: its robots tag reads noindex, nofollow. It carries no canonical tag and no structured data block at all. A reader who clicks it gets a support and feedback page - "Create and follow support requests and product feedback for OnePassApps." - while a crawler is told there is nothing here to index.
Both guide pages end with a "Common questions" section - the NewsFlow guide asks three of them, about listening without an account, about whether every story from a source is included, and about what it costs.
None of that is marked up as structured data. The JSON-LD on both guide pages is the same four nodes - Organization, WebSite, WebPage, BreadcrumbList - with no FAQPage and no QAPage anywhere in the document. The questions are in the page as headings and paragraphs; they are not in the page as questions and answers a search engine can quote.
curl -s https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/image | grep -o '<meta property="og:[^>]*>'
curl -s https://app.onepassapps.com/studios/image | grep -o '<meta name="twitter:[^>]*>'
curl -s https://app.onepassapps.com/og-image.png -o card.png && file card.png

No login, no uploads, nothing to install - the same browser tools the guides walk through, described in one page each. Start with the Image Studio, or browse the app guides.
Disclosure again: I work on OnePassApps, the team behind app.onepassapps.com.

articles.title: One documentation site from five sources
articles.description:
If your repository mixes languages, you almost certainly ship four kinds of documentation that four different tools generate: the HTTP API reference from OpenAPI, the C and C++ pages from Doxygen, Go and Rust pages from godoc and rustdoc, and the guides sitting in a Markdown folder that every tool renders differently. Each generator brings its own theme, its own search, and its own idea of where output belongs.
The fix is boring and effective: treat documentation as a build artifact. Leave every source where it already lives, then run a single build that turns all of them into one static site.
Static HTML has three properties that matter in 2026. It hosts anywhere: a bucket, a CDN, a small VPS, or a folder inside the repo. It needs no runtime, so it cannot rot when a server dependency breaks. And it can be read by anything, including the agents people now point at documentation.
A single build matters because readers do not care which generator produced which page. They want one search box, one navigation tree, one place where the version number is correct. If the API reference says 2.4.0 and the guide says 2.3.1, trust is gone.
A realistic project needs at least three of these sources:
OpenAPI or Swagger definitions for the HTTP API.
Doxygen XML for C and C++ code.
godoc for Go packages.
rustdoc for Rust crates.
Markdown for guides, tutorials, and changelogs.
MCP server definitions, if the project exposes tools to agents.
Each source already has a canonical extractor. Doxygen parses C and C++ comments into XML. godoc reads Go doc comments. rustdoc ships with cargo. OpenAPI is a YAML file. The only real decision is what renders the final site.
Doxygen plus a theme is still the standard for C and C++, and it now emits usable HTML on its own. Sphinx owns the Python world and handles Markdown through MyST. MkDocs with Material is the default for Markdown-first projects and is easy to wire into CI. Redoc and Swagger UI render OpenAPI well but stop there; they do not know about the rest of your documentation.
There is also a newer option worth a look: Sourcey, a free, self hosted documentation generator that takes OpenAPI, MCP, Doxygen, godoc, rustdoc, and Markdown in the same build and outputs static HTML. It is AGPL-3.0, installs with npx sourcey init, needs Node 22 or newer, and ships four themes with custom CSS. The detail I care about is that the same build also emits llms.txt, OpenAPI, and API catalogs, so agent facing readers get machine readable versions without a second pipeline. You can see the engine at https://sourcey.com/docs and the source at github.com/sourcey/sourcey.
Keep sources under docs/ and let the build own build/site:
docs/
  guides/*.md
  openapi.yaml
  doxygen/Doxyfile
src/                # godoc and rustdoc read from here

A CI job runs the extractors first, then the site build, then deploys build/site to your host. Cache the extractor outputs; Doxygen on a large C++ tree is the slow step, and it does not need to rerun when only a guide changed.
Two rules keep this honest. First, the version string comes from one file, not from prose. Second, a broken link fails the build, not the reader's afternoon.
Client side search over static files works fine up to a few thousand pages. Past that, prebuild the index at build time and ship it as a static asset.
The agent question is newer. If your product exposes an MCP server or an API that agents call, your docs are part of the interface. Agents do not click; they fetch. Serving llms.txt, a clean OpenAPI file, and plain HTML without JavaScript requirements costs almost nothing and removes a whole class of failures. A documentation build that emits these by default saves you from bolting them on later.
Pick the one build that already understands your largest source. Add the other sources one at a time. Deploy the static output somewhere boring. Then spend the remaining time on the guides, because the generator was never the hard part.
Documentation is a product surface. Treat the build like code: versioned, tested, deployed on every merge. The rest is details.

articles.title: When Programmatic SEO Works (and 3 Signs It Won't)
articles.description:
When programmatic SEO works, it turns a spreadsheet of structured data into thousands of ranking pages that attract real search traffic, without a content team. But the line between a traffic engine and a domain-burning liability is thinner than most founders think. If you get the data, the demand, or the template wrong, you don't break even, you go backwards.
This guide walks through exactly what makes programmatic SEO tick, the three project types that actually work, and the validation steps most people skip. GrowGanic's autonomous pipeline solves the scaling part; the thinking behind it is laid out here.
You have a database. You have real search demand. The template you build can create unique, useful pages at scale. Those three conditions must all be true. Miss one, and you're generating digital noise, not assets.
Put plainly, the strategy fails without scalable data, clear intent, and validated keyword patterns. seoClarity drives the point further, long-tail pages built from thin data become dead weight the moment Google's quality thresholds tighten.
It's permanent. You can't easily recall 10,000 pages once they're indexed. If they're low-quality, you've polluted your own site. Google's classifiers don't forget. Each one dragged down the average, and the domain never recovered.
That's why we designed GrowGanic's scoring engine to flag thin pages before they ever touch a CMS. The gates aren't magic, they're just the same checks a decent editor would run. But they run every time, on every page, without exceptions.
Programmatic SEO creates many SEO-optimized pages at once from existing data and pre-programmed rules. That's the definition Zapier's own team published, and it holds. It's not a trick. It's not black-hat. It's just a systematic way to build pages when the data already lives somewhere else.
Think of Zapier's "Connect X to Y" pages. Airbnb's city-level listings. Tripadvisor's destination guides. Indeed's job pages. Each one comes from a database. Each one targets a search term that real people type. That's the pattern.
The opposite is thin affiliate spam: pages with zero original data, stitched together with synonyms, hoping to rank for "best [x] in [y]" without any human having reviewed the thing. Programmatic SEO succeeds when every page has at least one genuine atomic fact that exists nowhere else in that exact combination. For more on that, we've written a full breakdown in What Is Programmatic SEO? The Founder's Guide to Scaling Pages. (yes)
It's a scalability play, not a revenue shortcut. If you can export your data to a spreadsheet with consistent columns, you have the raw material. The columns become the variables. The page becomes the output.
Mangools defines it similarly: an automated or semi-automated approach that can target thousands of pages. The key is that automation doesn't strip away the usefulness. Every page must solve a real searcher problem.
Not all programmatic pages are created equal. We group them into three categories based on the data and intent they serve. The distinction matters because each type needs a different template design and a different validation check.



Type
Data Source
Search Intent
Real-World Example




Location-based
Geographic coordinates, service areas, local NAP
"dentist in Austin", transactional, high local intent
A dental chain's city pages


Entity-combination
Product features, category lists, comparison logic
"best CRM for real estate agents", comparison or recommendation
A SaaS comparison site


Template-driven resource
Structured steps, integration lists, job databases
"how to connect X to Y", how-to or transactional
Zapier's integration pages



Seothe research backs this: location pages and product variations are the most common winners because the data is naturally rich. The danger zone lies with entity-combination pages where the template assumes a comparison is helpful but the searcher wants a table, not a narrative.
You need clean, accurate NAP data for every location. You need a template that generates unique content by pulling in nearby landmarks, local testimonials, or service variations. If your template just swaps the city name, you've built a penalty magnet.
Local SEO tools handle this well. GrowGanic isn't the best for pure local play, we don't auto-build citations. But if your location pages also serve as content hubs with neighborhood guides, we can generate the supporting content that makes those pages distinctive.
Entity-combination pages thrive when you have a comparison rubric and unique data points per pair. For example, a CRM comparison page for real estate agents should cite actual feature differences, pricing, and user reviews, not just a templated sentence saying "X is a great CRM for Y."
We built GrowGanic's proprietary content generation to handle this. The engine pulls live research and fact-grounds every claim. That means a "best CRM for real estate agents" page gets real data, not filler. It's not a script swapping words, it's a pipeline that treats each page like a standalone article.
This is a sequence. Each step depends on the one before it, so we're putting it in order.
 Audit your existing data. Do you have a database of locations, products, services, or integrations? If not, programmatic SEO probably isn't your first move. Start by building the asset that generates that data.
 Validate search demand. Run keyword research on the pattern. "Best [tool] for [industry]" must show search volume and clear intent. Ahrefs' tools can surface these patterns quickly.
 Define the template. Map the data fields to the page structure. What stays the same? What changes? The template must allow enough variation to keep the pages distinct.
 Build the generation pipeline. This could be a custom script, a CMS plugin, or an autonomous engine like GrowGanic. The pipeline handles the research, generation, optimization, and publishing in one loop.
 Monitor and iterate. Track rankings, clicks, and conversions. When a page underperforms, adjust the data or the template. This is not a set-it-and-forget-it strategy, it's an asset that needs maintenance.
We automated steps 2 through 5 inside GrowGanic's pipeline. You feed the domain, and the engine discovers demand patterns, generates unique pages, scores them for quality, and ships them to your CMS. If you're a solo founder with no time for manual monitoring, the fully autonomous SEO engine guide spells out the whole loop.
No. The entire method rests on structured data. If your data is just a list of ideas, you're not doing programmatic SEO, you're doing mass content creation, and that rarely ends well. The database is what gives each page a unique reason to exist.
They treat them exactly like any other page. If the content is thin, duplicate, or irrelevant, they ignore it or penalize it. Google's guidelines are clear: generate pages for users, not search engines. The scale doesn't matter. The value per page does. Search Engine Journal has a strong breakdown of the crawl budget and indexing behavior.
You can't fix zero-search-volume pages later. They're dead on arrival. So the validation step is non-negotiable.
Look for patterns with long-tail modifiers and clear modifiers, location, industry, use case. "CRM for real estate agents" is strong. "CRM for happiness" is not. The pattern must match a real user query. Moz emphasizes the importance of clustering keywords that share the same template skeleton.
Our on-page SEO checklist covers the template requirements in detail. Everything from title tag structure to internal linking matters more when machines write the pages, because no human editor is there to catch the drift.
We won't publish the gate architecture, that's the moat. But we can describe what the pipeline does at a high level.
For location pages, the mechanism layers geographic data with service descriptions and local schema markup. The engine draws from location-specific cues so no two pages read identically.
For entity-combination pages, the engine extracts entities, constructs a comparison logic path, and anchors every claim in a cited fact. Search Engine Land has covered similar approaches. The critical piece is avoiding the trap where every comparison page says the same thing with different nouns.
For template-driven resource pages, the engine fills in the blanks from a structured database and auto-links to related resources. Every page gets internal links that strengthen the cluster.
A common failure mode is generating pages that look identical to Google's classifiers. Even if the text varies slightly, the structural fingerprint can flag them. That's why our scoring engine evaluates Google readiness and AI-search readiness in a single pass. The same template that ranks well on Google also needs to be cited by generative engines.
Entity-combination pages require the deepest research. The model has to understand that "best CRM for real estate agents" implies a comparison of CRM features against the specific workflows of agents. That's not a simple substitution. It's a reasoning step, and most generic AI content fails it. We wrote about that in Why AI Content Doesn't Rank (And the Fix Everyone Missed).
The most common mistake is building pages for patterns with zero search volume. A subtler trap, and the one that kills sites, is using a template that produces pages with 80% identical content. Google's thin-content thresholds don't care that you meant well.
The most expensive failure is intent mismatch. Searchers want a comparison table, but the page gives them a 2,000-word listicle. They bounce. Google notices. Rankings tank.
The template was essentially "[City] dentist" with swapped city names and no original content. Another case: 500 product comparison pages with unique review snippets and side-by-side specs ranked within 90 days. The difference was the atomic facts per page.
There is another layer: even valid data and demand aren't enough if the page doesn't earn links. Without links, the pages exist in a crawl budget black hole. That's the infrastructure problem we built GrowGanic to route around, the engine publishes and auto-refreshes pages as SERPs shift. But outbound link building stays manual.
If your template produces a carbon copy of an existing H1, you're competing on identical signals with worse authority. You lose every time.
The fix is brutal: you kill the pages that don't rank within three months. We bake that into our auto-refresh loop: if a keyword drops, the article re-optimizes itself. If it fails to recover, the cycle ends. No sentimental attachment.
This article was researched, written and published by GrowGanic, which does the same on a business's own site: it picks the searches the business can win, writes the articles and publishes them on WordPress, Shopify, HubSpot or a hosted blog. The first article is free at growganic.io.
