articles.title: ElevenLabs launched 13 products this week. Only 3 matter if you build voice agents.
articles.description:
Disclosure: this piece contains an affiliate link. If you sign up through it, I earn a commission at no extra cost to you.
ElevenLabs held its New York Summit on 11 November and announced 13 new products and upgrades. The headline is that it stopped being a voice tool. It is now a platform for voice agents, and the announcements split into two groups: things you can use today, and things that are for large enterprises with a sales call in between.
I tested the tools that claim to do the same work I do, so here is the split that matters if you build agentic workflows.
1. ElevenAgents Campaign Manager — live now. Announced 9 November, and it is the one I would try first. It runs outbound campaigns: you give it contacts and a goal — a qualified lead, a confirmed appointment — and it works each contact toward that goal, retrying when nobody picks up, calling back when someone asks for Thursday at 4pm, and stopping when a person opts out. It runs on the agents and phone numbers you already have in ElevenAgents, and contacts go in by CSV or API. Phone calls and WhatsApp voice and messaging work today; email and SMS are coming soon. It ran live beta campaigns across insurance, banking and ecommerce before launch.
This is the loop I build by hand in n8n today: call, check the outcome, retry on a schedule, keep the context between touches. Campaign Manager puts that loop inside the voice platform. The honest read is that the voice agent is the front door and something still has to do the work behind it — the CRM lookup, the booking, the follow-up. That is where n8n sits in my stack, and it is still where it sits after this launch.
2. Scribe v3 and Scribe v3 Live — live now. Announced 10 November. Scribe v3 is the recorded-audio transcription model, covering 102 languages. Scribe v3 Live is the low-latency real-time variant, with speaker labelling as it goes, and it is live in ElevenAgents today. Both are in ElevenAPI. If you run voice agents, transcription quality is the part that decides whether the agent understands the caller at all, and this is the piece of the Summit that is already in the product rather than on a roadmap.
3. ElevenAI — free early access, open now. A workplace app that listens to spoken conversations, including in-person meetings, and turns them into notes, summaries and action items. It can also give live assistance during a call. ElevenLabs built notice and consent mechanisms into it, which matters — a meeting recorder that does not ask first is a liability, not a feature. Early access is free and open with the announcement. This is the one to try with no budget and no sales call.
The rest of the Summit is real, but it is not for a solo builder today, and I will not pretend otherwise.
The Marketplace is a curated catalog of partner-built industry apps — healthcare, financial services, insurance, education, retail, government — from more than 20 partners at launch, including Salient for borrower servicing calls, Gail by Lula for insurance inquiries, and Zendesk for customer service. You can browse the apps and contact the developers today. You cannot buy through it yet: purchasing through existing ElevenLabs commitments is planned to start in 2027.
Model customization lets selected enterprises work with ElevenLabs researchers to fine-tune open-source language models and ElevenLabs voice models on data from their own live deployments, tuned to metrics like customer satisfaction. It begins in the coming months, for selected enterprises first. Scribe v3 Medical — a transcription model built for healthcare terminology — already exists, and a financial-services model is in development. If you are not a large enterprise, this is a roadmap item, not a product you can sign up for.
The Interaction Engine is a preview: a system that manages turn-taking, interruptions and model selection inside a conversation. Memory (an agent keeps context across interactions, so callers stop repeating themselves) and Routines (multi-step work before, during and after a conversation) are coming to ElevenAgents. None of the three is shipped yet.
The Partner Program itself is now 550+ partners across 44 countries, including Google Cloud, IBM, Deloitte, DXC and Genesys. ElevenLabs also expanded its NVIDIA work — Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is in ElevenAgents, with 15 MW of Vera Rubin compute planned on top of existing Blackwell Ultra systems. A Unity SDK for ElevenAgents landed 5 November, so game players can talk to NPCs out loud — desktop and WebGL supported, iOS, Android and XR in beta. None of that changes what I build this week.
Campaign Manager is a real product, not a demo. It shipped after live beta campaigns, it runs on the agents and numbers you already have, and the retry and callback logic is the part that usually takes a builder a week to get right.
Scribe v3 Live is in the product today. Real-time transcription with speaker labelling, inside ElevenAgents, no waitlist mentioned.
ElevenAI early access is free and open. No sales call to try the one consumer-shaped product in the whole announcement.
The API is still the product. ElevenAPI carries the new models, and the whole stack is built to be called from outside — which is why it fits an n8n workflow instead of fighting it.
Nothing about ElevenLabs broke this week. The hard part is the gap between the announcement and the product.
Three honest limits:
Most of the Summit is not shippable yet. Marketplace purchasing waits until 2027. Customization starts in the coming months for selected enterprises. Memory, Routines and the Interaction Engine are coming, not live. If you buy on the keynote alone, you are buying a roadmap.
Campaign Manager is phone and WhatsApp only for now. Email and SMS are coming soon, and new customers have to go through sales rather than signing up in the app. Existing ElevenAgents users find it under Campaigns in the Agents sidebar.
The enterprise pricing is undisclosed. No prices were given for the customization work or the Marketplace. The self-serve plans are public — Free at $0, Starter at $6, Creator at $22, Pro at $99, Scale at $299, Business at $990 a month — but the Summit's biggest items have no number attached.
None of that is a reason not to use it. It is a reason to use the three things that are live, and to wait on the rest until it ships.
ElevenLabs fits if you run voice agents in real workflows — outbound calls with a goal, meeting notes that need to be right, transcription in more than one language — and you want the voice layer to be an API you call from n8n rather than a dashboard you babysit.
It fits agencies that run outbound for clients: Campaign Manager is the first piece of this launch that does a job an agency bills for, today.
It does not fit if you only need text-to-speech for a video or a voiceover. The free tier covers that, and the Summit news is about agents, not voices. And if you are a solo builder waiting on the Marketplace or model customization, the honest answer is to try ElevenAI and Scribe v3 now and check back when the enterprise pieces ship.
ElevenLabs' programme pays 22% of payments on Starter, Creator, Pro and Scale plans for the first 12 months of a referred subscription, and 11% on the Business tier, through PartnerStack. Enterprise purchases earn nothing. Commissions clear about 90 days after the payment they come from. If you try it through my link, that is the arrangement: https://whoisalfaz.me/go/elevenlabs
And if the voice agent you build sits behind n8n schedules, check the 3.0 guide before December. The Cron node your workflows use today is gone in 3.0: https://whoisalfaz.me/blog/how-to-upgrade-to-n8n-3-without-breaking-workflows/
ElevenLabs is now a platform for voice agents, not a voice tool. Three of the 13 announcements are live and worth your time this week. The rest is a roadmap — a good one, but a roadmap.
Alfaz Mahmud Rizve — GTM & RevOps Architect. I build autonomous revenue systems for scaling agencies and SaaS: SEO & organic growth, high-speed Next.js apps, and self-healing n8n workflows. whoisalfaz.me

articles.title: How to Build an MVP Without Wasting 6 Months
articles.description:
Originally published at muhammadmoiz.dev.
To build an MVP without wasting six months, start from one painful problem and one type of customer, write down the single job your product must do, cut every feature that doesn't serve that job, and put a working version in front of real users within weeks rather than quarters. Anything you can do by hand behind the scenes, do by hand at first. The goal of a minimum viable product is learning what customers will actually use and pay for, not shipping a smaller copy of your dream app.
This guide walks through how to create an MVP step by step, how to decide what to cut, and the mistakes that turn a six-week project into a six-month one.
Eric Ries, who popularised the term in The Lean Startup, describes the MVP as the version of a product that lets a team learn the most about its customers for the least effort. The term itself is older: it is generally credited to Frank Robinson in 2001, with Steve Blank and Ries spreading it later.
Two parts of that definition matter more than people expect:
"Learn" is the output. An MVP is a tool for answering a question, such as "Will restaurant owners pay monthly for this?" or "Will people upload their files to us instead of emailing them?" If you can't name the question, you aren't building an MVP yet.
"Least effort" is relative. Ries himself stresses that there is no formula for how small an MVP should be. For some ideas it's a landing page and a payment link. For others, like anything that handles money or health data, the minimum still has to be secure and reliable.
A useful test: if your first version answers your riskiest question, it is viable. If it also answers ten questions nobody asked, it isn't minimal.
Slow MVPs rarely come from slow coding. They come from decisions made before the first line of code. The usual causes:
Building for every future customer. Multiple user roles, team accounts, an admin dashboard with analytics, and five integrations, all before one person has signed up.
Perfecting things users haven't asked for. Custom design systems, animations, and settings pages for preferences nobody has.
Automating work that happens ten times a month. Writing an invoicing engine when you could send ten invoices by hand.
Scope that changes every week. Without a written, frozen scope, every conversation adds a feature.
Waiting for a big launch. Holding the product back until it feels "ready", then launching to silence.
Ries gives a good example of the cost of guessing: his team at IMVU once spent weeks on a feature nobody wanted, when a simple ad test could have shown the lack of demand far sooner. The fix for all five causes above is the same. Decide what you need to learn, and build only that.
"Independent wedding card sellers lose orders because customers can't see designs and prices online" is a usable problem. "A platform for events" is not. Pick one customer type you can actually reach this month.
Usually it is one of three: people don't have this problem, they won't switch from what they do now, or they won't pay. Your MVP exists to test that one assumption first.
Map the shortest path from "user arrives" to "user gets value". For a booking product, that's: see availability, pick a slot, confirm. Everything outside that path goes on a "later" list.
Paul Graham's essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" is full of examples: Airbnb's founders recruited hosts door to door in New York, and Stripe's founders quietly set up merchant accounts for early users by hand. You can do the same. Approve signups manually, send reports by email, handle payments with a payment link, and take orders over chat.
Pick a fixed window, for example four to eight weeks, and cut scope to fit the window rather than stretching the window to fit the scope. Write the scope down and treat changes as trade-offs: something comes in, something goes out.
Graham's point about launches is blunt: big launches rarely matter, and what counts is a small core of users who genuinely like the product. Ship to 10 to 50 people you found yourself, watch how they use it, and talk to them weekly.

Photo: Patrick Perkins on Unsplash
This is the part founders find hardest, so here's a practical way to sort features. Ask of each one: "If this were missing, would a user in our core flow fail to get value?" If the answer is no, it waits.



Feature
In the MVP?
What to do instead




Sign up and log in
Usually yes
Use a managed auth provider instead of building your own


The core flow (book, order, upload, track)
Yes
This is the product


Payments
Only if testing willingness to pay
A hosted checkout or payment link


Admin dashboard
Minimal
A simple internal page, or the database console


Team accounts and roles
Rarely
Add when a paying customer asks


Native iOS and Android apps
Rarely
A responsive web app or PWA first


Analytics and reporting
No
Basic event tracking plus talking to users


Notifications
Maybe one
One email or push for the moment that matters


Integrations
Rarely
Manual export or a single webhook



A real example: when I co-founded and built Shahi Bulawa, a wedding card and e-invitation store, we went from zero to launch in about a month. Instead of building a full cart and checkout, each product leads customers to WhatsApp to request a quote or a free mockup. The Next.js catalogue, an admin panel and SEO-friendly pages were in scope; a complex ordering system was not. The store got around 15 orders a month from the first month. You can read the full Shahi Bulawa case study.
The best MVP stack is the one your developer can ship fastest and that won't need a full rewrite if the idea works. For most web MVPs, that means:
A mainstream framework such as Next.js or React, so hiring help later is easy.
A managed backend such as Firebase or Supabase for auth, database and storage, so nobody spends weeks on infrastructure.
Hosted payments rather than custom billing logic.
Simple hosting with automatic deploys.
AI app builders like Lovable, Bolt and Replit can get a prototype on screen in days, and for testing demand they are often a great value starting point. The catch is what happens when real users and real data arrive. We've covered the common security holes in AI-built apps separately; if you go this route, plan for a review before you take payments or store personal data.
Minimal is not the same as insecure: Cutting features is fine. Cutting security is not. Even a two-week MVP needs proper access rules on the database, secrets kept off the client, and validated input on every form. A data leak in month one can end a product before it starts.
Every project differs, but a focused web MVP often follows a shape like this:
Week 1: Scope. Problem statement, riskiest assumption, core flow, written feature list, and a "later" list.
Weeks 2 to 5: Build. Core flow first, then auth, then the minimum admin tools. A working preview every week.
Week 6: Private launch. Ten to fifty hand-picked users, manual onboarding, direct feedback.
Weeks 7 onward: Iterate. Fix what blocks users, add only what several users ask for, and decide whether the core assumption held.
If you want a sense of budget for each stage, see our breakdown of web app development cost in 2026 and the fixed options on the pricing page.
Building an MVP is a business decision before it is a technical one. Before you hire anyone or open an AI builder, you should be able to answer:
What single question will this MVP answer?
Who are the first 20 users, by name or by channel?
What is the one flow they must complete?
What will we do by hand for now?
What result would make us stop, change direction, or keep going?
If you can answer those, a capable developer can usually get a first version live in weeks. If you can't, no amount of code will save the six months.
If you'd like help scoping and shipping your first version, take a look at how I approach product development from idea to launch.
What is an MVP? (Lean Startup Co., quoting Eric Ries)
Do Things That Don't Scale, Paul Graham (July 2013)
Minimum viable product (Wikipedia)
Shahi Bulawa case study
Cover photo: Kvalifik on Unsplash
I'm Muhammad Moiz, a full-stack developer who builds web apps, SaaS and POS systems, and takes AI-built apps (Lovable, Bolt, Replit) to production. Get in touch.

articles.title: How to import a Flowise export into Cuttlely
articles.description:
Already have flows? Bring them over.
Cuttlely opens a chatflow or agentflow that you exported from Flowise as a JSON file. A browser wizard checks the file, lists the fixes it made, and opens the flow on the right canvas. You pick your credentials again, check the graph, and save. It's one flow at a time. Import from the Chatflows page for a new flow. Import from the gear menu on an open canvas of the same type and it replaces what's on that canvas, so Save overwrites that flow. Nothing is saved until you select Save.
Here's what you need:
Cuttlely 1.7.3 or later, installed and signed in. Haven't set it up yet? The quickstart gets you there.
The exported JSON file for each flow you want to move.
Your model keys. Keys don't travel in the file, so you'll add them in Cuttlely under Credentials.
The import runs in the browser wizard. There's no import API or CLI for it.
In Flowise, open the flow on its canvas.
Select the Settings gear in the canvas header.
Select Export Chatflow. On an agent canvas, the item is Export Agents.
Flowise downloads a JSON file named after the flow, such as Bakery helper Chatflow.json. The file holds the flow's nodes and edges. Flowise leaves password, file, and folder fields out of the export, and it strips saved credential ids too.
Cuttlely also accepts a saved flow whose flowData holds the nodes and edges, and template files that have nodes and edges. A whole-workspace export won't import. That's the file with several flows, tools, and variables in it. Export each flow on its own instead.
In Cuttlely, open Chatflows. Select Import at the top right, then select Import Flowise JSON. On a chatflow canvas, the gear menu has Import Flowise JSON too.
The Flowise migration wizard opens on its Upload step. Select Choose Flowise JSON and pick your file.

Start the wizard by choosing a Flowise chatflow JSON file. API keys are not copied.
On Scan, read what the wizard found. It counts the nodes and edges and lists what it fixed, such as a credential it cleared. Select Next.
On Credentials, note each card that needs a credential. Select Next.
On Nodes, look over the list. It shows older nodes that still work but are on their way out, and nodes Cuttlely can't place. Select Next.
On Result, select Open migrated canvas. Green means the wizard found nothing left for you to do. Amber means the canvas can open but something still needs you. Expect amber on most imports, because the wizard clears every saved credential.
The flow opens on the canvas that fits it. A chatflow goes to the chatflow canvas, and an agentflow goes to the agentflow canvas. Select a credential on each card the wizard named. With the default compact cards, select the card and set its credential in the side panel.

The imported flow opens on the canvas with its connections in place. Connect your OpenAI credential before you run it.
Select Save. The first save creates the published flow. Your next canvas save is a draft.
Want the rule-by-rule detail on what Scan checks? It's in Flowise migration wizard.
Don't put an imported flow to work straight off the wizard. Go over the canvas first and make sure each card connects to the cards you expect. Scan lists the edges the wizard removed so you can connect them again by hand, but check every connection yourself rather than relying on that list.
Then try the flow in the canvas chat. The chat runs your draft, so you can test it before anything goes live.
Here's what comes across:
Nodes. A node whose name is in Cuttlely's node catalog opens with its settings. The catalog has about 300 nodes. On a chatflow, a node saved with no version or an older one is refreshed to the current node.
Retiring nodes. Older nodes that are on their way out still open, and the wizard lists them.
Chatflows and agentflows. Each opens on its own canvas. Older multi-agent and sequential-agent flows open on the legacy agentflow canvas. They run and save there, but that canvas isn't offered for new work.
Custom tools. On Tools, Load reads an exported tool JSON file and opens it in the Add New Tool dialog, ready to save.
Some things won't come across. The partial list:
Keys, passwords, and saved credential ids. Cuttlely removes them before the canvas opens.
A whole-workspace export. Import one flow at a time.
LlamaIndex nodes. The wizard names each one and doesn't open the file.
A node Cuttlely doesn't have, or a node saved without its input and output lists. The wizard names it and doesn't open the file.
The Arize, LangFuse, LangSmith, LangWatch, Lunary, Opik, Phoenix, and AssemblyAI configuration cards. The wizard drops each one with a note on Scan and still opens the file. Set up tracing in Chatflow Configuration > Analytics, and transcription in Speech to Text.
Matching or creating credentials inside the wizard. You pick them on the canvas after it opens.
The saved zoom and position of the canvas.
The full list, including moving a whole install with its database, is in Bring your existing flows.
Select Publish when the flow is ready. On a chatflow or agentflow, the Publish dialog can run a few questions against your draft first. Every save is kept in version history. Both are covered in Drafts and Publish.
New to Cuttlely? Run the quickstart and you'll have it running on Docker before you open the wizard. If this got your flows across, star Cuttlely on GitHub so other devs can find it.

articles.title: Deleting your losers buys 4.1 points of hit rate: an audit protocol for model retirement
articles.description:
Every prediction system eventually grows a lifecycle manager: models get born, promoted, demoted and killed. Ours has 8,789 model rows and a retirement pipeline that runs every two hours. For a long time the number we published was computed over whatever models happened to still exist at query time — a mistake whose size is measurable.
46,160 graded predictions carry a boolean hit. The all-cohort rate is 57.05% (26,334 correct). The rate over models still in a live lifecycle state is 61.17% (19,281 of 31,520). Nothing about the models changed between those queries — only the WHERE clause did. A 4.12-point swing produced entirely by bookkeeping. In a system that retires models automatically, survivorship bias is not an edge case; it is the default output. What follows is the audit protocol we now run before any retirement decision.
There is no single "deleted" state. A model leaves the visible cohort through six different doors, and the aggregate rate treats each differently.

Three things stand out. First, the worst cohorts are also the smallest. demoted holds 2,937 model rows but only 1,014 graded predictions — 0.35 per model. pending_retrain holds 56 models and 318 predictions at 28.30%. These are not measured failures; they are barely-measured ones. A rule that fires on 0.35 observations per model is not selecting on quality, it is selecting on noise.
Second, eliminated is a real signal. 801 models, 7,950 graded predictions, 45.11% — 11.98 points below the evolving cohort on a sample worth reading.
Third: 4,854 graded predictions reference 525 model_id values that no longer exist in ai_models at all. Their score, 56.61%, is close to the pool average, and any metric written as JOIN ai_models silently drops every one of them. We also keep an ai_models_archive table with 4,054 rows, while archived_at is NULL on all 8,789 live rows — the primary table cannot tell you when anything was retired.
The protocol: publish two numbers from one query so they cannot drift apart — the headline, and its complement over the full historical cohort including rows whose model row is missing.
-- Cohort audit: the same graded rows, seen through two different filters.
WITH graded AS (
    SELECT p.id,
           p.model_id,
           p.hit,
           p.created_at,
           COALESCE(m.lifecycle_status, 'hard_deleted') AS lc
    FROM ai_predictions p
    LEFT JOIN ai_models m ON m.id = p.model_id
    WHERE p.settled = TRUE
      AND p.hit IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT 'all_cohort'      AS view,
       COUNT(*)          AS n,
       SUM(hit::int)     AS hits,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2) AS hit_rate
FROM graded
UNION ALL
SELECT 'live_only', COUNT(*), SUM(hit::int),
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2)
FROM graded
WHERE lc IN ('evolving', 'active', 'incubating', 'validating')
UNION ALL
SELECT 'retired_cohort', COUNT(*), SUM(hit::int),
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(hit::int) / COUNT(*), 2)
FROM graded
WHERE lc IN ('eliminated', 'demoted', 'archived');

     view      |   n   | hits  | hit_rate
---------------+-------+-------+----------
 all_cohort    | 46160 | 26334 |    57.05
 live_only     | 31520 | 19281 |    61.17
 retired_cohort|  8964 |  3931 |    43.85

The rule we now enforce: the delta between all_cohort and live_only is itself a monitored metric. Call it the retirement gap. When it grows, the pipeline is deleting measured failures faster than unmeasured models — flattering the published number without improving the system. Month by month:

The gap is not constant. It is smallest in the month when almost nothing had been retired and largest when a quarter of the pool was already gone. The full series runs between 50% and 62%, and part of the recent stability is the deletion of 23% of the evidence.
Hard deletion destroys the denominator. 525 model ids vanished from ai_models while their predictions stayed, so every JOIN-based metric silently excludes 4,854 rows — worse than a wrong number, because nothing in the output declares it.
Status filters are applied at read time, not write time. The same physical rows produce 57.05% or 61.17% depending on a WHERE clause chosen by a dashboard author, and no schema-level signal marks that the choice exists.
The leaderboard adds a minimum-sample filter on top. Of 4,681 models with any graded prediction, only 660 reach 20 and 170 reach 50; the median is 6. A "top models by hit rate" view is therefore almost entirely models whose whole record is under ten games, and sorting it descending returns 100% records: 388 with fewer than five graded predictions, 18 more between five and nine.
Here is the part that should end the argument. If every model were exchangeable at the pool rate of 0.5705, the expected number of perfect records is Σ p^n over the actual sample sizes:
models with n < 5   : expected 634.5 perfect records, observed 388
models with n >= 5  : expected  25.3 perfect records, observed  18

Observed is below the coin-flip expectation in both bands. A 4-for-4 record is not evidence of skill here — it is less impressive than chance would produce. Any rule that ranks on raw rate ranks a mixture of noise and sample size, and the models it rewards are the ones that guessed few times.
The fix is not "stop filtering" — some views legitimately want the live cohort. The fix is to make the filter explicit, permanent and reversible, so excluded rows stay addressable. Retirement becomes an event, never a delete.
"""Retirement ledger: retirement is an event, never a delete."""
import hashlib, json, datetime as dt

def _h(prev: str, payload: dict) -> str:
    body = json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"))
    return hashlib.sha256((prev + body).encode()).hexdigest()

def retire(cur, model_id: int, new_state: str, reason: str, evidence: dict):
    """Append one row. Never UPDATE ai_models.status, never DELETE."""
    cur.execute(
        "SELECT state, entry_hash FROM model_lifecycle_ledger "
        "WHERE model_id = %s ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1", (model_id,))
    row = cur.fetchone()
    prev_state, prev_hash = (row if row else ("born", "0" * 64))

    payload = {
        "model_id": model_id, "from_state": prev_state,
        "to_state": new_state, "reason": reason,     # 'eliminated_low_n'
        "evidence": evidence,                        # n, hits, rate, window
        "at": dt.datetime.utcnow().isoformat(timespec="seconds"),
    }
    cur.execute(
        "INSERT INTO model_lifecycle_ledger "
        "(model_id, from_state, to_state, reason, evidence, entry_hash, prev_hash) "
        "VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s)",
        (model_id, prev_state, new_state, reason,
         json.dumps(evidence), _h(prev_hash, payload), prev_hash))
    # projections may change; history may not
    cur.execute("UPDATE ai_models SET lifecycle_status = %s WHERE id = %s",
                (new_state, model_id))

With that ledger, the cohort view stops being a guess:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_model_cohort AS
SELECT m.id AS model_id,
       m.lifecycle_status AS current_state,
       COALESCE(f.first_retired_at, TIMESTAMPTZ 'infinity') AS retired_at,
       f.retirement_reason
FROM ai_models m
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT MIN(at) AS first_retired_at,
           (ARRAY_AGG(reason ORDER BY at))[1] AS retirement_reason
    FROM model_lifecycle_ledger l
    WHERE l.model_id = m.id
      AND l.to_state IN ('eliminated', 'demoted', 'archived')
) f ON TRUE;

Now "as of date D" is a temporal join instead of a status filter: a model retired in September still contributes its September predictions to every point-in-time metric, and the historical series can no longer be rewritten by a later decision. Three invariants belong in CI, each of which our bad state violated:
COUNT(*) FROM ai_predictions p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ai_models m WHERE m.id = p.model_id) must be zero. Ours was 4,854.
archived_at must be non-NULL for every row whose state is archived. Ours was 0 of 170.
Every state change needs a ledger row, and the chain must verify from genesis. Ours had 1,185 rows with reactivated_at set and no recorded reason.
Judge a retirement rule on the predictions it would have removed, not on the leaderboard it produces afterwards. Report four numbers together for every candidate cohort: n, hits, rate, and the rate of the cohort that survives. A rule removing 8,964 rows at 43.85% from a pool running at 57.05% raises the published number by 3.18 points while deleting 19.4% of the evidence. Whether that trade is defensible depends on whether the rule fired on measured failure — and with demoted averaging 0.35 graded predictions per model, ours mostly did not.
The honest summary of our pool: 63.6% of model rows (5,587 of 8,789) have never produced a single graded prediction, the median model has six, only 170 clear fifty, and 253 models were fathered by parents that were later eliminated. A system that kills a parent but keeps its descendants runs a selection loop it cannot audit, because the descendants inherit a training word whose measured performance was negative and nothing records the inheritance.
Retirement is a data operation, not a UI operation. If deleting a row changes the headline metric, that metric is a function of your bookkeeping rather than your model quality — and the cheapest way to improve it is always to delete more.
Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

articles.title: A balanced rota can still fail: a two-person scheduling example
articles.description:
A rota can give everyone the same number of assignments and still leave a shift uncovered. The problem often starts with a reasonable shortcut: assign the next shift to the person with the lowest current workload.
Here is a small, fictional example that exposes the limitation.



Person
Morning
Afternoon
Maximum assignments




Ada
Available
Available
1


Ben
Available
Unavailable
1



Both shifts need one person. At the start, Ada and Ben have equal workloads. If a greedy tie-break assigns Ada to the morning, the afternoon is left without an eligible person: Ben is unavailable, and Ada has reached her limit.
Yet a complete schedule exists: Ben in the morning, Ada in the afternoon.
Availability and maximum assignments are hard constraints. A schedule must satisfy them before its workload balance is useful.
For a slightly larger example, the checks might be:
Every shift has its required number of people.
Every assigned person is available for that shift.
Nobody exceeds their own assignment limit.
One person cannot cover two assignments in the same time group.
After those checks, compare feasible schedules using an explicit objective. One simple choice is to minimize the difference between the largest and smallest assignment counts, then use the sum of squared counts as a tie-break.
That is a definition of fairness for this model. It does not account for shift difficulty or individual preferences unless those are represented in the inputs.
For the two-person example, checking all combinations is small enough to write directly. This standalone JavaScript runs in Node.js and uses no packages:
const people = [
  { name: "Ada", available: ["morning", "afternoon"], max: 1 },
  { name: "Ben", available: ["morning"], max: 1 },
];

const feasible = [];
for (const morning of people) {
  for (const afternoon of people) {
    const assignments = [morning, afternoon];
    const available = morning.available.includes("morning") &&
      afternoon.available.includes("afternoon");
    const withinLimits = people.every(person =>
      assignments.filter(p => p === person).length <= person.max
    );
    if (available && withinLimits) {
      feasible.push({ morning: morning.name, afternoon: afternoon.name });
    }
  }
}
console.log(feasible);
// [{ morning: "Ben", afternoon: "Ada" }]

This example checks availability and assignment limits. It has four combinations, so completing the search is easy. Larger instances need better ordering and pruning, and they still need an explicit stopping rule.
A useful scheduling interface should distinguish these outcomes:



Outcome
What the result establishes




Optimal
A feasible schedule meets a proven lower bound or a complete search established the best objective.


Feasible, search limit reached
The shown schedule satisfies the modeled constraints; a better schedule might exist.


Infeasible
A constraint check or a complete search established that no schedule satisfies the modeled constraints.


Unknown, search limit reached
The search stopped without finding a feasible schedule. This does not establish infeasibility.



The final two states are easy to confuse in a UI. A time limit is a statement about how much searching happened, not a proof about every possible schedule.
The same distinction is useful in packing, timetabling and small resource-allocation tools.
An exported schedule is easier to review when it travels with its assumptions. Keep the availability table, individual limits, time groups and solver status alongside the assignments. If an input changes, recompute the result before sharing it.
For an initial check, use a tiny example where you already know the answer. Then try an impossible case, such as two required assignments with a total capacity of one. Finally, test an invalid input and make sure an old successful result is not left looking current.
I used these checks while preparing Fair Schedule Planner, a small offline browser tool with editable availability, personal limits, shared time groups, CSV results and a workbook for recording assumptions. The supplied examples are fictional. The interface reports the search outcomes above.
If you want the ready-made interface and worksheets, the Fair Schedule Planner download is available on Payhip for $12 as a one-time purchase. A free PDF preview is available on the product page. The JavaScript example in this article is independent and free to use.
This article and the product were prepared with AI assistance. The example output was checked, and the product's documented functional checks cover availability, conflicting assignments, impossible inputs and exported result data.

articles.title: Use Jenkins Agents on EC2 to Scale Your Builds
articles.description:
Learn how to connect a second AWS EC2 instance as a Jenkins agent, run pipelines in parallel, and keep your Jenkins controller fast.
When I first set up Jenkins on an AWS EC2 instance, everything ran on that one server: pulling code, building Docker images, running tests, and deploying. It worked for small labs, but as soon as I ran two or three jobs together, the server became slow and builds started waiting in the queue.
The fix is simple and very common in real DevOps teams: use Jenkins agents. In this article I explain what agents are, why they help, and how to connect a second EC2 instance as a Jenkins agent step by step.
Jenkins has two types of machines:
Controller (formerly "master"): the main Jenkins server. It hosts the web UI, stores job configuration, manages credentials, and schedules builds.
Agent (formerly "slave"): a separate machine that actually runs the build steps. The controller sends work to it.
Simple way to remember it: the controller is the manager who assigns tasks, and the agents are the workers who do them.



Problem on a single Jenkins server
How agents solve it




Builds queue up when many jobs run together
Jobs run in parallel on different agents


Heavy builds (Docker, tests) slow down the Jenkins UI
The controller stays light and responsive


One server holds all tools (Java, Docker, Node, Maven)
Each agent can have its own tools


A broken build can affect the Jenkins server itself
Builds are isolated on separate machines


Hard to scale
Add more EC2 agents when you need more capacity



A good practice is to run zero or very few builds on the controller and let agents do the heavy work.
          GitHub (code)
               |
               v
   +-----------------------+
   |  Jenkins Controller   |   EC2 #1  (port 8080)
   |  (UI, jobs, schedule) |
   +-----------------------+
        |              |
      SSH            SSH
        v              v
 +--------------+ +--------------+
 | Agent EC2 #2 | | Agent EC2 #3 |
 | label: docker| | label: test  |
 +--------------+ +--------------+

The controller connects to each agent over SSH (port 22) and runs the build steps there.
A running Jenkins controller on an EC2 instance (http://<Controller-IP>:8080)
A second EC2 instance for the agent (Amazon Linux 2023 or Ubuntu, t2.micro or t3.small is enough for practice)
Both instances in the same VPC (using private IPs is the best practice)
A key pair (.pem file) to log in to the agent
Go to EC2 → Launch Instance

Name it jenkins-agent-1

Choose the same AMI and VPC as your controller
In the Security Group, allow SSH (port 22) from the controller's security group (not from the whole internet)
Launch the instance
Tip: allowing port 22 only from the controller's security group is safer than opening it to 0.0.0.0/0.
Connect to the agent instance and install Java, because Jenkins needs it to run its agent process.
# Amazon Linux 2023
sudo dnf update -y
sudo dnf install java-17-amazon-corretto -y
java -version

Install any tools your pipeline needs. For example, Docker and Git:
sudo dnf install git docker -y
sudo systemctl enable --now docker
sudo usermod -aG docker ec2-user

Create a working folder for Jenkins:
mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/jenkins-agent

The controller needs a way to log in to the agent.
Go to Manage Jenkins → Credentials → System → Global credentials → Add Credentials

Kind: SSH Username with private key

ID: agent-ssh-key

Username: ec2-user (use ubuntu for Ubuntu)
Private Key: choose Enter directly and paste the content of your .pem file
Click Create



Never store keys inside a Jenkinsfile or a Git repository.
Go to Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New Node

Name: agent-1, select Permanent Agent, click Create

Fill in the settings:



Setting
Value




Number of executors

2 (how many builds can run at once)


Remote root directory
/home/ec2-user/jenkins-agent


Labels
docker linux


Usage
Use this node as much as possible


Launch method
Launch agents via SSH


Host
Agent's private IP



Credentials
agent-ssh-key


Host Key Verification Strategy
Non-verifying (for practice) or Known hosts file (better)



Click Save

Open the node page and check that the status shows "Agent successfully connected and online"




Note: Labels are very useful. They let a job choose which type of agent it needs.
Go to Manage Jenkins → Nodes → Built-In Node → Configure and set Number of executors to 0.
Now all builds are forced to run on agents, and your Jenkins UI stays fast.
Tell the pipeline which agent to use with the agent { label '...' } block.
pipeline {
    agent { label 'docker' }

    stages {
        stage('Checkout') {
            steps {
                git branch: 'main', url: 'https://github.com/myuser/cloudcart.git'
            }
        }

        stage('Build Docker Image') {
            steps {
                sh 'docker build -t myuser/cloudcart:latest .'
            }
        }

        stage('Verify') {
            steps {
                sh 'hostname && whoami && docker images'
            }
        }
    }

    post {
        success { echo 'Build finished on the agent!' }
        failure { echo 'Build failed. Check the console output.' }
    }
}

Run the job and open the Console Output. You will see a line like Running on agent-1 in /home/ec2-user/jenkins-agent/workspace/.... That confirms the build ran on the agent, not on the controller.
pipeline {
    agent none

    stages {
        stage('Build') {
            agent { label 'docker' }
            steps { sh 'docker build -t myapp .' }
        }
        stage('Test') {
            agent { label 'linux' }
            steps { sh 'echo Running tests...' }
        }
    }
}




Problem
Likely cause and fix




Agent shows offline

Check that Java is installed on the agent and port 22 is open from the controller's security group


Permission denied (publickey)
Wrong username or wrong private key in the Jenkins credential


docker: permission denied
Add the user to the docker group (sudo usermod -aG docker ec2-user) and reconnect the agent


Job stays in queue: "waiting for next available executor"
The label in the Jenkinsfile does not match the node label


Connection timeout
The controller and agent are in different VPCs or the security group rule is missing



Use small instances (t3.small) for agents, since builds are short-lived
Stop the agent instance when you are not practicing, to avoid charges
Use private IPs to avoid data transfer costs between instances
For automatic scaling, explore the Amazon EC2 plugin for Jenkins. It launches agents on demand and terminates them when the build is finished
Keep the controller light: 0 executors on the built-in node
Use labels (docker, linux, test) to match jobs to the right agents
Allow SSH only from the controller's security group
Store keys in Jenkins Credentials, never in code
Keep agent tools (Java, Docker, Git) updated
Monitor agent disk space, since Docker images can fill it quickly
Moving from a single Jenkins server to a controller plus agents setup is one of the easiest ways to make your CI/CD faster and more reliable. Builds run in parallel, the Jenkins UI stays responsive, and you can add more EC2 agents whenever your workload grows.
If you already have Jenkins running on EC2, try launching one more instance today, connect it as an agent, and run your pipeline on it. It takes less than 30 minutes and teaches you how real-world CI/CD is scaled.

llama.cpp Just Hit 1.0 — Local AI Apps Finally Have a Stable Foundation
articles.description:
llama.cpp Just Hit 1.0 — Local AI Apps Finally Have a Stable Foundation


After three and a half years of commit-number builds, llama.cpp released version 1.0.0 on November 13, 2026 — and the headline is not a new model or a speed boost. It is a promise: the public API is now stable, and breaking changes will arrive only with a major-version bump.
If you build anything that runs AI models on a user's own machine — a desktop app, a private chatbot, a coding assistant, a mobile app, or an OpenAI-compatible inference server — this is the most important local AI news of the year. The engine underneath your app just grew up.
First, a clarification for anyone new here: llama.cpp is not a language model. It is an open-source inference engine written in C and C++, built on top of the ggml tensor library. Its job is to take a compatible model — usually packaged in GGUF format — and run it efficiently on whatever hardware is available: a laptop CPU, a phone, a GPU, or a server.
It is also the engine quietly powering most of the local AI world. Ollama, LM Studio, and a long tail of apps that run models on ordinary hardware all build on llama.cpp. When it changes, the whole local AI ecosystem feels it.
The biggest change is a pruning. Version 1.0 uses the major-version milestone to remove the deprecated public API: 35 deprecated functions are gone, along with the warmup setter (llama_set_warmup) and the defragmentation-threshold option. At the same time, the NextN speculative-decoding API moves from the llama-ext.h extension header into the main llama.h header — placing it inside the public API covered by the new stability rules.
The companion tensor library ggml also ships as v1.0.0 at the same time, with its own deprecated API and legacy operations pruned.
The versioning rules are refreshingly specific, and they are tied to the public C API exposed through the project's include directory:
MAJOR — a breaking change to the public C API.
MINOR — a backward-compatible feature, backend update, model addition, or API addition.
PATCH — a bug fix with no API change.
A move from v1.0.0 to v1.0.1 should be a plain bug-fix update. That is the whole point: you can now upgrade with confidence instead of pinning a commit hash and hoping nothing moved under you.
As project creator Georgi Gerganov put it: "Every new integration means more developers depending on our library interfaces and therefore having a flexible but stable API is paramount."
The release is not only a contract — it ships real improvements too:
OCP FP8 KV-cache support through the f8_e4m3 type, with optional static per-tensor scales — smaller memory footprints for long conversations.
A host-memory MoE expert cache with a configurable CPU share, so mixture-of-experts models run better on machines without huge GPUs.
Three new text architectures: Kimi-K3.1-Pro, Ripple, and xing4_0.
llama-server security hardening — fixes for server-side request forgery (SSRF), CORS, and DNS-rebinding attacks, plus HF_TOKEN now restricted to huggingface.co hosts.
A new /v1/audio/speech endpoint and a redesigned web UI for llama-server, the OpenAI-compatible API server many apps talk to.
Official quick-start installation scripts for Unix-like systems and Windows.
The project now supports more than 150 model-architecture variants, and pre-release artifacts cover Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, and iOS — with Docker, Debian, Homebrew, conda-forge, MacPorts, Winget, and XCFramework channels listed in the release notes.
The timing is not an accident. Local AI has moved far beyond running a small model on a laptop as a curiosity. Developers now ship desktop applications, private chatbots, coding assistants, multimodal systems, and mobile apps on top of local inference — and open models keep getting stronger.
Take Edge0-145B, a 145-billion-parameter open model that runs on a laptop: the frontier of open models is now genuinely usable on consumer hardware. A stable llama.cpp means apps built on models like that have a foundation they can depend on, instead of a moving target.
Local inference also solves problems the cloud cannot:
Privacy — your data never leaves the device, which matters for health, legal, and business documents.
Cost — no per-token API bill for every request your app makes.
Offline use — your app works on a plane, in a dead zone, or behind a firewall.
Control — no provider can change the model, the price, or the terms underneath you overnight.
If you want to try it, the official quick start is now simpler than ever. Clone the repo and build:
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build --config Release

Or skip the build entirely and grab a pre-built release for your platform from the llama.cpp GitHub releases page. Then start the OpenAI-compatible server with any GGUF model and point your existing client code at it — no code changes needed if you already speak the OpenAI API.
One warning before you upgrade: 1.0 is a stable contract, but it is not a drop-in upgrade for every existing app. If your code calls any of the 35 removed deprecated functions, it will break at compile time. Check the release notes, fix the calls, and then enjoy never having to do that again without a major-version warning.
For three and a half years, llama.cpp versioned itself with raw commit numbers — builds like "12360" that told you nothing about compatibility. From here on, it follows semantic versioning, and the project has committed to it in public.
That is what a 1.0 is supposed to mean: not that the software is finished, but that the people building on it can finally plan around it. Local AI just got its stable foundation. Now go build on it.

Google's New AI Can Find Where Disease Begins in Your DNA
DeepMind's AI Found Cracks in RSA Encryption — Should You Worry?

articles.title: Depot vs Blacksmith Docker cache for GitHub Actions builds
articles.description:
The depot vs blacksmith docker cache question is really one about geography: Depot keeps your layers on a remote BuildKit builder with its own NVMe disk, and Blacksmith keeps them on a sticky disk that reattaches to the runner the job is already on. That decides the workflow edit, the cold-cache failure mode, and which line of the invoice the cache lands on.

Where each vendor keeps a Docker layer cache, and what it costs on top of runner minutes, at rates read 20 September 2026. A 50 GB cache is $25 a month on either vendor by a different route.
Depot touches Docker builds in two separate products, and it matters which one you buy. Its GitHub Actions runners carry a RAM-disk accelerator and Depot Cache; its container builds are a different service, where an ephemeral EC2 builder runs an optimized BuildKit with a persistent NVMe layer cache, 50 GB by default and up to 500 GB, and builds amd64 and arm64 natively without emulation.
Blacksmith does one thing here: it gives BuildKit a disk that survives the job. useblacksmith/setup-docker-builder@v2 mounts a sticky disk keyed by the cache-key input its v2 README requires, one key per build target, and useblacksmith/build-push-action@v2 builds against it, so the cache lives beside the runner rather than in a cache service. There is no second product to buy.
Every cell below was read from the vendor's own public pricing or documentation page on 20 September 2026. Where a vendor does not publish a number, the cell says "not published" instead of carrying a guess.




Depot
Blacksmith
Latchkey




Price per minute, 2 vCPU Linux x64
$0.006 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk, 2 GB RAM disk)
$0.004 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk)

$0.0025 (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)


Price per minute, 4 vCPU Linux x64
$0.012 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 130 GB disk, 4 GB RAM disk)
$0.008 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 80 GB disk)

$0.005 (4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 100 GB disk)


Free tier
None standalone: 2,000 runner minutes with the $20/month Developer plan, 20,000 with the $200/month Startup plan
3,000 free minutes a month, printed on every runner card
30-day trial, then 2,000 included minutes a month on Developer, 4,000 on Launch, 6,000 on Scale


Billing granularity
Per-second usage tracking, with whole minutes billed at the end of the month and no one-minute minimum
Not published
Per minute


Runner sizes and OS
2 to 64 vCPU on Linux x64 and arm64 (Graviton4); Windows Server 2022 and 2025, with no Hyper-V; macOS at 8 vCPU
2 to 32 vCPU on Linux x64 and arm64; Windows Server 2025 at 2 to 32 vCPU in public beta; macOS M4 at 6 and 12 vCPU
2, 4, 8 and 16 vCPU, Ubuntu 24.04 on x86_64 only. arm64, Windows and macOS are not offered


Cache: type, limit, persistence
Depot Cache, 25 GB included on Developer and 250 GB on Startup, then $0.20/GB/month; reported at up to 1,000 MiB/s; entries are not isolated by branch
Colocated cache intercepts actions/cache, 25 GB free per repo per week; sticky disks are ext4 volumes, 5 per job, evicted after 7 days idle, $0.50/GB/month
Size not published. latchkey-dev/cache-action@v1 replaces actions/cache with a restore step and a save step, keeping path and key (no restore-keys); entries are isolated per organization, versioned by OS, kept 14 days; a failed restore warns rather than failing the job


Docker build acceleration
A RAM disk on every runner, 2 GB at 2 vCPU rising to 32 GB at 64 vCPU, plus remote BuildKit builders as a separate product: 16 vCPU and 32 GB by default, 50 GB of NVMe layer cache expandable to 500 GB

useblacksmith/setup-docker-builder@v2 and useblacksmith/build-push-action@v2; layers sit on a sticky disk per cache key and are garbage-collected after 8 days unused

latchkey-dev/docker-cache-action@v1, layers held in a Latchkey-managed private registry per organization


Concurrency limits
Not published
None imposed, per the runner docs
Developer 20, Launch 40, Scale 80 busy runners per workspace; idle warm runners do not count


Where jobs run
Ephemeral EC2 instances in Depot's AWS account, or in your own account on Depot Managed; remote builders run beside the runner
Blacksmith's own regions: Ashburn, Phoenix, Amsterdam and Frankfurt
Latchkey's own AWS estate on m6a-class hosts, one job per runner, no inbound access, destroyed after the job


Self-healing or retries
Not offered
Not offered
Built in: transient failures are diagnosed and retried inside the run


Setup change required
Change the runs-on label; for remote builds add depot/setup-action@v1 and swap in depot/build-push-action@v1. The repository must be owned by a GitHub organization
Install the GitHub App, change the runs-on label, then swap two actions in the Docker job
A runs-on label change. GitHub organization accounts only



A Docker layer cache is only useful if it is near the machine that reads it, and the two vendors solve that in opposite directions. Blacksmith moves the disk to the job: a sticky disk is an ext4 volume that reattaches to whichever runner takes the next run with the same cache key, so BuildKit sees a warm local filesystem. Depot moves the job to the disk: the build runs on a remote builder with NVMe attached, and your runner sends context and receives an image.
The consequences show up in three places. The edit: Blacksmith is two action swaps in the Docker job, Depot is a setup action plus a project id. The failure mode: a sticky disk idle for seven days is evicted and the next build is cold. And the bill, which both marketing pages skip.

A sticky disk per cache key, 5 disks per job
A Latchkey-managed private registry per organization


First run after a cold start
Cold: the builder cache is empty for a new project
Cold: Blacksmith documents that the first Docker run is uncached
Cold: the registry has no layers for a new repository


Eviction
Not published for Depot Cache; storage is billed past plan inclusions

What the cache costs on top of runner minutes
$20/month Developer plan includes 25 GB; $0.20/GB/month after that; build minutes billed separately at $0.04/min past 500 included
$0.50/GB/month of sticky disk; the 25 GB colocated actions/cache allowance is free
Included in the plan


Native multi-architecture
amd64 and arm64 built natively on the builder, no emulation
arm64 runners exist, so a matrix builds each architecture on its own runner
Not offered: x86_64 only



Not benchmarked yet; the runner benchmark report will replace this section. We have not run the same workload on these runners ourselves, and until we have, there is no number here worth quoting.
The cheap way to get a real answer is to point one slow job at each candidate for a week, because runner selection is per job and the Actions run log gives you the timings for free.
Both vendors publish a claim, and both are marketing rather than measurement. Blacksmith's documentation says "Our customers have reported 2x to 40x improvements in build times" from Docker layer caching: a reported range, not a benchmark. Depot says its runners are "up to 3x faster than a GitHub-hosted runner" and its cache gives "10x faster caching". Neither names the workload, so neither transfers to your Dockerfile.
The number you can trust is your own cache hit rate: count how many layers say CACHED in the build log on a normal pull request. If most do, a faster cache is not your bottleneck and a cheaper runner minute is worth more. If none do, read buildx failed to reserve cache first, because a cache that is not being written is not a vendor problem.
Start with the runner minutes, at the workload every comparison here uses: 10,000 Linux minutes at 2 vCPU plus 2,000 macOS minutes on a private repository.

2,000 macOS minutes

$160 at $0.08/min
$188

$25 at $0.0025/min
Not offered: $124 on GitHub-hosted
$149 plus $5 to $49 a month for the plan



On runner minutes Blacksmith is a third cheaper than Depot at both published Linux sizes, $0.004 against $0.006 at 2 vCPU and $0.008 against $0.012 at 4 vCPU, and it is the only one with a standing free tier. Depot charges exactly GitHub-hosted list price and sells more machine for it. Latchkey's own plan is $5 to $49 a month on top of that compute, and its 2,000 to 6,000 included minutes are not netted off, so the figure is gross on both counts.
Now the cache, where the two land in the same place by different routes. A 50 GB layer cache on Blacksmith is 50 GB of sticky disk at $0.50 per GB per month, which is $25 a month. The same 50 GB on Depot is the $20 Developer plan, which includes 25 GB, plus 25 GB of overage at $0.20 per GB per month, which is $5: $25 a month again. The shapes differ. Blacksmith scales linearly with the disk you keep; Depot is mostly a plan fee until you pass 25 GB.
If you use Depot's remote builders and not just its runners, there is a third meter. Build minutes are tracked by the second and billed separately: the $20 Developer plan includes 500 of them, overage is $0.04 a minute, and the Large builder consumes them at 2x, Extra Large at 4x. Two hundred builds a month at three minutes each is 600 build minutes, so 100 bill at $0.04, which is $4 on top of the plan. That is cheap until a build takes twenty minutes.
Take uptime as unmeasured: no Actions SLA appears on either vendor's pages. What both do publish is enough to predict the bad days. Blacksmith states that the first Docker run is uncached and that a sticky disk idle for seven days is evicted, so a repository that builds weekly is permanently cold. Depot Cache is shared across branches rather than isolated per branch, which is faster and less strict than GitHub's scoping.
The failure neither addresses is the build that dies mechanically halfway through: a registry timeout, a rate limit on a base image pull, a disk full of layers. Those bill the minutes they burned, fail the job, and wait for a person to press re-run, which bills again. Docker Hub pull rate limit and registry mirror cover the two that hit Docker jobs hardest.
You want the build off the runner. A remote builder with 16 vCPU and 32 GB means a 2 vCPU runner can drive a large build, which is the opposite of the usual "buy a bigger runner" answer.
You build amd64 and arm64 from one workflow and are tired of QEMU. Depot builds both natively on the builder rather than emulating one of them.
Your cache is large and you would rather pay for it by the gigabyte past a plan allowance than manage disks and their idle eviction.
Your jobs are short and numerous, because per-second tracking with no one-minute minimum removes rounding that a lower rate does not.
One caveat before you commit: Depot documents that its Windows runners have no Hyper-V on EC2, so Docker on Windows is unlikely to work there.
You want the lowest runner rate of the two: $0.004 against $0.006 at 2 vCPU, with 3,000 free minutes a month on top.
You want the smallest possible change. Two action swaps inside the Docker job, and the build still runs where it ran before.
Your Docker job also does other work, such as tests against the image it just built, and you would rather keep that on one machine than split it across a runner and a builder.
You want the cache and the runner from one vendor, on one invoice, with no separate build-minute meter to model.
Note the trade you are accepting: a sticky disk is per cache key with five disks per job, so a repository that builds many distinct images needs its keys planned rather than pasted.
Both start with a runs-on change, and each wants two more lines in the Docker job. Blacksmith keeps the build local and swaps the builder underneath it; Depot installs the CLI and replaces the build action, after which the build leaves the runner. Runner selection is per job, so point one Docker job at each for two weeks and compare real numbers instead of vendor claims.
jobs:
   image:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: blacksmith-4vcpu-ubuntu-2404
     steps:
       - uses: actions/checkout@v7
+      - uses: useblacksmith/setup-docker-builder@v2
+        with:
+          cache-key: docker/Dockerfile
-      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
+      - uses: useblacksmith/build-push-action@v2
         with:
           context: .

   image-on-depot:
-    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    runs-on: depot-ubuntu-24.04-4
     permissions:
       contents: read
       id-token: write
     steps:
       - uses: actions/checkout@v7
+      - uses: depot/setup-action@v1
-      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
+      - uses: depot/build-push-action@v1
         with:
+          project: your-depot-project-id
           context: .

For most teams the honest answer is Blacksmith, because the change is smaller, the runner rate is a third lower, and a warm local disk is a good enough cache for a Dockerfile that has not been split across a dozen images. Depot is the better buy when the build itself has outgrown the runner: native multi-architecture images, a layer cache measured in hundreds of gigabytes, or a build you want executed on a 16 vCPU machine while the job that drives it stays on a cheap one. The two cache bills land in the same place at 50 GB, $25 a month either way, so cost is not the deciding axis at that size and architecture is. What neither does is notice that the build failed because a registry timed out at minute nine, repair it, and carry on, which on a Docker-heavy pipeline is the line item that grows quietest.
Blacksmith mounts a sticky disk, an ext4 volume keyed by an input you set on useblacksmith/setup-docker-builder@v2, and BuildKit writes its layer cache onto it. The disk reattaches to whichever runner takes the next run with that key, so the cache is local. Blacksmith documents that layers unused for 8 days are garbage-collected, the disk is evicted after 7 days idle, and the first Docker run is uncached.
On stock GitHub-hosted runners the usual route is cache-to: type=gha, which writes layers into the same 10 GB per-repository store actions/cache uses, so a large image evicts everything else. Both vendors replace that store: Blacksmith puts layers on a sticky disk, Depot on a remote builder's NVMe. Verify either by counting CACHED lines in the log, not by trusting the setup step.
Both products share by design, and scope it differently. A Blacksmith sticky disk is shared by cache key, so two jobs passing the same key see the same layers, five disks per job. Depot Cache is shared per project and explicitly not isolated by branch. On stock GitHub-hosted runners, entries restore only from the same branch or the default branch, which is why cross-job sharing appears to work on main and not on a pull request.
The three usual causes are a cold first run, a cache key that changes every run, and a write that failed silently. Blacksmith documents the first, and a new Depot project starts with an empty builder. For the third, the GitHub cache backend returns an error buildx reports as a reservation failure, which buildx failed to reserve cache reproduces.

articles.title: GitHub Actions on section missing from a workflow file
articles.description:
A GitHub Actions on section missing from a workflow file fails with "No event triggers defined in on", a message with no line or column because there is no key to point at, and it usually comes from a file that was emptied, or had its whole trigger block commented out, to switch it off. GitHub reports such a file instead of ignoring it, so restore an on: block at the root, or stop the workflow properly with gh workflow disable or by deleting the file.

The published schema requires only jobs at the workflow root. The trigger requirement is applied by GitHub, outside the parser that ships in the runner.
Every push to every branch produces a failed check against a workflow you did not think was running. That is the shape worth recognizing, because a workflow with no usable trigger does not quietly sit there: it is evaluated, found unusable and reported, on every push, forever. The file is often one somebody meant to disable. Commenting the whole thing out, emptying it while leaving it in place, or deleting the contents and keeping the name all produce the same result, which surprises people who expected an empty file to be ignored.
``Quoted from susam.net, Minimal GitHub Workflow, a recorded experiment on a zero-byte workflow file
on`



## Common causes

### The trigger block was commented out to disable the workflow

The commonest origin by a distance, and the one place the wording of the edit decides which message you get. Comment out the key along with its events and no key is left, which is this message. Comment out only the events, as below, and the key survives with nothing under it, which the ladder answers differently. Either way the file fails against every push rather than doing nothing, which is the opposite of the intent.



```Illustrative workflow fragment
# the trigger key survived, every event under it did not
on:
#  push:
#    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo hello

A commit that strips the contents and leaves the path in place. The diff reads as a deletion in review, and the zero byte file is still evaluated on every push.
One extra level of indentation puts it inside another key. The YAML is valid, the block looks right in isolation, and the root genuinely has no trigger.
A template, a fragment or an editor configuration file stored in the workflows directory. Everything in that directory is treated as a workflow, so a file that was never meant to be one fails as one.
If it should run, restore a trigger block at the root of the file.
If it should not run for now, disable the workflow rather than editing it.
If it should never run again, delete the file.
If it is not a workflow, move it out of the workflows directory.
Check the indentation of the trigger key against the jobs key. Both belong at column one, and a trigger that is indented further is inside something else regardless of how correct the block under it looks.
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

Disabling leaves the file intact and stops it being considered, which is what commenting out the events was trying to achieve. It is reversible from the same command.
gh workflow disable ci.yml
gh workflow enable ci.yml

Templates and fragments belong beside it, not in it. A directory whose every file is a workflow is one fewer thing to explain to the next person who adds a file there.
Never disable a workflow by commenting out its trigger block.
Treat an emptied workflow file in a diff as a file that still runs.
Keep only real workflows in the workflows directory.
Check that the trigger key and the jobs key sit at the same indentation.
Follow the workflow root definition in the schema that ships in the runner and the list of properties is short: the trigger key, a name, a description, a run name, defaults, env, permissions, concurrency and jobs. Exactly one of them carries the required flag, and it is jobs. The trigger key is listed as an ordinary optional property.
The editor copy of the schema in the language services repository has the same root definition with the same single required property, which is why an editor extension does not warn you about a file with no trigger. Both published parsers will read such a file without objecting.
The refusal therefore happens somewhere else. GitHub evaluates the file when it decides which workflows a push affects, and a file that offers no usable event is reported at that point. That component is not published, so the honest statement is that the rule is GitHub behavior rather than parser behavior.
The message it produces is the one quoted above, and what it leaves out is the diagnosis. There is no file path, no line and no column, which is unusual for this validator: the key is not there to point at. A recorded experiment that walked a workflow file up from zero bytes got those two lines from the empty file, and something else from the next rung, where the key exists with nothing under it. That rung gets the ordinary shape, a position and an unexpected empty value, because an empty value is a value. So the distinction that matters is whether the key survived, and parentheses and numbers in your annotation mean it did.
The rest of this page is the other half: why the file looks fine to every tool you have locally, and which edits produce it.



Layer
Requires a trigger
What it does with a file that has none




YAML parsers generally
no
parses it, no complaint


The published workflow schema
no, only jobs is required
reads it, no complaint


The editor schema copy
no, the same root definition
no warning in the editor


GitHub, when deciding what a push runs
yes
reports it against every push



Three of the four rows are quiet, which is why the failure only ever appears once the file is pushed, and appears on every push after that.
There is widespread advice to quote the trigger key because YAML will otherwise read it as a boolean. That advice has a real origin and it does not apply to this parser, which is worth stating plainly because acting on it wastes time you could spend on the actual cause.
The runner YAML reader resolves plain scalars using the YAML 1.2 core schema, and the source says so in a comment with a link to the specification. Its boolean matcher accepts six spellings and no others: true, True, TRUE, false, False and FALSE. The words on, off, yes and no are not among them, so the trigger key is read as the ordinary string it looks like.
The advice comes from YAML 1.1, where those four words are booleans, and from the many tools that still implement it. A script that loads your workflow with a 1.1 parser really does see a key that is not the trigger key, and linters warn about it for that reason. That is a fact about your tooling, not about GitHub, and quoting the key is harmless but it will not fix a missing trigger.
```YAML 1.2 core schema, as implemented in the runner reader
true   True   TRUE   false   False   FALSE
on:



## The edits that produce it

Commenting out the trigger block is the first. Somebody wants to stop a workflow temporarily, comments out the events and leaves the key, and now the file has a trigger key with nothing under it. Reports of this describe a failure on every push to every branch, which is exactly what it should do, and it is startling because the intent was to make the workflow stop.

Emptying the file is the second. A commit that removes the contents of a workflow and leaves a zero byte file behind produces the same thing, and the diff looks like a deletion, so reviewers read it as one.

Indentation is the third and the least obvious. A trigger key that has drifted one level in, so that it sits under something else rather than at the root, is a perfectly valid mapping in the wrong place. The root then has no trigger key, and the misplaced one is a stray key inside whatever now contains it.

The remedy for all three is the same and it is not to edit the trigger block. If you want a workflow to stop running, delete the file or disable the workflow, which are both operations that leave nothing behind to be evaluated on every push.



```shell
# stop a workflow without leaving a file that fails on every push
gh workflow disable ci.yml

# or remove it entirely
git rm .github/workflows/ci.yml

A workflow with no usable trigger does not produce a run with jobs in it, so there is no log to capture. The observable artifact is a failed check attached to a commit, and a capture of ours would show our repository name and our commit, which carries no information about yours.
The parts of this page that can be established from published sources are established from them: the single required property at the workflow root is read out of both copies of the schema, and the six boolean spellings are read out of the reader that implements the YAML 1.2 core schema. The part that cannot be, which is what GitHub does with the file, is labeled as GitHub behavior rather than dressed up as parser behavior.
Nothing here is repairable by a runner. No runner is ever handed this workflow, because the decision is made before any job is created.
Not by the published schema, which marks only the jobs key as required at the workflow root, and the editor copy of that schema agrees. The requirement is applied by GitHub when it decides which workflows a push affects, which is why no local tool warns you.
Not for GitHub. The runner reader follows the YAML 1.2 core schema and its boolean matcher accepts only true, True, TRUE, false, False and FALSE. The advice comes from YAML 1.1 parsers, which many other tools still use, so quoting helps those tools and changes nothing here.
Because every file in the workflows directory is evaluated when a push arrives, and one that offers no usable event is reported then. Emptying a file does not remove it from consideration, so the failure repeats on every push until the file is deleted or the workflow is disabled.
No, and the annotation tells you which you have. A key present with an empty value is answered with a line, a column and an unexpected empty value, because an empty value is still a value. The message about no event triggers carries no position at all, which is the state where the key itself is absent.
Disable the workflow, or delete the file. Both leave nothing that has to be evaluated on each push. Commenting out the events is the one option that keeps the file in play while making it unusable.
