Confirm price, duration and current skills measured before you schedule. Local pricing varies, so the official page wins over any blog.
A short exam rewards pacing. Answer short questions first, flag long scenarios, and return to them.
If you are comparing entry-level cloud credentials, AZ-900 vs AWS Cloud Practitioner puts the two fundamentals exams side by side.
We built SecLern around a pattern: people who fail fundamentals exams usually did not run out of hours; they spent them passively. Three weeks of video feels like preparation and leaves you recognizing terms without being able to define them. Microsoft Learn already teaches AZ-900 well, so we do not replace it. What a course cannot do is tell you that you are weak on governance and strong on cloud concepts. The habit that matters is 45 minutes a day plus a short question set, with misses written down.
SecLern's AZ-900 path follows the loop this article describes: answer questions by domain, read why every option is right or wrong, and turn misses into notes and drills. Timed simulations return a readiness grade per domain, so you can see whether you are at the 85% mark before you book. The free tier includes the first module, 30 questions a day, 3 labs and PBQs, and unlimited flashcards, no card needed. Pro is $15 a month or $99 a year with a 7-day trial (card required); Exam Sprint is $29 once for 90 days. See pricing.
Is 2 weeks enough to study for AZ-900?
Yes for many candidates. Two weeks at about 1.5 hours a day is roughly 20 hours, in the middle of the 15 to 25 hour estimate. It is tight from zero with no IT background, where 20 to 30 hours over four to six weeks is more realistic. Book only after two timed simulations at 85% or better in every domain.
How hard is AZ-900 with no IT experience?
It is not technically hard, but it is vocabulary-dense: storage tiers, identity, governance and pricing models arrive faster than you can absorb them. Budget 20 to 30 hours over four to six weeks. There are no prerequisites, and the questions ask you to describe concepts rather than configure anything in the Azure portal.
Can you pass AZ-900 in 3 days?
Only if you already work with Azure. Three days at four hours a day is 12 hours, enough to refresh vocabulary you use weekly and not enough to learn it from scratch. If cloud is new to you, use the three-week plan; a retake costs more than the extra study time.
How many questions are on the AZ-900 exam?
Microsoft does not publish a fixed question count for AZ-900, so there is no number to memorize. Expect multiple-choice and interactive items inside the 45-minute window. Flag long scenarios, answer short questions first, and check the official exam page before you schedule.
Does the AZ-900 certification expire?
No. Microsoft's certification expiration page states that Fundamentals certifications, including Microsoft Certified: Azure Fundamentals, do not expire. That makes AZ-900 a one-time exam rather than an annual commitment, though Microsoft can still retire an exam version and replace it with a newer one.
Should you take AZ-900 or go straight to AZ-104?
Take AZ-900 first if cloud is new to you; it builds the vocabulary AZ-104 assumes. If you already administer Azure subscriptions, networks or identities at work, skip it and start AZ-104, a role-based administrator exam with hands-on expectations. AZ-900 is not a formal prerequisite for AZ-104.

articles.title: Patrones de Arquitectura de Software: Guía Comparativa y su Uso en Frameworks Modernos
articles.description:
Propósito


Identificar las características, ventajas y aplicaciones de los principales patrones de arquitectura de software, y analizar cómo los frameworks modernos los implementan, así como la relación entre las decisiones arquitectónicas y el éxito de un proyecto.
a. Patrón de Capas (Layered)
b. Patrón Cliente-Servidor
c. Patrón Modelo-Vista-Controlador (MVC)
d. Patrón Filtro de Tuberías (Pipes and Filters)
e. Patrón Intermediario (Mediator)
f. Patrón Igual a Igual (Peer-to-Peer)
g. Patrón Bus de Eventos (Event Bus)
h. Patrón Pizarra (Blackboard)
El patrón Pizarra no es simplemente un almacén de datos compartido. Su estructura completa requiere tres componentes fundamentales:
La pizarra (blackboard): contiene el estado del problema y las soluciones parciales.
Las fuentes de conocimiento (knowledge sources): son módulos independientes que leen el estado de la pizarra y contribuyen con nuevas soluciones parciales.
El componente de control (control component o motor heurístico): es el encargado de evaluar el estado actual de la pizarra y decidir qué fuente de conocimiento debe ejecutarse a continuación.
Sin este componente de control, el patrón colapsa y se convierte en un simple repositorio de variables globales o una base de datos compartida, perdiendo su naturaleza de resolución de problemas no determinista. El control es lo que permite que el sistema progrese hacia la solución sin un algoritmo predefinido.
2. Lista Comparativa de Patrones


A continuación se presenta la comparativa de cada patrón con su definición, estructura, ventajas, desventajas y ejemplos de aplicación.
a. Capas (Layered)
Definición: Divide la aplicación en capas horizontales según las responsabilidades; cada capa solo interactúa con la capa adyacente inferior.
Estructura: Capas apiladas presentación → negocio → persistencia → datos. Capas cerradas que obligan a pasar por todas las otras capas; capas abiertas permiten saltos.
Ventajas: Separación clara de responsabilidades; fácil de probar y mantener; curva de aprendizaje baja; es buena para migrar sistemas heredados.
Desventajas: Puede generar capas embudo sin lógica real; añade latencia; dificulta el despliegue independiente; el monolito por capas es rígido.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Aplicaciones web empresariales; sistemas heredados a la nube; ERPs tradicionales; aplicaciones Java EE / Spring MVC.
b. Cliente-Servidor
Definición: Separa roles: el cliente inicia solicitudes, el servidor las procesa y responde.
Estructura: Dos capas, cliente con interfaz y algo de lógica / servidor con datos, o N capas. Servidor con o sin estado.
Ventajas: Datos centralizados; seguridad y respaldos más simples; roles claros; soporta múltiples tipos de clientes.
Desventajas: El servidor central es cuello de botella y punto único de fallo; en dos capas hay alto acoplamiento entre UI y lógica; cambios costosos.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Aplicaciones web; servidores de archivos; sistemas de correo; acceso a bases de datos; FTP, HTTP.
c. Modelo-Vista-Controlador (MVC)
Definición: Separa la aplicación en modelo (datos y reglas), vista (interfaz) y controlador (entrada y flujo).
Estructura: El controlador recibe la entrada y opera el modelo; el modelo notifica a la vista; la vista renderiza. Un modelo puede tener varias vistas.
Ventajas: Separación de preocupaciones, desarrollo en paralelo; pruebas unitarias más fáciles, un ecosistema maduro y reutilización de modelos.
Desventajas: Sobrediseño en apps pequeñas; controladores que se inflan, sincronización vista-modelo requiere mecanismos extra.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Spring MVC; ASP.NET Core MVC; Laravel; Ruby on Rails; Django; AngularJS (versión clásica).
d. Filtro de Tuberías (Pipes and Filters)
Definición: Descompone el procesamiento en filtros independientes conectados por tuberías que transforman datos secuencialmente.
Estructura: Filtros sin estado que reciben, procesan y emiten datos; tuberías que solo conectan y transmiten; sin lógica de enrutamiento.
Ventajas: Altamente modular; filtros reutilizables, reordenables y reemplazables; soporta paralelismo y distribución; escalado por filtro.
Desventajas: Cambios exigen pruebas de extremo a extremo; incompatibilidad de formatos añade sobrecarga; manejo de errores e idempotencia complejos.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Compiladores, análisis léxico/sintáctico; pipelines de datos (ETL); procesamiento de logs; procesamiento de imágenes; Unix pipes.
e. Mediador (Mediator)
Definición: Introduce un componente central que encapsula la comunicación entre objetos, evitando referencias directas entre ellos.
Estructura: El mediador mantiene referencias a los colegas; los colegas solo hablan con el mediador; este enruta, transforma o coordina mensajes.
Ventajas: Reduce drásticamente el acoplamiento muchos-a-muchos; lógica de interacción centralizada; más fácil de modificar y depurar.
Desventajas: El mediador puede volverse un "objeto dios"; centralización crea punto único de fallo; puede convertirse en un cuello de botella.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Diálogos GUI; salas de chat; agentes de servicio en sistemas distribuidos; torres de control aéreo.
f. Igual a Igual (Peer-to-Peer, P2P)
Definición: Cada nodo actúa como cliente y servidor a la vez; no hay control central; los nodos colaboran directamente.
Estructura: Nodos simétricos que mantienen recursos y responden a otros. P2P puro, sin centro, o híbrido, con nodo de descubrimiento.
Ventajas: Escalabilidad excelente, cada nodo añade consumo y servicio; robustez por descentralización, y sin punto único de fallo.
Desventajas: Difícil aplicar seguridad y regulación uniformes; descubrimiento y consistencia complejos; problemas de privacidad y derechos de autor.
Ejemplos de aplicación: BitTorrent; Gnutella; Bitcoin; Skype arquitectura temprana; redes de intercambio de archivos; blockchain.
g. Bus de Eventos (Event Bus)
Definición: Los componentes se comunican asíncronamente mediante eventos publicados en un bus; los emisores y receptores no se conocen.
Estructura: Bus central que distribuye eventos; generadores publican sin esperar respuesta; consumidores se suscriben y procesan asíncronamente. Modelo publicar y suscribir.
Ventajas: Bajo acoplamiento; añadir consumidores no afecta a generadores; soporta asincronía y concurrencia; altamente escalable.
Desventajas: Flujo de control difícil de rastrear; depuración y pruebas complejas; el bus puede ser cuello de botella; cambios de esquema impactan ampliamente.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Eventos de UI; microservicios asíncronos (Kafka, RabbitMQ); IoT; trading financiero; sistemas de notificaciones.
h. Pizarra (Blackboard)
Definición: Varias fuentes de conocimiento independientes colaboran sobre un almacén compartido hasta resolver un problema sin algoritmo determinista.
Estructura: Pizarra con estado y soluciones parciales; fuentes de conocimiento independientes; componente de control que evalúa el estado y decide el orden de activación de las fuentes.
Ventajas: Adecuado para problemas complejos con múltiples estrategias; fuentes desarrollables y reemplazables por separado; sin algoritmo único necesario.
Desventajas: Estado compartido difícil de controlar como variables globales; riesgo de condiciones de carrera; lógica de control compleja.
Ejemplos de aplicación: Reconocimiento de voz; interpretación de imágenes; fusión de recomendadores heterogéneos; sistemas expertos de IA.
Es importante distinguir entre patrones de diseño de software y estilos arquitectónicos de distribución. Spring Boot es un framework que facilita la creación de aplicaciones stand-alone y, por sí solo, tiende a producir monolitos modulares. Los microservicios no son un patrón de diseño de software, sino un estilo arquitectónico de distribución. Spring Boot no "implementa" microservicios; se utiliza dentro de una arquitectura de microservicios, a menudo apoyado por Spring Cloud (Eureka para descubrimiento de servicios, API Gateway para enrutamiento, etc.).
- Spring Boot
Patrones centrales: MVC + Capas (monolito modular). Los microservicios son un estilo arquitectónico de distribución, no un patrón que Spring Boot implemente por sí solo.
Práctica concreta: Spring MVC implementa aplicaciones web en capas; convención sobre configuración reduce código boilerplate. Para microservicios se requiere Spring Cloud, que añade descubrimiento de servicios (Eureka), balanceo de carga, API Gateway y trazabilidad distribuida.
- ASP.NET Core
Práctica concreta: Soporte MVC nativo con límites claros entre controlador, vista y modelo; inyección de dependencias integrada que promueve el desacoplamiento en capas; mecanismo de filtros que encapsula preocupaciones transversales.
- Laravel
Práctica concreta: MVC como núcleo desde su diseño; el motor de plantillas Blade asume la responsabilidad de la vista; Artisan CLI genera esqueletos de controladores, modelos y otros componentes.
- Angular
Práctica concreta: Organiza la interfaz como un árbol de componentes; inyección de dependencias para gestionar servicios; soporta micro-frontend mediante Module Federation / Native Federation.
- React
Práctica concreta: Es una biblioteca de vistas, no impone MVC; Flux y Redux proporcionan gestión de estado con flujo unidireccional; Context API para estado compartido ligero.

  5. Opinión Personal: ¿La Arquitectura Determina el Éxito o Fracaso de un Proyecto?


Sí, considero que la elección de arquitectura es uno de los factores clave del éxito o fracaso de un proyecto, aunque también influyen otros factores o condiciones. La evidencia de la industria, documentada en post-mortems y estudios de casos, muestra que una arquitectura correcta pero mal ejecutada también lleva al fracaso: equipos que eligen una arquitectura limpia pero llenan la capa de lógica de negocio con consultas SQL y anotaciones específicas del framework terminan con capas que no funcionan como tales. Por otro lado, sistemas entregados con arquitecturas simples de tres capas han demostrado ser extremadamente estables y evolucionar durante años. La clave no es la sofisticación de la arquitectura, sino que el equipo entienda y respete sus restricciones, con la guía adecuada.
La arquitectura sirve a los requisitos, al equipo y a las restricciones de tiempo. Un equipo de cinco personas desarrollando una herramienta interna no tiene sentido que adopte P2P; un MVP que necesita validar el mercado rápidamente ve el sobrediseño como un retraso en el aprendizaje. La esencia de la decisión arquitectónica es hacer compensaciones apropiadas bajo las restricciones actuales, no perseguir la solución teóricamente óptima. ASP.NET Core y Laravel son populares precisamente porque encuentran el equilibrio entre una arquitectura suficiente y flexible.
La arquitectura no es un fin en sí mismo, sino una herramienta de gestión de riesgos. La verdadera pregunta no es "¿cuál es la mejor arquitectura?", sino "¿qué riesgos técnicos (escalabilidad, tiempo de mercado, complejidad operativa, costo de mantenimiento) estamos dispuestos a asumir con esta elección para satisfacer los objetivos del negocio?". Una buena elección arquitectónica hace que el cambio sea barato y que los riesgos sean identificables y acotados; una mala elección hace que el cambio sea caro y que los riesgos se materialicen en forma de deuda técnica, retrasos o fallos en producción. Por ello, la arquitectura debe ser entendida, respetada y ajustada según las circunstancias, y su evaluación debe hacerse siempre en función de los riesgos que el negocio está dispuesto a tolerar.

articles.title: pstack 完全ガイド ─AIエージェントに雑なコード     を書かせない技術─
articles.description:
AIエージェントに仕事を頼むと、自信満々の報告と一緒に検証されていない大量のコードが届いて困ったことはありませんか？

AIエージェントを使い始めた人はもちろん、日常的に使いこなしているエンジニアでも、「どうすれば品質を担保できるのか」「どこまで自律的に仕事を任せられるのか」という疑問は共通の課題ではないでしょうか

pstack は、元React コアチームのエンジニア poteto（Lauren Tan）氏が、日々の開発で使っているスキルを公開したものです

本書は、pstackの思想から実践までを体系的に解説した初心者から中上級者までを対象とする実践ガイドです。

単なるスキルの使い方にとどまらず、AIエージェントの仕事の進め方そのものを見直し、検証可能で信頼できる開発ワークフローをどう構築するかまで踏み込みます。

この本を読むと、明日からAIへの仕事の任せ方が変わります

- 寝る前に仕事を頼み、朝には検証済みのPRが作成されている
- AIの「直しました」を、実行結果や動作確認の証拠つきで受け取れる
- コードレビューする必要性が減り、動画やスクショのチェックだけでマージできる
  (機械的な検証を自動化し、人間がレビューすべき範囲を減らせる)
- 属人的なプロンプトの工夫から脱却し、再現性のある開発手順を構築できる

pstackが目指しているのは、AIにたくさんコードを書かせることではありません。書く量を減らし、質を上げることです。

そのために「証拠がなければ完了と認めない」「書いた本人に採点させない」「足す前に引く」といった考え方が、各スキルやプレイブックに組み込まれています。

本書では、入口となる /poteto-mode の使い方とプロンプトの書き方から始め、22のプレイブック、34のスキル、24の原則を一つずつ解説します。

さらに、似たスキルの使い分け、寝ている間にエージェントに仕事を任せる方法、日本語でそのまま使えるプロンプトのレシピ集、よくある失敗と対処法も収録しました。Cursor だけでなく、Claude Code で使うときの違いも説明しています。

初心者にはpstackを迷わず使い始めるための入門書として、中上級者にはAIエージェントの運用や検証戦略を見直すための実践書としてオススメです

articles.title: Why Direct Browser Thumbnail Uploads Fail: CORS, Private Buckets, and Presigned Limits
Fintech Training Artifact Storage Explained Through Private Browser Upload and Signed URLs
articles.description:
The page says training_artifact_receipt_missing. On-call sees a completed training run, an expected object key, and no durable receipt proving that the browser upload became the artifact the next stage will read. This is the operational difference between Supabase Storage, a direct S3 presigned upload, and any other browser-to-storage path: the immediate action is to stop promotion of that run, not to retry an opaque upload and hope.
Short answer: for private fintech training artifacts, use a backend-generated presigned URL, upload bytes directly from the browser, and record a separate receipt before declaring the run complete. Supabase Storage is the easier fit when a frontend team needs an integrated product and self-managed browser origins; direct Amazon S3 or Cloudflare R2 is the better fit when the team needs full storage controls. Infrai is worth trying for private upload and signed-access handoffs when one key and one bill across backend services matter, provided the required CORS policy is already handled outside the frontend team's workflow.
That boundary is deliberate. The storage provider accepts bytes and later serves a private object through signed access. Your application still owns authorization, tenant-to-key mapping, retention intent, and the state transition from "upload authorized" to "artifact accepted." Don't make a presigned URL carry all of those meanings.
The easiest option depends on who owns the browser-to-storage boundary. A React or Next.js page should ask its backend for permission, receive a short-lived signed URL, and send the file directly to storage. That avoids proxying a large training artifact through the application server while keeping the storage credential out of the browser.



Option
Delivery simplicity
Access-control boundary
Better choice when
Main catch




Supabase Storage
Integrated application workflow
Application and storage policies stay close
The frontend team wants one product surface
It is less attractive when storage must remain a provider-neutral boundary


Amazon S3 presigned upload
More infrastructure to configure directly
The platform team controls the storage account
Lifecycle and detailed native controls are requirements
The team owns IAM, CORS, lifecycle, and operational integration


Cloudflare R2 direct browser upload
Direct provider setup
The platform team owns signing and origin policy
R2 is already the chosen object store
Delivery remains coupled to that provider's configuration surface


Google Cloud Storage
Direct provider setup
The platform team controls the cloud project
GCS is a platform standard
It is outside Infrai's listed storage vendor coverage


Infrai
One HTTP surface, with no storage SDK required
The backend authorizes presigning; objects remain private
Multiple backend capabilities should share one credential and billing boundary
Frontend teams cannot self-configure CORS through the exposed capability



Infrai's useful advantage here isn't a claim that object storage has become novel. It is operational consolidation: one key and one bill can cover storage and the other backend services in the same system, instead of adding another credential dashboard and invoice to the runbook. Infrai also exposes one REST API over plain HTTP, with no SDK to install, so any language or runtime can request the handoff. Its public, unauthenticated discovery surface provides the method, path, full request and response schema, billing details, and runnable examples in 10 languages. That reduces a specific runbook risk: the implementation and the operator can inspect the same contract instead of translating between an SDK abstraction and the request that crossed the wire.
The catch is real. Infrai is not suitable when the product depends on frontend-owned CORS changes, public assets, static website hosting, permanent public links, Google Cloud Storage, Backblaze B2, cross-region replication, or bulk cross-cloud migration. Stick with direct S3 or R2 when native control is the priority, and with Supabase Storage when its integrated application model removes more work than a provider boundary would.
The late signal is "the training stage could not open its artifact." By then, the useful question is no longer whether an upload request once succeeded. On-call needs the run ID, tenant ID, unique object key, expected checksum, retention class, and the last confirmed state. Without that receipt, a missing object, an overwritten object, and an uncommitted application record all collapse into the same page. Work backward one transition: the earlier signal should fire when an upload authorization exists but no verified receipt arrives within the expected upload window. That alert points at the handoff, while there is still enough context to act. A second signal should catch a receipt whose object key or checksum does not match the run manifest. Keep promotion blocked in either case. If the authorization record says issued, the object verification says present, and the receipt is absent, the action is to reconcile the application transition; issuing another upload URL would create a second attempt before the first identity is settled.
This is the idempotency reflex: retries may repeat intent, but they must not change identity. Generate a new key for every attempted artifact, such as a tenant prefix followed by a run ID and an artifact ID. Reusing model.bin is unsafe because this capability has neither object versioning nor object lock; a later write can replace the earlier bytes, and there is no built-in recovery of that prior object. There is no conditional If-Match write either, so strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database transaction.
No mystery state.
Receipts decide readiness.
The smallest useful implementation is a backend handler that authorizes the caller, constructs the unique key, and asks for a presigned operation. The example below focuses only on the provider call. It sets the method explicitly, reads the key from the environment, retries HTTP 429 with Retry-After when available, and forwards the provider's JSON unchanged so it doesn't invent response fields.
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func requestPresign(ctx context.Context, bucket, key string) ([]byte, error) {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    route := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}"
    path := strings.ReplaceAll(route, "{bucket}", url.PathEscape(bucket))
    path = strings.ReplaceAll(path, "{key}", url.PathEscape(key))
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, path, strings.NewReader("{}"))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }

        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-time.After(delay):
                continue
            }
        }

        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign request returned %s: %s", resp.Status, body)
        }
        return body, nil
    }

    return nil, fmt.Errorf("presign request remained rate limited")
}

The browser uses the returned presigned URL for the byte transfer and must not attach the Infrai Authorization header to that URL. After upload, the backend should verify the private object and atomically store the receipt before it marks the training run ready. The receipt, not a browser progress bar, closes the gap that the alert watches.
Choose the timer from observed artifact sizes and network conditions, then separate "slow" from "missing." I'm not sure a single threshold will fit both small evaluation bundles and large checkpoints; percentile distributions split by artifact class would resolve that. Start the warning below the page threshold, and require the hard failure to persist long enough for a verification attempt to complete. Don't tune from the average alone. A large checkpoint on a European mobile connection and a small evaluation bundle are different operational populations, and combining them can produce a threshold that is useful for neither. Record authorization age, bytes expected, artifact class, receipt state, and verification outcome, then review the distribution after a real delivery window before moving the page.
For this system, every receipt should carry an explicit retention class and deletion due date. Configure storage lifecycle from that class, but retain the application record that explains why the object exists and when deletion was requested. The capability's lifecycle minimum is one day, so it does not fit hour-level expiry. Multipart fragments also have no automatic cleanup rule, which means aborted multipart work needs an owned cleanup process.
Use key prefixes for tenant, training run, and artifact class because server-side metadata search is unavailable and listing can filter only by prefix. Prefixes help operators narrow a recovery check; they are not authorization. The backend must still derive the allowed tenant scope from the authenticated principal and must never accept an arbitrary bucket or key from the browser.
There is a harder limit for regulated retention. No versioning, object lock, or WORM control means this path alone cannot prove that a financial training artifact was never altered. If policy requires immutable evidence, use an external immutable archive or a specialist storage setup with the required controls. Also verify region availability, data-processing terms, and regulatory fit directly before choosing a European deployment; the available material does not establish that compliance decision, and your mileage may vary by regulator and data class.
Private downloads through signed URLs fit review and controlled model promotion. Public-read access does not: public URLs remain null, so this isn't an image host or a static-site origin.
The final failure mode is the monitor itself. A threshold shorter than ordinary upload time pages on healthy transfers; a threshold longer than the promotion deadline reports the incident after the damage. Alert first on the broken state transition, then add duration. Route warnings to the owning queue and reserve a page for a blocked promotion or a sustained backlog with an approaching deadline.
Test the monitor with three cases: an authorization with no receipt, a receipt with the wrong expected identity, and a completed verified receipt. The first two must block promotion. The third must stay quiet. Review false positives by artifact class and connection profile, because suppressing noisy pages globally can hide the one class whose delivery window actually regressed.
This is also where the provider choice shows up in the runbook. A direct cloud setup exposes more controls but leaves more configuration and credentials with the team. The consolidated HTTP boundary reduces that integration surface, yet it does not take ownership of application state, CORS policy, immutable retention, or compliance review. Keep those lines explicit and the page becomes actionable.
If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage comparison and signed-upload guide, then confirm the live discovery schema before implementing the request.

How Long to Study for Security+? Hours by Background
articles.description:
This article was first published on the SecLern blog.
How long to study for Security+ depends on your starting point. Most candidates should plan on 100–150 focused hours, which is roughly 7–15 weeks at 10–15 hours a week. Complete beginners usually need 150–200 hours, or 10–20 weeks at the same pace. Those are planning estimates, not CompTIA requirements. For the SY0-701 exam, CompTIA's certification page lists a maximum of 90 questions in 90 minutes and a passing score of 750 on a 100–900 scale.
Most candidates need 100–150 focused study hours for CompTIA Security+; candidates starting from zero usually need 150–200 hours.
Weeks = total focused hours ÷ realistic weekly hours, so a 120-hour plan at 12 hours a week takes 10 weeks.

CompTIA recommends Network+ plus two years of IT administration experience with a security focus before Security+.
SecurityX (CAS-005) and AWS Security Specialty are separate exams, so Security+ hour ranges do not transfer to either.
Plan on 100–150 focused study hours if you already work in IT, and 150–200 hours if you are starting from zero.
The table converts those ranges into calendar time at three common weekly loads. They are planning estimates based on how much of the exam is new at each starting point, not figures CompTIA publishes.

CompTIA's own baseline is higher than most candidates expect: the Security+ certification page recommends CompTIA Network+ plus two years of IT administration experience with a security focus before you sit the exam. If you do not have that background yet, use the beginner or help-desk row.
The hours model survives version changes; the syllabus does not. Study the objectives for the exact code you book, and confirm that code and the current exam price on CompTIA's page before you set a date. If you are weighing SY0-701 against SY0-801, this version comparison covers what changed.
Because a two-week pass and a six-month grind usually describe different people, not different tricks.
Two weeks at 8 hours a day is 112 hours. That sits inside the experienced-candidate range and far outside the beginner range, and fast-pass posts often leave out the 8 hours a day. The inputs that actually move the calendar:
Prior knowledge. A help-desk technician already knows authentication, permissions and network basics. A career changer meets all of it at once.
Weekly hours. 15 hours a week for 10 weeks and 5 hours a week for 30 weeks are the same 150 hours with very different retention.
Practice quality. Answering questions and reviewing misses shows you what you do not know; rewatching videos mostly feels productive.
Exam version. Objectives change between codes, so advice written for a retired exam may not match the one you book.
Reschedules. Some "six months" stories include a moved exam date.
None of that means the fast posts are lying. It means their calendar was built on a baseline you cannot read from a screenshot. Run a diagnostic, fix a weekly schedule, then pick the date.
Most working adults should study 10–15 focused hours a week; at that load, a 120-hour plan takes 8 to 12 weeks.
The formula is weeks = total focused hours ÷ realistic weekly hours. A 120-hour plan at 12 hours a week is 10 weeks. The same plan at 6 hours a week is 20 weeks, which is why your weekly availability, not the total, should drive the exam date.

Focused hours means active work: answering questions, doing labs and PBQs, reviewing your error log, and sitting timed practice. A video course playing in the background does not count, even though the clock runs the same way.
Split the load across five or six sessions and protect one block for reviewing what you missed. If the exam is already booked, set aside the final 10–14 days for timed practice and weak-domain review, then divide the remaining hours across the domains by weight. How to study while working full time has a schedule built for the 7–10 hour row.
With no IT experience, plan on 150–200 focused hours: about 15–20 weeks at 10 hours a week, or 10–14 weeks at 15 hours a week.
"No experience" has a specific meaning here. It means no help-desk or IT support work, no networking foundation, and no recent security coursework. If that describes you, the first 20 to 30 hours go to vocabulary and networking basics, because exam-style questions are not useful until terms like hashing, VLAN and least privilege mean something.
A sequence that works: skim the official objectives for your exam code, learn core security concepts, refresh networking (protocols, ports, subnetting), move into threats and architecture, then operations, and finish with timed practice.
Book after your practice scores are stable, not when you finish a video course. A readiness check that names your weakest domain is a better gate than finishing a playlist.
Three to five months is a normal timeline from zero. A longer calendar only helps when the hours inside it are active.
Allocate study hours in roughly the same proportions as the exam weights, so Security Operations gets the largest block at 28% of SY0-701.
The weights below come from CompTIA's Security+ page. The hour column is arithmetic on a 120-hour plan: an example allocation, not an official formula.

Security Operations is the largest domain, and it is also where monitoring, log analysis and many PBQ-style tasks live, so give it the biggest block and the most lab time. General Security Concepts is the smallest at 12%, but it supplies the vocabulary the other four domains assume, so beginners should not treat it as a warm-up.
The weights are a starting point, not the plan. Once you have practice results by domain, move hours toward whatever is lowest. Equal hours for every domain is usually the wrong split. Verify the weights against the objectives for your exam code, because CompTIA can rename domains and shift percentages between versions.

A 12-week plan at 10–12 focused hours a week lands inside the 120–150 hour range for candidates with some IT background, and it leaves two full weeks for timed practice.
Weeks 1–2: objectives and vocabulary. Read the official objectives for your exam code end to end, then start core security concepts and a networking refresh. Aim for 10–12 hours a week and write your own definition for every term you meet.
Weeks 3–5: threats, vulnerabilities, mitigations, architecture. Those two domains are 40% of SY0-701, so they get three weeks. Add hands-on labs and PBQs instead of rewatching videos, and read how to actually pass the performance questions before your first one.
Weeks 6–8: security operations. Monitoring, incident response and vulnerability management. Answer questions by domain and keep an error log with the reason you missed each one.
Weeks 9–10: program management and oversight, plus weak domains. The 20% domain is easy to postpone and easy to lose points on. Spend the rest of these two weeks on whatever your practice results put at the bottom.
Weeks 11–12: timed full exams. Two or three full simulations under the real time limit. Review every wrong answer the same day and stop adding new topics.
Compress to 8 weeks only if you already have networking or security work behind you: keep the order, give operations two weeks and program management one. Stretch to 16 weeks by adding two weeks to threats and architecture and two to weak-domain review. The final two weeks stay timed practice either way.
One month is enough only if you already have Network+ or CCNA-level networking, or security work experience, and can study 15–20 or more hours a week.
The math is unforgiving for beginners. Four weeks at 10 hours a week is 40 hours. Four weeks at 20 hours a week is 80 hours, which sits at the very bottom of the experienced range and is less than half of the 150–200 hour beginner range.
The risks in a one-month sprint are predictable: memorizing terms without being able to apply them, skipping PBQs because they take longer than multiple-choice questions, and burning out in the final week. The riskiest move is booking on a practice score that is still climbing.
If your exam is already on the calendar and you are short on hours, rescheduling costs less than a retake. If you cannot move it, spend what is left on timed practice and your two weakest domains rather than trying to cover everything once.
You are ready to book when you can explain each official objective in your own words and your timed practice scores have held steady across several attempts.
Coverage. You have read every objective for your exam code and can say something specific about each one.
Stable scores. Two or three timed practice exams land in the same range. One good mock is noise.
Hands-on reps. You have done labs and PBQs, not only multiple-choice questions.
A shrinking error log. Your reasons for missing questions have shifted from "never seen this" to "misread the question."
Domain balance. No domain sits far below the others.
SecLern's free 10-question Security+ readiness check returns a score and your weakest domain without an email or a card, which is enough to decide between booking now and adding three weeks.
Once you decide, book through CompTIA's official page, where the exam code, price and appointment details live.
No. SecurityX and AWS Certified Security Specialty are separate exams with their own objectives, and Security+ hour ranges do not transfer to either.
CompTIA SecurityX (CAS-005) is a separate, expert-level CompTIA certification, and CompTIA's SecurityX page publishes its own objectives and exam details. AWS Certified Security Specialty is an AWS exam, not a CompTIA one; the AWS Certified Security Specialty page lists its own domains, and your study time depends heavily on how much hands-on AWS work you already do.
Use the same method: estimate hours from your background, divide by realistic weekly hours, then weight the domains. Just get the right objectives and practice questions for that exam. For the AWS exam, AWS Certified Security Specialty: SCS-C03 explained covers the scope and objectives.
We built SecLern around a boring observation: the problem is usually not a shortage of hours. It is that the hours were passive. A 14-hour video course feels like studying, and it is comfortable, but it never tells you which domains you can actually answer questions about. Our advice is to spend one hour before you pick a date: take a short diagnostic, log every miss by domain, and let that shape the calendar. The hour ranges in this article are not a personality test. Ten hours a week with no background is an honest 20-week runway. Fifteen hours a week with a CCNA is an honest 8 weeks. What is dishonest is booking a date and hoping the material absorbs by osmosis.
SecLern's CompTIA Security+ (SY0-701) study page turns this hours model into daily work: original practice questions with an explanation for every answer, browser-based labs and PBQs, and full timed simulations with readiness grades. The free tier needs no card and includes the first module of the path, 30 questions a day, 3 labs and PBQs, and unlimited flashcards. Pro is $15 a month or $99 a year with a 7-day trial (card required), and Exam Sprint is $29 once for 90 days of Pro-level access if your date is already booked. Details on pricing.
How long does it take to study for Security+ with no experience?
With no IT experience, plan on 150–200 focused hours for Security+. At 10 hours a week that is 15–20 weeks, or roughly 3.5 to 5 months; at 15 hours a week it drops to 10–14 weeks. The first 20 to 30 hours go to vocabulary and networking basics before exam-style questions pay off. Confirm the objectives for your exam code on CompTIA's page.
How many hours a day should I study for Security+?
CompTIA publishes no official daily number for Security+. Most working adults do well with 10–15 focused hours a week spread over five or six sessions, which is roughly 1.5 to 2.5 hours per session, plus one review block. Short daily sessions beat one long weekend cram because you retain more of what you actively practiced.
Can I pass Security+ in two weeks?
You can pass Security+ in two weeks only with a strong head start. Two weeks at 8 hours a day is 112 hours, which fits the range for experienced admins and security staff. A beginner needs 150–200 hours, so two weeks would mean 11 to 14 hours every single day. Take a readiness check before you commit to a sprint.
How long does it take to study for SecurityX?
No Security+ hour estimate transfers to SecurityX. SecurityX (CAS-005) is a separate, expert-level CompTIA certification with its own objectives, so start from CompTIA's SecurityX page, estimate how much of that material is genuinely new to you, and divide by your weekly hours. Plan it from its own objectives, not by scaling Security+ numbers.
Is AWS Security Specialty study time the same as Security+?
No. AWS Certified Security Specialty is an AWS exam with its own domains, and it assumes working knowledge of AWS services, while Security+ is vendor-neutral and covers five broad domains. If you build in AWS daily your hours will be lower; if you do not, budget substantial lab time. Check the objectives on AWS's exam page.
How long does it take to study for cybersecurity overall?
There is no single number for cybersecurity overall, because it is a sequence rather than one exam. Most people build fundamentals with CompTIA A+ or Network+, then move to Security+, and the total depends on your starting point and the hours you can sustain each week. Plan the next exam, not the whole career.

articles.title: Why "I'll Fix It Later" Is the Most Permanent Lie in Software
articles.description:
Imagine this. You are fixing a critical bug in production. You trace the error back to a specific file, scroll down, and find a comment left by a previous developer.
It says: // TODO: This is a temporary hack. Refactor this later.
You check the git blame. The comment is from 2019. The author of that comment was... you.
Welcome to the club. We’ve all left that comment. We’ve all promised ourselves, "I'll just ship this to fix the immediate issue, and I'll clean it up next sprint." But next sprint never comes.
This is the story of how our codebases slowly become haunted houses, and why "I'll fix it later" are the most permanent words in software engineering.
The Loan We Take From Our Future Selves
Like any loan, it accrues interest. And in software, the interest rate is brutal.
A quick hack to bypass a slow database query? That might save you 2 hours today. But next month, when traffic spikes and the app crashes, that "temporary" hack will cost the team 3 days of panicked refactoring and late-night rollbacks.
Here is the uncomfortable taxonomy of the technical debt we all create:
Type of Debt    How It Starts   The Real Cost
javascript
What happened next: The demo was a success. The ticket to "remove the hack" was created. Then it was moved to the next sprint. Then it was deprioritized. Three years later, someone discovers that a specific subset of production users are receiving fake mockData because nobody remembered the environment variable check.
Why do we do this to ourselves?
Business pressure: The PM needs the feature by Friday. The "right" way takes two weeks. The "hack" takes two days.
The "It Works" fallacy: The code compiles, the tests pass, and the user gets their feature. The invisible cost of the mess is deferred.
Fear of the unknown: Refactoring a working (but ugly) system feels risky. What if we break it? It's easier to just build on top of the mess.
How do we stop the bleeding?
Make it visible.


The Boy Scout Rule.


Fix it when you touch it.


Automate the cleanup.



Let's discuss
What is the oldest // TODO comment you've ever found in a codebase? Did you fix it, or did you just walk away?
Does your team have a dedicated "Tech Debt" sprint, or is it just a myth you tell juniors?
What's the most catastrophic consequence of a "temporary fix" you've ever witnessed in production?
Let’s hear the horror stories. Because sometimes, the scariest ghost in the machine is the one you created five years ago.

articles.title: Verified MRR vs self-reported revenue: designing a startup database where AI explains numbers, never invents them
articles.description:
I am building MRRSignal, a public startup revenue database ranked by payment-provider-verified MRR. This is the design problem I keep coming back to: in a product about financial facts, the boundary between a fact and an explanation has to be structural, not a disclaimer in the footer.
A generated paragraph can be useful. It should never quietly become the source of a number.
Most startup revenue on the internet is self-reported. A founder posts a screenshot or a milestone, and readers decide whether to believe it. MRRSignal moves the source: revenue is read from the founder's connected payment provider through a read-only key, encrypted with AWS KMS. A founder cannot replace the figure with a number typed into a profile.
That makes the origin of the number explicit. It does not make the number self-explanatory - a good page still has to say what metric it shows, what period it covers, and when it was refreshed.
MRRSignal produces three different things, and the interface treats them differently:
Verified figures - revenue read from the connected payment provider. This is source data.
A statistical revenue projection - a modelled path, clearly an estimate.
A weekly AI outlook - generated text that explains the verified inputs in words.
The rule is simple: nothing an AI writes changes the revenue number or a startup's rank. Projections and outlooks sit downstream of verified data, and the UI labels them so a reader never confuses an estimate with a fact.
Startup communities are global, but most revenue tools assume one payment provider and one currency. MRRSignal supports 49 payment providers - global services like Stripe, Braintree, Chargebee and Paddle alongside regional ones such as Razorpay - and normalizes everything to USD. Founders compare on the same scale without being forced onto the same billing stack. Geography should not look like a data-quality problem.
Public transparency is not the same as publishing everything. Listing is opt-in, and founders choose between an exact MRR figure and a revenue band. A band is enough to find peers at your stage without revealing more than you want. Connecting a provider for your own dashboard never silently becomes consent to a public profile.
If you were designing this interface, how would you make source facts, statistical projections and AI-generated explanations visibly different - without burying the user in disclaimers?
I am the founder of MRRSignal. You can see the product at https://mrrsignal.com - it is free to list during beta.

articles.title: 6 Critical F5 BIG-IP Flaws: Affected Versions and Fixes
articles.description:
Last updated: 22 November 2026. F5 disclosed these flaws on 18 November 2026 and revised some advisories on 19 November, so details may have changed since. I could not open F5's own support articles from my environment, so the facts below come from security vendors, government advisories and news reports that cite F5. SeeHow this was checked.
On 18 November 2026, F5 published advisories for six critical vulnerabilities in the data plane of BIG-IP, the part that handles live traffic. All six are stack-based buffer overflows. An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM), which interrupts traffic until it restarts, and F5 says the flaws may also allow remote code execution. F5 lists no workaround. The fix is an engineering hotfix. Each flaw needs a specific feature on a virtual server, which means you can check whether you are exposed without guessing.
Six CVEs, all rated 9.8 (CVSS 3.1) and 9.3 (CVSS 4.0).
No authentication needed, but each needs a trigger configuration on a virtual server.
The management interface is not the attack path, so locking it down does not help.
No exploitation has been reported by F5 at the time of the sources I read, and the CVEs were not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog when one vendor checked.
Fixes are engineering hotfixes only. No scheduled release containing them was listed.



CVE
F5 article
Trigger on a virtual server
Product




CVE-2026-123637
K000163937
APM per-request policy containing both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents
BIG-IP APM


CVE-2026-121805
K000163946
iRule using PEM::subscriber on client traffic
BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes, CNF


CVE-2026-120292
K000163940
HTTP profile plus an iRule using MR::message route

All BIG-IP modules, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes


CVE-2026-120285
K000163939
HTTP profile plus an iRule using PSC::ip_address

All BIG-IP modules, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes, CNF


CVE-2026-116953
K000163941
iRule using GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic
All BIG-IP modules, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes


CVE-2026-120722
K000163945
iRule using DNS::scrape on client traffic
BIG-IP DNS, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes



Five of the six are iRule commands. A device that does not use these commands, and does not run the APM policy combination, does not meet the trigger. That is the most useful fact in the whole advisory, and it also means the answer is in your own configuration.
A note on the count: most sources, including H-ISAC and the UK NHS alert, say six critical flaws. BleepingComputer's article names five (it leaves out DNS::scrape, CVE-2026-120722) and describes a sixth, CVE-2026-126822, as a separate high-severity APM SAML flaw. The Canadian Cyber Centre lists K articles for all six critical CVEs above. I treat six as the count.
The Canadian Cyber Centre advisory lists affected versions as "prior to" the fixed build:



Branch
Fixed build




BIG-IP 21.1.0
BIGIP-21.1.0.4.0.19.3-ENG


BIG-IP 17.5.0 to 17.5.1
BIGIP-17.5.1.11.0.61.12-ENG (or BIGIP-17.5.1.10.0.80.35-ENG on specific starting builds)


BIG-IP 17.1.0 to 17.1.3
BIGIP-17.1.3.7.0.21.4-ENG (or BIGIP-17.1.3.6.0.14.20-ENG on a specific starting build)


BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes 2.2 / 2.3 / 2.4
BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1, BNK-2.4.2-EHF1


BIG-IP CNF 2.2 / 2.3 / 2.4
CNF-2.2.5-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1, CNF-2.4.2-EHF1



Which hotfix build you get depends on your current build, and F5 documents that mapping in K000164239. Do not pick a build from this table alone. BIG-IQ, F5OS, F5 Distributed Cloud, NGINX and F5 AI Gateway are reported as not affected. F5 does not evaluate versions at End of Technical Support, so treat those as exposed if a trigger is configured. If you run a custom engineering hotfix today, you need a new one from F5 Support.
F5 also says engineering hotfixes do not get the extensive QA of scheduled releases and carry no warranty. Plan a maintenance window with a rollback, test on a standby, and do not assume a hotfix is a drop-in.
The steps below follow the read-only checks described by Rescana, which is a security vendor and not F5. Run them on the device with an account that can read the configuration.
Check the version and provisioned modules:




tmsh show sys version
tmsh list sys provision one-line

Export every iRule and search for the five commands:




tmsh -q -c 'cd /; list ltm rule recursive' > /var/tmp/irules.txt

I wrote a small script for the search and ran it against a sample file with one rule per command, plus near-miss lines. It matched all five commands (and a commented-out mention) and ignored MR::message_foo and DNS::scrapeX:
#!/bin/sh
# Usage: f5-irule-scan.sh irules.txt
# A hit means "review this rule", not "this device is exploitable".
f="${1:?usage: $0 irules.txt}"
grep -nE '(PEM::subscriber|MR::message[[:space:]]+route|PSC::ip_address|GENERICMESSAGE::route|DNS::scrape)([^A-Za-z0-9_:]|$)' "$f"

3:        set s [PEM::subscriber config ]
8:        MR::message route
13:        log local0. "ip [PSC::ip_address]"
18:        GENERICMESSAGE::route "pool1"
23:        DNS::scrape
28:        # old: PEM::subscriber was removed

The script exits 1 when it finds nothing. That is not a clean bill of health on its own: rules created by automation may live in /config/bigip.conf or /config/partitions/*/bigip.conf, and the APM trigger is a policy, not an iRule. I tested the script on sample text, not on a real BIG-IP export.
Find out which virtual servers use the matching rules, and whether the HTTP profile is on the same virtual server for the two HTTP-profile flaws:




tmsh -q -c 'cd /; list ltm virtual recursive rules profiles destination'

For APM, open the Visual Policy Editor and look for a per-request policy that contains both the Client Information and Endpoint Security agents, then list which virtual servers use per-request policies:




tmsh -q -c 'cd /; list ltm virtual recursive per-flow-request-access-policy'

On Kubernetes, export your iRule resources from Git or with kubectl and run the same search, and record the BNK or CNF version for each cluster.
I did not run any of the tmsh commands, because I have no BIG-IP to test on. Check the syntax on your version before using them in a runbook.
Rank devices by exposure. A matching virtual server that faces the internet or a partner network comes first.
Get the hotfix build for your branch and current build from F5, using K000164239.
Patch the standby of each high-availability pair, fail over, verify with tmsh show sys version, then patch the former active unit.
If you cannot patch yet, the only precondition-removing options are to detach or rewrite the matching iRule or to restrict source addresses to the affected virtual server. F5 lists no mitigation, so this is vendor-neutral advice from Rescana. Test it first, because those iRule commands usually do real work, and removing an APM posture check weakens a security control.
Make sure failover works. HA reduces the impact of a TMM crash, but the peer runs the same configuration, so it does not remove the flaw.
No indicators of compromise have been published. These are monitoring leads from Rescana:
TMM restarts. Core files go to /shared/core, and logs are in /var/log/tmm and /var/log/ltm. Alert on any restart and on unexpected failovers.
Repeated restarts tied to one client source or one virtual server deserve a call to F5 Support.
After a crash, review configuration change logs, /var/log/audit, and any new or altered iRules.
If you suspect compromise, collect a QKView and the core files before rebooting, then rotate TLS keys, certificates and stored credentials.
Because the possible impact includes code execution, a crash is worth treating as an incident until you know why it happened.
F5 disclosed more than the six critical issues that day. Three more APM TMM crashes (CVE-2026-125272, CVE-2026-126822 and CVE-2026-121812) are fixed by the same hotfixes. Three others are fixed in scheduled releases 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6: CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8) and CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST token expiry, 8.1). For the iControl SOAP issue, F5's listed mitigation is limiting access to trusted networks, and that can break high-availability setups if you block self-IPs.
A different APM flaw, CVE-2026-94127, was disclosed on 22 September 2026 and exploited. It is a separate heap-based issue with a different trigger and is not one of these six. If you did not patch that one, start there.
Yes, per F5, but only against a virtual server that has the trigger feature configured.
No. These are data-plane issues. F5 says the management interface is not exposed. Restricting who can reach the affected virtual server does.
F5 lists none for the six critical flaws. Only engineering hotfixes are available.
F5 has not said so in the sources I read, and one vendor reported no public exploit code and no KEV listing as of 18 November. That can change quickly. Check CISA's catalog and F5's advisories again before you set your patch timeline.
BIG-IQ, F5OS, F5 Distributed Cloud, NGINX products and F5 AI Gateway are reported as not affected by these six.
Apache mod_http2 CVE-2026-119618
Windows 11 Narrator Lock Screen Zero-Day (FastUnlock)
composer audit: Find Vulnerable Dependencies
22 November 2026: first version.
To recheck on each update: F5's advisories (K000164058 and K000164239), any change to the affected product lists, CISA KEV status, reports of exploitation, and a scheduled release that includes the fixes.
The Hacker News: F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCE
Rescana: F5 BIG-IP iRule and APM flaws, patch now
Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: F5 security advisory AV26-1178
BleepingComputer: F5 releases emergency patches for critical BIG-IP RCE flaws
H-ISAC Vulnerability Bulletin: Six Critical F5 BIG-IP Flaws Could Lead to RCE

articles.title: Figma MCP with Claude Code: What 15,280 Calls Taught Me
articles.description:
Originally published on pzhydkykh.com.
Figma MCP lets Claude Code read and edit Figma files through the Model Context Protocol. I design and build websites with Claude Code every day, so I counted every Figma MCP call it made for me from 14 July to 17 November 2026: 15,280 calls. Almost all of them drew into Figma. The design-to-code tool most guides are about ran 14 times.
From 14 July to 17 November 2026 Claude Code made 15,280 Figma MCP calls in my sessions, across two servers.
Figma Console MCP, which works through the Desktop Bridge plugin, made 14,059 of them in 143 sessions; figma_execute alone ran 9,994 times.
The official Figma MCP server made 1,195 calls in 19 sessions, and get_design_context, its design-to-code tool, only 14.
About one call in three was a screenshot: 3,429 of them, because every drawing gets checked before I see it.
Writing to the canvas through the official server is in beta, free during the beta and planned as a usage-based paid feature.
Every Claude Code session leaves a transcript on disk, and every tool call Claude makes is in it with the tool's name. I wrote a short script that reads all my transcripts from 14 July to 17 November 2026 and counts the calls whose tool belongs to a Figma MCP server, by server, by tool and by session.
The work behind those sessions is ordinary studio work: client websites on Framer and Astro, my own site, Figma screens for clients, blog covers and LinkedIn images. One limit: the count shows what Claude called, not how good the result was. Where I can point to the result, I do.
I used two Figma MCP servers side by side. Figma Console MCP is a community server that talks to Figma Desktop through a plugin called Desktop Bridge. The official Figma MCP server is Figma's own, connected to Claude Code over HTTP.

figma_execute 9,994, figma_capture_screenshot 3,062, figma_take_screenshot 367, figma_list_open_files 291

The split is not about quality. The console server runs any Plugin API code I need in the file that is open on my Mac, which suits long drawing scripts. The official server has its own write tool, use_figma, and Figma's own docs still say that "Writing to the canvas is currently in beta and free to use during the beta period." The same page adds that it will eventually become a usage-based paid feature.
Most guides to Figma MCP with Claude Code start from a finished design and turn it into code. My numbers point the other way. figma_execute, the tool that runs Plugin API code inside the file, made 9,994 calls: that is Claude drawing frames, text, shapes and auto layout into Figma, not reading them out.
The second biggest group is screenshots, 3,429 on the console server and 268 on the official one. That is my working loop, not waste. Claude draws, takes a screenshot of the frame, looks for overlaps, clipped text and spacing that is off, fixes it and checks again. Roughly one screenshot for every three drawing calls is what it takes for a frame to be ready for my eyes.
Why draw in Figma at all, when Claude Code could write the page straight away? Because I prefer to show a Figma file first. A desktop screen, a phone screen and a board of states are faster to discuss and change than a deployed page, and the client can leave comments on the exact spot. Code comes after the design is approved.
Here is the real work behind the count, all of it public:
Every cover on this blog. One script, covers.js, holds a flat geometric drawing per article. Claude runs it in my Figma file through the bridge and exports each frame as a 1,000 px PNG; when the bridge is off, a small renderer draws the same script without Figma, which is how this article's cover was made.
LinkedIn post images. The images and carousels for my posts 01, 03, 04, 06 and 07 were built into the same Figma file by small builder scripts, then exported as images and PDFs.
The common thread: Claude writes a script once, and the script draws the same way every time. When a cover looks off, I fix the drawing in the script and run it again, instead of nudging shapes by hand.
get_design_context is the official tool for turning a selected Figma layer into code. Figma describes it as the tool that "Gets the design context for a layer or selection in Figma." By default it returns React and Tailwind. In four months it ran 14 times in my sessions, and get_metadata another 14.
The reason is how I build. Most of my sites are on Framer, where the design is rebuilt natively on the Framer canvas, or on Astro, where Claude writes components against the site's own tokens and existing components. For those, a screenshot of the approved frame and the design tokens tell Claude more than generated React it would have to rewrite anyway. Design to code still matters for me, but it is a small part of the Figma work, not the core of it.
These are the problems that cost me real time, so you can skip them:
The bridge must be open in the right file. Figma Console MCP talks only to files where the Desktop Bridge plugin is running. When the plugin was open in another file, Claude drew into that file. I now pass the file key with every call and check the list of open files first.
"Cannot unwrap symbol". When a result holds figma.mixed, for example the font size of a text with mixed styles, returning it from the plugin fails with this error. Convert such values to plain strings or numbers before you return them.
Only a few localhost ports. The plugin can only fetch from localhost ports 9223 to 9232. My covers script and its exports go through a small local file server on port 9228 for that reason.
A write tool that is not there. On the Figma forum, users report that use_figma or generate_figma_design is missing from the tool list while read tools work. In a February 2026 thread the fix that worked for several users was adding the remote server to Claude Code directly with claude mcp add instead of using a connector.
No new images and only cloud fonts. Figma's docs say use_figma cannot add new images on its own and fonts must be uploaded to your Figma account; fonts installed only on your computer are not available.
If I set up Figma MCP with Claude Code from scratch today, I would do it in this order:
Add the official server directly: claude mcp add --transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp, then sign in when Claude Code asks. It covers reading designs and, during the beta, writing to the canvas.
Load Figma's figma-use skill before drawing. In my skill count it was called 11 times and figma-generate-design 4 times; both carry the Plugin API rules that keep drawings in real auto layout.
Add a bridge server when you need full Plugin API control in an open desktop file, such as running a long drawing script, and always pass the file key.
Make Claude check its own work. Ask for a screenshot after every drawing step and a fix before it reports back. That is where my 3,429 screenshots went.
Keep drawings in scripts. A script you can rerun beats a hundred one-off prompts, and it makes the output the same every time.
I wrote up which Claude Code skills actually get called in Best Claude Code skills for web design. If you would rather have the website itself designed in Figma and built this way, I design and build Framer and Astro + Sanity sites for AI, fintech and B2B startups.
Figma MCP is a set of Model Context Protocol servers that let an AI agent such as Claude Code read Figma files and, with the write tools, create and edit content in them. Figma runs an official server, and community servers such as Figma Console MCP work through a desktop plugin.
Run claude mcp add --transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp in your terminal and sign in to Figma when Claude Code asks. Several users on the Figma forum found that the write tools only appeared after adding the server this way rather than through a connector.
Yes. The official server's use_figma tool runs Plugin API code in your file, and bridge servers such as Figma Console MCP do the same through a desktop plugin. In my sessions, drawing into Figma made up almost all of 15,280 Figma MCP calls.
Figma says writing to the canvas is in beta and free during the beta period, and that it will eventually become a usage-based paid feature. Check Figma's developer docs for your plan and seat before you rely on it.
Usually the server was added through a connector or an older install. Remove old Figma MCP entries, add the remote server directly with claude mcp add, sign in again and restart Claude Code. A Figma staff reply on the forum adds that writing needs a Full seat with edit access.
It can be, and get_design_context returns React and Tailwind by default. In my own work it ran only 14 times in four months, because on Framer and Astro sites a screenshot of the approved frame and the design tokens are usually enough.

articles.title: I distilled 65 viral short dramas into a "writing DNA" and built an AI pipeline that re-skins them beat by beat
articles.description:
Vertical short dramas (ReelShort, DramaBox…) are a multi-billion-dollar market
A hit episode opens with a visual hook in 3 seconds, stacks an information hook
engineered.
So I distilled 65 overseas vertical dramas — about 3,420 episodes and 55,000
Drama Forge, an open-source pipeline that turns one proven hit into a
Upload a hit sample, and the pipeline:
Deconstructs it into a six-dimension report plus a per-episode beat map:
what each beat does (humiliation / restraint / reversal / face-slap),
its emotional intensity, where the paywall sits.
Re-skins it into 10 concept variants. The core promise ("contract
marriage → real love", "hidden identity revenge") stays locked; only the
surface genre swaps — mafia, werewolf, billionaire, royal.
Produces a full script package per concept: direction card, character
bios, season outline, a coherent block of opening episodes, and two
ad-creative episodes. After final review, it keeps writing to the season
finale in resumable background batches.
Grades everything with an editor-in-chief review pass.
The key discipline is beat-level mirroring: each new episode mirrors the
A 60-episode script package is 10+ long LLM calls. Naive implementations die
Streamed structured output everywhere (streamObject + a 15-minute
undici agent). Non-streaming calls get killed by intermediaries after ~10
minutes of silence.
tRPC with JSONL heartbeats (pingMs: 4000) so long requests never go
quiet.
Async jobs with server-side checkpoints: the browser submits and polls;
every batch is persisted, so a restart resumes from the exact missing
episodes. Idempotent merges by episode number make retries free.
Missing-episode self-healing: LLMs sometimes return 4 episodes when
asked for 5. Each batch retries up to 3 rounds and refuses to advance the
pipeline until the set is complete.
Stack: React 19 + Hono + tRPC 11 + Drizzle + MySQL, all TypeScript.
The model doesn't need to be "creative". It needs rails: a beat map to mirror,
Repo (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/epongzhao-sketch/drama-forge
The corpus-distilled DNA ships in the repo. A newer rule pack, corrected
If you work in short-drama production and want to see what a full package
looks like, open an issue — I'll show you one.

articles.title: Tutoriel n8n : sauvegarder et versionner vos workflows (export JSON, CLI, Git et restauration)
articles.description:
Un workflow n8n qui tourne en production, c'est souvent des heures de réglages : les bons filtres, les prompts de l'agent IA ajustés au fil des semaines, les cas particuliers gérés un par un. Et pourtant, beaucoup d'équipes n'en ont aucune copie en dehors de l'instance. Une mauvaise manipulation, une mise à jour ratée ou un serveur perdu, et tout est à refaire.
Ce tutoriel couvre quatre niveaux de protection, du plus simple au plus robuste : l'export manuel, l'export en ligne de commande, la sauvegarde automatique par un workflow, et le versionnement dans Git. On termine par le point que tout le monde oublie : savoir restaurer.
Un workflow n8n est un document JSON : nœuds, paramètres, connexions, réglages. Mais il ne contient pas les secrets. Les credentials (clés API, mots de passe, jetons OAuth) sont stockés à part, chiffrés avec la clé de chiffrement de l'instance (N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY).
Concrètement, une sauvegarde complète, c'est trois choses :
les workflows (JSON) ;
les credentials (exportées chiffrées) ;
la clé de chiffrement, conservée en lieu sûr, séparément. Sans elle, les credentials exportées sont illisibles par une autre instance.
Dans un workflow ouvert, le menu « … » en haut à droite propose Download. Vous obtenez un fichier .json que vous pouvez réimporter plus tard avec Import from File, ou simplement coller dans un éditeur vide (n8n accepte le JSON copié-collé).
C'est utile avant une grosse modification : on télécharge, on modifie, et on a un point de retour. Mais ça repose sur la discipline de chacun, donc ça ne suffit pas pour la production.
À savoir aussi : selon votre version et votre offre, n8n conserve un historique des versions de chaque workflow, consultable depuis l'éditeur. Pratique pour revenir en arrière, mais cet historique vit dans la même base de données que le reste : ce n'est pas une sauvegarde externe.
Sur une instance auto-hébergée, la CLI de n8n exporte tout d'un coup :
# Tous les workflows, un fichier par workflow
n8n export:workflow --all --separate --output=backups/workflows/

# Toutes les credentials (restent chiffrées par défaut)
n8n export:credentials --all --separate --output=backups/credentials/

Avec Docker, on lance la même commande dans le conteneur, puis on récupère le dossier :
docker exec -u node n8n \
  n8n export:workflow --all --separate --output=/home/node/backups/workflows/

(Adaptez le nom du conteneur et montez /home/node/backups sur un volume pour retrouver les fichiers sur l'hôte.)
Une option --decrypted existe pour exporter les credentials en clair. Évitez-la, sauf migration ponctuelle et maîtrisée : un fichier de secrets en clair qui traîne dans un dossier de sauvegarde, c'est exactement ce qu'on veut éviter.
Planifiez ces commandes avec un cron système, copiez le résultat hors du serveur (stockage objet, autre machine), et vous avez déjà une vraie sauvegarde.
Si vous préférez rester dans n8n, un petit workflow peut faire le travail :
Schedule Trigger : chaque nuit, par exemple à 2h (pensez à définir le fuseau horaire du workflow).
Nœud n8n (l'API publique de n8n, avec une clé API créée dans les paramètres) : opération Get many sur les workflows.
Code ou Edit Fields : pour chaque workflow, préparer un nom de fichier stable, par exemple {{ $json.id }}-{{ $json.name }}.json, et le contenu JSON.
Destination : nœud GitHub (créer ou mettre à jour un fichier), Google Drive, ou stockage S3.
Sortie d'erreur vers une notification : une sauvegarde qui échoue en silence est pire que pas de sauvegarde, parce qu'on croit être protégé.
Deux précautions :
utilisez un nom de fichier basé sur l'ID du workflow, pas seulement sur son nom, pour ne pas écraser deux workflows homonymes ;
ce workflow ne sauvegarde que les workflows. Gardez la sauvegarde des credentials et de la clé de chiffrement côté serveur (niveau 2).
Une fois les workflows exportés un fichier par workflow, les pousser dans un dépôt Git privé apporte ce que les sauvegardes seules n'ont pas : l'historique lisible des changements. On voit qui a modifié le prompt de l'agent IA, quand, et on peut comparer deux versions.
Un script minimal, lancé après l'export :
cd backups
git add workflows/
git commit -m "Sauvegarde n8n $(date +%F)" || echo "Aucun changement"
git push

Ne commitez jamais les credentials déchiffrées ni le fichier .env contenant N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Ajoutez-les au .gitignore dès le départ.
Pour les équipes qui ont plusieurs instances (développement, test, production), n8n propose aussi une fonctionnalité de source control et environnements basée sur Git, réservée à certaines offres. Vérifiez dans la documentation officielle si elle est incluse dans la vôtre avant de construire votre propre mécanisme.
Une sauvegarde n'a de valeur que si on sait la restaurer. Faites l'exercice au moins une fois, sur une instance de test :
n8n import:credentials --separate --input=backups/credentials/
n8n import:workflow --separate --input=backups/workflows/

L'instance de test doit utiliser la même N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY que l'instance d'origine, sinon les credentials importées ne fonctionneront pas.
Après l'import, vérifiez trois choses :
les workflows importés sont désactivés tant que vous ne les avez pas relus (évitez qu'une copie de test envoie de vrais e-mails à vos clients) ;
les credentials se connectent bien ;
les webhooks pointent vers la bonne URL, qui change d'une instance à l'autre.
[ ] Clé N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY conservée hors du serveur, dans un gestionnaire de secrets
[ ] Export automatique quotidien des workflows (CLI ou workflow dédié)
[ ] Credentials exportées chiffrées, jamais en clair dans Git
[ ] Copie hors du serveur
[ ] Alerte en cas d'échec de la sauvegarde
[ ] Une restauration testée au moins une fois
C'est le genre de fondation peu visible qu'on met en place chez Flux Intelligent avant de confier des tâches importantes à des agents IA : quand un workflow devient critique pour l'activité, il mérite la même protection que le reste de vos données. Si vous voulez faire le point sur vos automatisations existantes, vous pouvez demander un audit.

articles.title: What SOLID Taught Me About Life, Not Just Code
articles.description:
I used to overthink everything. I wanted to lead every project, hold every thread, and be right every time. I gave to people with my whole heart, whether or not they deserved it.
Then I learned SOLID, and one day I realized these five principles weren’t describing my code. They were describing real life.
S: Single Responsibility Principle
In code: A class should have one reason to change. When one module does everything, everything breaks together.
My old behavior: I wanted to lead in everything, and I wanted everything in my hands. I called it “being responsible.”
In reality I was a God class: one person, a hundred responsibilities, zero room for anyone else to do their part. And a God class has a hundred reasons to break.
Now: I lead where I’m strong, and I let other people own their part. A team works better when each person has one job and the trust to do it.
in Tunisia , my homeland we say :
=>Sharing responsibilities makes everything easier.
O: Open/Closed Principle
In code: Open for extension, closed for modification. You can add new behavior without breaking what already works.
My old behavior: I overthought everything. Every time a doubt showed up, I went back and modified a decision that was already working. And like modifying working code, every edit risked breaking it and created new doubts.
Now: Once a decision works, I treat it as closed for modification. When new information or a new doubt arrives, I extend instead: I add a next step, a plan B, a small adjustment, without rewriting what I already decided. Less noise in my head, and decisions that actually stand.
“الذهب يرق يرق وما يتقطعش”
=>You can change and adapt without losing the core.
L: Liskov Substitution Principle
In code: If you replace a parent type with a subtype, the program must still behave correctly. A subtype can’t demand more than its parent did, or deliver less.
My old behavior: I wanted to be the leader, and I never said “I was wrong.” But a leader comes with a contract: people expect you to own your mistakes. My version of leading only worked as long as I was never wrong. I had quietly added a condition the parent type never had, and dropped a promise it did make.
That’s a Liskov violation: I carried the “Leader” label, but I behaved differently exactly when it mattered, so the people depending on me got a surprise.
Now: I learned that “sorry” is part of the contract. A leader who can say “I was wrong” behaves like a real leader, so people can depend on me without surprises.
“Practice what you preach.”
I: Interface Segregation Principle
In code: Don’t force a client to depend on methods it doesn’t need. Expose small, focused interfaces, not a giant one.
My old behavior: I’m a giver. I gave with my whole heart to everyone, everywhere, and everyone got the full interface: my time, my energy, my attention, my yes, even when they only needed one method.
Now: I learned that “no” is a valid method, and that not everyone, and not everywhere, gets full access to me. Different people get different parts of me. I’m still a giver, but now I choose which interface each person gets.
“الماء الماشي للسدرة، الزيتونة أولى به”
=>Direct your resources where they are needed.
D: Dependency Inversion Principle
In code: High-level modules shouldn’t depend on low-level details. Both should depend on abstractions.
In everyday life: Think of a lamp. It doesn’t care whether its electricity comes from solar panels, a gas plant, or a wind farm. It depends on one thing: the socket. The socket is the abstraction. The power plants are details, and they can change without the lamp ever noticing.
My old behavior: My decisions were plugged straight into the power plant. They depended on low-level details: my mood that day, what someone said, how people reacted. When the detail changed, my decision changed with it.
Now: I plug into the socket: my values. Moods, opinions, and reactions are still there, but they are details. My decisions and those details both answer to the same standard, so things can change around me without everything going dark.
“Don’t put all your eggs in one basket.”
The Real Lesson
Every principle pointed to the same thing:
S: You don’t have to carry everything.
O: Don’t keep rewriting what works; add to it.
L: Honor what your role promises, including owning your mistakes.
I: Not everyone needs, or deserves, all of you.
D: Base your decisions on your values, not on moods or reactions. 
I came to SOLID to write cleaner code. It made me a better person instead.
Which principle do you recognize in yourself? Share it in the comments, and add your own proverb. I’d love one in Arabic , French or your native language too.
For developers: If you want to apply SOLID in your code (and with AI), I built open-source skills for it: clean-code-skills on GitHub. I also wrote about how they work here: Clean Code in the Age of AI Agents: 5 Principles and 2 Skills I Built .
