articles.title: Web AR Checklist: 8 Browser Numbers I Measure Before Launch
articles.description:
TL;DR
WebGL 2.0 and a secure context are hard stops. Check them against your own analytics browser list, not a support badge.
Constraints are requests. Read track.getSettings() back instead of trusting what you asked for.
Your frame budget is arithmetic, not measurement: 33 ms at 30 fps, 16.7 ms at 60.
Device pixel ratio is the multiplier nobody writes down. 1280x720 at ratio 2 is twelve times the pixels of 640x480.
The transfer size of the WASM module is the number that reaches users, not the file size.
Handle NotFoundError, not just NotAllowedError, or desktop users with no webcam get told they denied permission.
MediaPipe dropped its non-SIMD build in November 2026. TensorFlow.js still ships three binaries and picks at load time. Check which one your page actually fetched.
Measure for minutes on your oldest phone, not seconds on your laptop.
Every web AR page I have shipped failed in the same place. The demo ran on my laptop and fell over on somebody's two-year-old Android.
The fix was never a better runtime. It was having eight numbers written down before launch instead of after. This is that list, in the order I run it.
This is a harness. There are no frame rates from my own devices in this post, because the numbers that matter are the ones your effect produces on your device list, and mine would only tell you about my hardware.
So: specified here, all eight checks, the arithmetic you can redo on paper, and the browser behaviour each one depends on, with a link to the documentation that defines it. Produced here, nothing. You run it.
Face AR in a browser composites through WebGL, so WebGL 2.0 is the floor. Everything else here is pointless if this one fails.
The headline number looks safe. caniuse puts WebGL 2.0 at 97.29% global support, with no partial-support asterisk. The gap sits where you would expect: iOS Safari had it disabled by default from version 12 through 14.8, and only shipped it on by default in iOS 15. If your analytics still show a tail of old iPhones, that tail is the 2.7%.
How to run it: take your own analytics browser list, not a generic support claim, and check each entry against that table. Then feature-detect at runtime rather than trusting the user agent string.
const probe = document.createElement("canvas")
const hasWebGL2 = probe.getContext("webgl2") !== null

Use a throwaway canvas, as above. getContext() returns null both when the context type is unsupported and when the canvas has already been set to a different context mode, so running the probe on a canvas that something already called getContext("2d") on reports WebGL 2.0 as missing on a browser that supports it fine. That one cost me an afternoon.
Good answer: every browser in your top 95% of sessions returns a context. Bad answer: a tail of old iPhones and in-app webviews that you find out about from support tickets. caniuse does not break webviews out, so that one you have to test yourself.
getUserMedia() is a secure-context feature, and MDN states the consequence plainly: "in insecure contexts, navigator.mediaDevices is undefined, preventing access to getUserMedia()". The call is not available at all, so you get a TypeError on property access rather than a rejected promise.
Secure context is not the same as HTTPS. MDN counts HTTPS, file:/// and localhost, which is exactly why this breaks after dev and not during it.
How to run it: load every route that opens a camera over the real scheme users will get, including any embedded frame. A frame needs allow="camera", and the Permissions-Policy header has to permit the origin.
Good answer: the permission prompt appears on every route, first try. Bad answer: it works on your dev machine over localhost, which is a secure context, and dies on a staging host that is not.
Constraints are requests. The browser honours them when hardware allows and quietly gives you something else when it does not, so read the track back instead of assuming.
How to run it: after the stream resolves, log track.getSettings() and compare width, height and frameRate against what you requested. Treat them as possibly absent rather than destructuring blind, because MDN notes that listed properties may be missing when the browser does not support them or the context does not provide them.
Use min, max or exact only when you genuinely want the call to fail instead of degrade. Those three are inherently mandatory, and MDN is specific about what failure looks like: the promise rejects with OverconstrainedError "and the user will not be prompted". No permission dialog, no camera, no obvious reason. Plain values and ideal are the ones that degrade.
Good answer: settings match the request on your low-end reference phone. Bad answer: you asked for 1280x720, you got 640x480, and your effect placement was tuned for the first one.
Not a numbered check, but it belongs here, because three of these come straight out of check 3.
Developers search error names verbatim, and these are specified rather than invented. Six of the seven below are DOMException rejections from getUserMedia(). TypeError is the JavaScript built-in, not a DOMException, so a handler that switches on instanceof DOMException misses it entirely.
The user denied access, or a permissions policy blocks the input. Treat it as a user-facing state with a retry path, never as a crash.
MDN's entry for this one also still says it covers an insecure browsing context. That half is stale: in an insecure context navigator.mediaDevices is undefined, so you never reach a rejection. Do not write your insecure-context handling against this error.
No media tracks of the type you asked for exist. This is the desktop user with no webcam, and it is the one I see omitted most often. A page that handles NotAllowedError and not this one tells someone who has no camera that they denied permission, and then sends them into their browser settings to look for a toggle that will not help.
No device met the constraints you marked mandatory. It carries a constraint property naming the one that could not be met, so log that property rather than the message. Note that this can fire before any permission grant, which makes it a fingerprinting surface as well as an error.
Permission was granted, then a hardware error at the operating system, browser or page level blocked the device. On laptops this is usually another application holding the camera.
Your constraints object was empty or every member was false, or you called the method in an insecure context where navigator.mediaDevices does not exist. The second cause is the common one, and see the note under NotAllowedError.
The two I catch generically. AbortError is "permission and hardware were both fine, and it still did not work". SecurityError is user media support disabled on the document, by a mechanism each browser decides for itself. Neither has a useful retry path, so both go to the same fallback as NotReadableError.
This is the number most teams never write down, and it is arithmetic rather than measurement. At 30 frames per second the whole pipeline gets 1000 / 30, which is 33 ms per frame. At 60 frames per second it is 1000 / 60, or 16.7 ms. That budget covers capture, inference, effect rendering and compositing, not only the part you wrote.
How to run it: hang the timing off requestVideoFrameCallback so you time against delivered video frames instead of animation ticks. It is on HTMLVideoElement, it is in all three engines, and Firefox only shipped it in 132, so feature-detect:
if (!("requestVideoFrameCallback" in HTMLVideoElement.prototype)) {
  // fall back to requestAnimationFrame and accept the mismatch
}

Two things about the timing itself that I got wrong for longer than I would like.
First, the callback already hands you now and a metadata object, so you do not need performance.now() on the entry side. That metadata carries presentedFrames, which is a far better dropped-frame detector than inferring drops from timing deltas, and processingDuration, which is decode time rather than your time.
Second, performance.now() is coarsened. MDN gives 5 microseconds when the document is cross-origin isolated and 100 microseconds when it is not. A rolling median is still worth keeping, because it rejects the frame that collided with a GC pause or a layout, but it does not buy you resolution below that floor. Quantisation is a deterministic floor on the clock, not zero-mean noise, so the median lands on the same grid every sample did. If your per-frame work is near a tenth of a millisecond, time across N frames and divide, or turn on cross-origin isolation and check crossOriginIsolated.
Good answer: a median well inside the budget, with headroom for the render. Bad answer: a median at 31 ms, which looks fine in a spreadsheet and stutters the moment a background task takes the GPU.
Resolution choices scale geometrically, and two of them compound.



What you set
Pixels per frame
Relative cost




640x480
307,200
1x


1280x720
921,600
3x


1280x720 at device pixel ratio 2
3,686,400
12x



640x480 is 307,200 pixels a frame. Moving to 1280x720 makes it 921,600, which is three times the work. Rendering that at a device pixel ratio of 2 doubles each axis again, so the processed area reaches 3,686,400 pixels, twelve times the cheapest setting.
The ratio is the one people forget, because the display applies it and your code never mentions it.
How to run it: log window.devicePixelRatio on your reference devices, then log the real canvas backing-store size. Cap the ratio at 1 where effect detail is not the point.
Good answer: you chose a number. Bad answer: the ratio chose it for you on a high-density phone.
Browser face tracking ships a WebAssembly module, and those files are large uncompressed. The current MediaPipe vision build is a fraction under 15 MB on disk. The figure that reaches your users is the transfer size, which is the compressed one.
How to run it: open the network panel, load the page cold with the cache disabled, and read the transferred column next to the resource size for the .wasm file, and for any .data companion file if your runtime still ships one, plus the Content-Encoding response header. If that header is missing on either, your host is serving it raw, and fixing that is the highest-return change available to you.
Purely as illustrative arithmetic, so you can see the shape: a 12 MB module at a compression ratio of 3.4 transfers as roughly 3.5 MB. Measure your own ratio. Do not borrow mine or anyone else's.
Good answer: Content-Encoding present, transfer size a fraction of file size. Bad answer: a multi-megabyte raw download in front of the first camera frame.
This check changed under me while I was writing, which is the best argument for running it yourself rather than reading about it.
The shape used to be simple: browser CV runtimes shipped a baseline WASM binary and a SIMD one, detected support at load time, and picked. That is still exactly what TensorFlow.js does, and it ships three, not two. Its README says it loads "the appropriate WASM binary" after "testing the capabilities of your runtime", across tfjs-backend-wasm.wasm, tfjs-backend-wasm-simd.wasm and tfjs-backend-wasm-threaded-simd.wasm. The threaded one needs cross-origin isolation, and without it you silently fall back to SIMD-only.
MediaPipe no longer does this. Up to and including @mediapipe/tasks-vision 1.2.0 the package shipped a vision_wasm_nosimd_internal binary and selected against it at load time. From 1.2.2, published 3 November 2026, that file is gone and the SIMD detection with it. Current builds assume SIMD. I found this by diffing the published packages, because the MediaPipe documentation does not mention SIMD at all, before or after.
So the check is no longer "did it get the fast one". It is: which files does your runtime expect, and did your bundler actually serve them?
How to run it: load the page cold and read the network panel for every .wasm request, including the ones that 404. If you want to branch yourself, wasm-feature-detect is the small way to do it, and it is live again after a quiet stretch, at 1.10.1 in November 2026:
import { simd, threads } from "wasm-feature-detect"
if (await simd()) { /* ... */ }

Two bundler traps worth knowing. The runtime fetches its .wasm relative to the JavaScript file, so your bundler has to serve it as a static asset at a predictable path, and the failure mode is a 404 rather than a build error. And TensorFlow.js documents a second one: if your minifier rewrites typeof foo == "undefined" into foo === void 0, which terser does under its typeofs option, you get "_scriptDir is not defined" thrown from a web worker, but only in browsers that qualified for the SIMD plus threading build. A failure that appears on fast machines only is a bad afternoon.
Good answer: every .wasm your runtime asks for returns 200, and you know which one. Bad answer: one 404 on a binary, a silent fallback, and a performance mystery you chase for a day.
The first frames after model load are always slower, and sustained load behaves differently from a cold start as the device heats up. A reading taken over two seconds tells you about neither.
How to run it: run the effect continuously for several minutes on your oldest supported device, sample the frame time throughout, and keep the distribution rather than one average. If you are in requestVideoFrameCallback, keep presentedFrames alongside it, because a thermal throttle shows up as dropped frames before it shows up in a median. Record the discarded runs too, including the one where you had a video call open in another tab, because that is a real user condition.
Good answer: the median holds across the window and you know the shape of the tail. Bad answer: a single screenshot of a good second.
Face tracking has to keep working across browser releases nobody on your team controls, and that maintenance has no end date. Check 7 is the small version of the argument: a dependency I do not maintain changed its binary layout three weeks ago, and the only way I learned was by diffing packages. Multiply that by every browser release.
I spent a long time on my own tracking layer before I accepted that, and I wrote up what moved me off it at more length.
The eight checks apply either way. They measure the page, not the runtime underneath it.
Pick your oldest supported phone. Run checks 1, 2 and 6 first, because each one is a hard stop rather than a slow page. Then write down your frame budget from check 4 and measure against it for five minutes rather than five seconds.
Keep the numbers in the repository next to the integration code, so the next person to touch it starts from a baseline instead of an opinion. And put a date on them. Mine from a month ago would already be wrong about check 7.

articles.title: How to Ship Clean Markdown Docs for AI Coding Agents (llms.txt, llms-full.txt & Next.js Routes Without External Crawlers)
articles.description:
If you maintain an SDK, API, or developer tool, you've probably watched an AI coding assistant hallucinate outdated flags because it tried to parse your heavily styled HTML docs—or got tripped up by client-side hydration.
Even though Google Search does not use llms.txt for ranking, publishing a clean /llms.txt index and /llms-full.txt Markdown bundle is genuinely useful for developers and coding agents pulling your docs into context.
The catch: most online llms.txt generators work by pointing a remote crawler at your public URL. That breaks immediately if:
You're working on localhost or a password-protected staging environment.
Your WAF/CDN rate-limits or blocks third-party scrapers.
The scraper ingests your <nav>, <footer>, and cookie banner into the output.
Here is a clean, local-first workflow to generate, structure, and serve /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt in a Next.js App Router project.
/llms.txt (Required index): A compact Markdown table of contents following llmstxt.org—one # H1 title, one > blockquote summary, curated ## H2 link lists with concise factual descriptions, and an ## Optional section for secondary pages.
/llms-full.txt (Optional full bundle): Concatenated clean Markdown of your primary docs so an agent can ingest the entire core reference in one request.
/llms-ctx.txt (Optional XML context): Prompt-friendly XML-wrapped context for direct LLM pasting.
/llms.txt





# AcmeSDK

> TypeScript SDK for real-time webhook verification and idempotent event queues.

## Core Documentation
- [Quickstart](https://docs.example.com/quickstart): Install the SDK and verify your first webhook signature in 5 minutes.
- [Authentication](https://docs.example.com/auth): API key scoping, rotation, and HMAC-SHA256 header verification.

## API & SDK Reference
- [Queues API](https://docs.example.com/api/queues): Enqueue jobs, configure retry backoff, and inspect dead-letter queues.
- [Error Codes](https://docs.example.com/api/errors): HTTP status codes and retryable vs. terminal error payloads.

## Optional
- [Changelog](https://docs.example.com/changelog): Release notes and migration guides.

Three mistakes to avoid: never use relative paths (always use full https:// canonical URLs), avoid vague link titles like "Click here" or "Learn more," and strip marketing superlatives from descriptions so every token carries technical signal.
/llms.txt Cleanly in Next.js App Router


You can drop static files straight into public/llms.txt, or serve them via a route handler with explicit text/plain; charset=utf-8 headers and CDN caching:
// app/llms.txt/route.ts
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';

const LLMS_TXT = `# AcmeSDK

> TypeScript SDK for real-time webhook verification and idempotent event queues.

## Core Documentation
- [Quickstart](https://docs.example.com/quickstart): Install the SDK and verify your first webhook signature in 5 minutes.
- [Authentication](https://docs.example.com/auth): API key scoping, rotation, and HMAC-SHA256 header verification.

## Optional
- [Changelog](https://docs.example.com/changelog): Release notes and migration guides.
`;

export async function GET() {
  return new NextResponse(LLMS_TXT, {
    status: 200,
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'text/plain; charset=utf-8',
      'Cache-Control': 'public, max-age=3600, s-maxage=86400',
    },
  });
}

robots.txt Cross-Check


Before deploying, confirm two things in /robots.txt:
You aren't accidentally disallowing /llms.txt or /llms-full.txt.
If you add bot-specific User-agent: rules (to allow search citation bots while blocking training crawlers), repeat your global Disallow: paths (/admin/, /api/private/) inside each allowed bot block so RFC 9309 doesn't override your wildcard protections.
If you want to paste a local Sitemap XML or raw HTML pages (automatically stripping <nav>, <script>, and <footer>), check BPE token counts across GPT/Claude/Gemini/DeepSeek, lint both llms.txt and robots.txt together, and export ready-to-paste Next.js routes without sending private docs to an external crawler, KivaroTools' in-browser llms.txt studio handles the whole pipeline locally with no sign-up. You can also browse the main KivaroTools browser suite if you prefer local-first developer utilities.
Verify curl -I https://yourdomain.com/llms.txt returns 200 OK and text/plain; charset=utf-8.
Keep primary links concise and move changelogs/archive pages into ## Optional.
Check that robots.txt allows /llms.txt and repeats protected Disallow: routes inside any custom bot blocks.

articles.title: Gen AI Cost Optimization on AWS: A Technical Guide to Building Cost-Efficient AI Applications
articles.description:
www.infimatrix.com 
Generative AI (Gen AI) has shifted from experimental pilots to core production workloads. However, as applications scale to support thousands or millions of queries, infrastructure costs primarily driven by Large Language Model (LLM) inference, fine-tuning and vector retrieval can rapidly escalate out of control.
On Amazon Web Services (AWS), optimizing Gen AI costs requires more than just picking a smaller instance. It demands an end-to-end architectural strategy spanning model selection, caching, dynamic routing, retrieval optimization and infrastructure provisioning.
Here is a technical guide to building and operating cost-efficient Gen AI applications on AWS.
Right-Sizing Models: The "Right Model for the Job" Strategy
The single biggest cost driver in Gen AI applications is using an over-parameterized model (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet or Anthropic Claude 3 Opus) for simple tasks that could be handled by lighter, specialized models (e.g., Claude 3 Haiku or Amazon Nova Micro).
Implementation Tactics:
Tier 1 (Simple Queries): Direct FAQ lookups or simple summaries to or Claude 3 Haiku.
Tier 2 (Moderate Tasks): Route standard reasoning tasks to Amazon Nova Lite or Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
Tier 3 (Complex Reasoning/Coding): Reserve high-parameter models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet / Opus strictly for edge cases requiring multi-step logic.
Fine-Tuning Small Language Models (SLMs): Instead of using prompt engineering on massive foundation models (FMs), fine-tune smaller open-weights models (e.g., Llama 3.2 1B/3B, Mistral 7B) on your specific domain dataset using Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. Deploying a fine-tuned 7B model on ml.g5.xlarge instances is often significantly cheaper per inference call than calling proprietary APIs at high volumes.
Optimizing Token Usage: Prompt & Cache Management
In Gen AI billing, tokens equal dollars. Reducing input/output token counts directly impacts your AWS Bedrock or SageMaker bill.
Implementation Tactics:
Cost-Effective RAG Architecture (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
RAG reduces hallucinations and enables grounded responses, but poorly optimized vector search and document chunking can lead to inflated storage, indexing and token costs.
Implementation Tactics:
Compute & Hosting Optimization on AWS
Whether you deploy proprietary FMs via Amazon Bedrock or self-host open-source models on Amazon SageMaker / EKS, choosing the right hosting model is critical.
Serverless vs. Provisioned Throughput on Amazon Bedrock:
AWS Inferentia2 (inf2 instances): Replace NVIDIA GPU instances with AWS Trainium/Inferentia2 chips. inf2 instances deliver up to 50% better performance-per-dollar over comparable GPU-based instances for LLM inference.
FinOps, Monitoring and Governance for Gen AI
You cannot optimize what you do not measure. Traditional AWS Cost Explorer metrics don’t give token-level visibility out of the box.
Implementation Tactics:
AWS Budgets & Cost Allocation Tags: Apply tags (CostCenter, Environment, ModelName, FeatureID) to Bedrock API calls, Lambda functions and SageMaker endpoints. Set up AWS Budgets alerts to notify engineering teams when daily token consumption exceeds expected baselines.
Rate Limiting and Guardrails: Implement Amazon Bedrock Guardrails not only for safety, but to reject invalid, malicious, or prompt-injection requests before they consume downstream inference tokens.
Here is a blueprint for a cost-optimized production Gen AI stack on AWS:
Summary Checklist for AWS Gen AI Cost Optimization
Turn on Prompt Caching: Reduce input token costs on static system prompts and RAG contexts.
Optimize RAG Payloads: Use rerankers to pass fewer, highly relevant chunks to the LLM.
Leverage AWS Silicon: Test AWS Inferentia2 (inf2) for self-hosted LLMs on SageMaker.
Set Up Token FinOps: Tag workloads, log custom token metrics in CloudWatch and set budget alarms.
Cost optimization in Gen AI is not a one-time setup; it is an ongoing FinOps discipline. By establishing token-level observability in CloudWatch and regularly evaluating new model releases, platform teams can maintain low operational expenditure while delivering fast, high-quality AI experiences to end users.
Written by the Infimatrix Cloud and AI team.
www.infimatrix.com

articles.title: Why is my NAT Gateway bill so high?
articles.description:
Why the charge appears


A team moves its application into private subnets and makes no change to request volume. The next bill still jumps. The application now sends image pulls, software updates, backups, and other outbound traffic through NAT gateways, and the gateways have an hourly cost even when traffic is quiet.
Separate the cost into gateway-hours and processed bytes. Multiple zonal gateways can increase the baseline, while a small number of busy jobs can dominate the per-GB line item. Cross-AZ or other transfer charges can also show up as separate billing lines.
In Cost Explorer, group by Usage type over the last 30 days and search for NatGateway-Hours and NatGateway-Bytes. Regional prefixes can vary. If you see a flat hourly baseline and an isolated spike in bytes, start with workloads that transferred data during that spike.
In CUR 2.0, filter line_item_usage_type for those tokens, then sum line_item_unblended_cost by Region and day. Group by line_item_resource_id where the export provides it. Keep data-transfer rows separate so you can compare the NAT charge with the cost of the network path.
Run these commands in the billed account. Replace uppercase placeholders with your own values.
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --region REGION

aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=VPC_ID

aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --region REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=VPC_ID

Match the NAT IDs to the route tables used by the affected subnets. For same-Region S3 and DynamoDB traffic, look for gateway endpoints and check that the relevant route tables are associated. Gateway endpoints have no additional endpoint charge and can keep matching traffic off the NAT path.
The hourly NAT charge continues while the gateway is provisioned. Check which workloads still need internet egress and which availability requirements the current layout serves before considering a topology change.
If you don't want to check these services one Region at a time, you can drop a Cost Explorer CSV or CUR 2.0 export (.csv / .csv.gz) into Bill Checkup — it parses 100% locally in your browser with zero AWS IAM permissions required and flags common idle charges automatically.

articles.title: We Refused to Build a Lottery Predictor, So We Published the Math Instead
articles.description:
Every lottery data project gets the same request eventually: "Can you predict the next draw?" We get asked it, we have refused it, and this post is why — with the actual numbers, in Python, so anyone can check our work.
The game here is Hong Kong Mark Six: 6 numbers drawn from 49, plus a special number drawn from the same 49. The dataset is every Macau draw from 2020-03-07 to 2026-11-24 (2,443 draws) and every Hong Kong draw from 2020-01-02 to 2026-11-24 (808 draws). Everything below is computed from that data. No predictions, no "hot tips" — just combinatorics and a chi-square test.
Pick 6 numbers out of 49. The number of possible combinations is:
from math import comb

comb(49, 6)  # 13,983,816

13,983,816. That is the size of the space. A single random pick matches all 6 numbers with probability 1 in 13,983,816. There is no strategy that changes this: every combination is equally likely, every draw.
The hypergeometric distribution gives the exact probabilities for a random 6-number pick:
from math import comb

def p_match(k):
    return comb(6, k) * comb(43, 6 - k) / comb(49, 6)

for k in range(7):
    print(k, f"{p_match(k):.6f}", f"~1 in {1/p_match(k):,.0f}")




Match
Probability
About




0 of 6
43.60%
~1 in 2


1 of 6
41.30%
~1 in 2


2 of 6
13.24%
~1 in 8


3 of 6
1.77%
~1 in 57


4 of 6
0.097%
~1 in 1,032


5 of 6
0.0018%
~1 in 54,201


6 of 6
0.0000072%
~1 in 13,983,816



Read that table the right way round: matching 3 numbers — the thing people celebrate — happens about once in 57 random picks. It feels like skill. It is arithmetic.
The jackpot alone contributes this much expected value per entry:
from math import comb

jackpot = 100_000_000  # HK$100 million
jackpot / comb(49, 6)  # 7.15

A HK$100,000,000 jackpot is worth HK$7.15 in expected value. At a HK$50,000,000 jackpot it is HK$3.58. The lower prize tiers add a few dollars more. The total expected return stays below the amount staked, because the prize pool is only a share of total stakes — the rest funds the operator, duty, and good causes. That is the whole business model, and it is why "expected value negative" is not an opinion but a structural fact.
Note what this calculation does not say. It does not say you cannot win. Someone wins the jackpot regularly — in the last 36 Hong Kong draws, 17 had a first-prize winner, and the largest single first-prize dividend was HK$81,142,980. It says that across all entries, the average return is less than the stake. Both statements are true at the same time.
Here is the test people usually skip. Take all 2,443 Macau draws — 17,101 numbers in total. If every number were equally likely, each should appear about 349.00 times (17,101 / 49). The most frequent number, 49, appeared 404 times. The least frequent, 14, appeared 310 times. That looks like a pattern. It is not:
# Appearances of numbers 1-49 in all 2,443 Macau draws (7 numbers each).
# Paste the real counts so anyone can rerun the test.
counts = [369, 368, 370, 330, 368, 345, 342, 347, 337, 371,
          366, 331, 314, 310, 362, 344, 357, 315, 359, 334,
          312, 366, 341, 359, 351, 346, 342, 326, 370, 372,
          349, 331, 321, 334, 336, 352, 352, 358, 355, 351,
          345, 358, 367, 372, 356, 355, 328, 353, 404]

total = sum(counts)               # 17,101
expected = total / 49             # 349.00
chi2 = sum((o - expected) ** 2 / expected for o in counts)
print(total, round(expected, 2), round(chi2, 2))  # 17101 349.0 49.46

The chi-square statistic is 49.46 with 48 degrees of freedom. The 95% critical value is 65.17. Since 49.46 < 65.17, we cannot reject the hypothesis that all 49 numbers are equally likely. The same test on the last 100 Macau draws gives 46.20, and on all 808 Hong Kong draws gives 50.13 — same conclusion, three times over.
The hottest number of the last 100 Macau draws, 17, appeared 24 times against an expected 14.29. That is the single most extreme cell in the window — and the chi-square test still says the whole table is consistent with chance. A 24 next to a 14.29 feels meaningful. Across 49 numbers, it is exactly the kind of outlier randomness produces.
Three things, and only three:
Describing the past. Number 49 appeared 404 times in 2,443 Macau draws. That is a fact about the past.
Checking your intuition. If you feel a number "comes up all the time," count it. The count is usually less dramatic than the feeling.
Learning statistics. Real draw data is a clean, honest dataset for practicing combinatorics, hypothesis testing, and the difference between a pattern and a coincidence.
What it cannot do is tell you the next draw. Every draw is independent. The math above is the reason, not the excuse.
Mark Six draw archive (Macau 2,443 draws, Hong Kong 808 draws): https://369123.cc

Draw statistics and number tools: https://369777.cc



Disclosure: this article was drafted with AI assistance and verified against the draw dataset by hand before publishing.

articles.title: Kaun Bol Raha Hai? — Voice Verification Meets Transaction Approval
articles.description:
Recognizing a voice doesn’t always mean you can trust the request. AI-generated speech makes it increasingly useful to check both who is speaking and what they’re asking you to approve.
I built Kaun Bol Raha Hai? (“Who’s speaking?”), a prototype that brings voice screening, speaker verification, and exact transaction confirmation into one workflow.
For transaction review, the customer receives a confirmation request showing the exact amount and merchant. They can deny the request or complete a spoken challenge before approving it. The interface supports English, Hindi, and Kannada.
Each request is tied to a transaction revision. If the agent changes the amount or merchant, the previous link is replaced and fresh approval is required.
Live integrations include:
DetectifAI Aletheia for synthetic-voice screening.
DetectifAI Eidos for speaker verification.
Google Speech-to-Text for transaction-challenge transcription.
Twilio and SMTP for optional SMS, OTP, and email flows.
The UI includes responsive layouts, interaction animations, and reduced-motion support. The repository also contains architecture diagrams, an integration guide, and automated checks through GitHub Actions.
Testing and current scope
The backend passes 81 automated tests, covering scenarios such as expired requests, missing verification results, and transaction changes while a check is running.
The screenshots show the actual application in demo mode, where voice results are simulated. All payments are simulated—the prototype does not move money. Reliable production deployment would also require shared persistent storage, stronger authentication, and further testing with real devices and live providers.
The main takeaway from building this project: voice authenticity, speaker identity, and transaction consent are separate checks. Bringing them together makes the review process clearer without treating any single signal as proof.
View the project on GitHub: https://github.com/VptrCipher/kaunbol

articles.title: Spring Security Explained: Filters, SecurityFilterChain and CSRF
articles.description:
When I started learning Spring Security, I thought securing a Spring Boot application was as simple as adding one dependency and writing a few annotations.
But then I encountered things like:

Try it yourself
Imagine Asha is building an online banking application.
Users should be able to:
Register an account.
Log in.
View their account balance.
Transfer money.
View their transaction history.
Now consider two situations.
Situation 1:
A user who hasn't logged in tries to access their account balance.
Should the application allow it?
Obviously not.
Situation 2:
A normal user logs in successfully and tries to access an administrator's dashboard.
Should the application allow it?
Again, no.
These are two different security problems.
Spring Security helps us handle both.
It is a framework that provides authentication, authorization, and protection against common web application attacks.
These two terms are frequently confused by beginners.
Let's understand them separately.
Authentication: Who are you?
Authentication verifies the identity of a user.
For example:
Asha enters:
Username: asha
Password: asha123

The application checks whether these credentials are valid.
If they are valid, Asha is authenticated.
Authorization: What are you allowed to do?
Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to access.
For example:
Asha
|
+-- Role: USER
    |
    +-- View Profile       ALLOWED
    +-- View Transactions  ALLOWED
    +-- Admin Dashboard    DENIED

Another user might have:
Ravi
|
+-- Role: ADMIN
    |
    +-- View Profile       ALLOWED
    +-- View Transactions  ALLOWED
    +-- Admin Dashboard    ALLOWED

Notice the difference.
Authentication answers:
"Are you really Asha?"
Authorization answers:
"Is Asha allowed to access this resource?"
Behind the scenes

                |
                v
          AUTHENTICATION
                |
                v
       Verify User Credentials
                |
          +-----+-----+
          |           |
        Valid       Invalid
          |           |
          v           v
     Authenticated   Reject
          |
          v
      AUTHORIZATION
          |
          v

          |

      |       |

      |       |
      v       v

Spring Security provides infrastructure to handle both operations.
Let's understand what happens when we add Spring Security to a Spring Boot application.
First, add the dependency:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

That's enough to bring Spring Security into a typical Spring Boot application.
Now start your application.
What happens?
By default, Spring Boot's security auto-configuration secures HTTP requests.
It provides default authentication behaviour, including a generated login page and a default user configuration when no custom authentication setup is provided.
You might see a generated password in your application startup logs.
For example:
Using generated security password: <generated-password>

The exact password will be different in your application.
Now try accessing any endpoint.
Instead of directly receiving the response, an unauthenticated browser request will generally be redirected to the login page.
Why?
Because Spring Security protects application endpoints by default.
This is useful because we start with a secure baseline instead of accidentally exposing every endpoint.
But what if we want some endpoints to be public and others to require authentication?
We need to customize the security configuration.
Before that, let's understand how Spring Security actually works.
This is probably the most important section of this post.
To understand Spring Security, we first need to understand something called a Servlet Filter.
A Servlet Filter is a Java component that can intercept HTTP requests and responses before they reach a Servlet.
Think about a security guard standing at the entrance of an office.
Before someone enters the office, the guard can:
Check their identity.
Verify their entry permission.
Reject unauthorized visitors.
Allow authorized visitors to proceed.
A Servlet Filter works similarly.
It can inspect an incoming HTTP request before allowing it to continue through the application.
A filter implements the jakarta.servlet.Filter interface.
For example:
import jakarta.servlet.Filter;
import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletResponse;

import java.io.IOException;

public class MyFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(
        ServletRequest request,
        ServletResponse response,
        FilterChain chain
    ) throws IOException, ServletException {

        System.out.println("Before request processing");

        chain.doFilter(request, response);

        System.out.println("After request processing");
    }
}

Output for a request that continues successfully:
Before request processing
After request processing

Let's understand the important part:
chain.doFilter(request, response);

This statement passes the request to the next filter in the chain.
Eventually, the request reaches the target Servlet.
If there are multiple filters, each one can perform some operation before and after calling chain.doFilter().
What if we don't call chain.doFilter()?
Then the request does not continue to the next filter or target Servlet through that chain.
For example:
public class MyFilter implements Filter {

    @Override
    public void doFilter(
        ServletRequest request,
        ServletResponse response,
        FilterChain chain
    ) throws IOException, ServletException {

        System.out.println("Request blocked");

        response.getWriter().write("Access denied");
    }
}

Output:
Request blocked

The request is stopped at the filter.
The controller never receives it.
This is exactly the kind of behaviour Spring Security uses to protect our application.
Now let's connect this to Spring MVC.
You probably know the normal Spring MVC request flow:
       CLIENT
          |
          v
     HTTP REQUEST
          |

   DispatcherServlet
          |

          |

     Controller
          |

      Response

The DispatcherServlet is the front controller of Spring MVC.
It receives incoming requests and decides which controller should handle them.
But here's the important question:
Should we allow every request to reach DispatcherServlet before checking whether the user is authorized?
No.
Imagine someone tries to access:
GET /api/admin/users

We should verify their permissions before allowing the request to reach the controller.
This is why Servlet Filters are useful.
Servlet filters execute before the target Servlet.
In a Spring MVC application, that target Servlet is normally DispatcherServlet.
The actual request flow looks like this:
              CLIENT
                 |
                 v
             HTTP REQUEST
                 |
                 v
       +--------------------+
       |   SERVLET FILTERS  |
       |                    |
       |   Filter 1         |
       |   Filter 2         |
       |   Filter 3         |
       +--------------------+
                 |
                 v
         DispatcherServlet
                 |
                 v
            Controller
                 |
                 v
              Response
                 |
                 v
               CLIENT

Now you can understand why Spring Security uses filters.
It can verify requests before Spring MVC starts controller processing.
Behind the scenes
The Servlet container, such as Tomcat, manages the Servlet filter chain.
When a request arrives, the container executes registered filters according to their configured order.
Spring Security integrates into this mechanism using a special filter called DelegatingFilterProxy.
We'll understand its responsibility next.
There are three important names here:
DelegatingFilterProxy
FilterChainProxy
SecurityFilterChain
Let's understand them one by one.
1. DelegatingFilterProxy
Spring Security is managed by the Spring ApplicationContext, but Servlet filters are registered with the Servlet container.
How do these two worlds communicate?
This is where DelegatingFilterProxy comes in.
It is a Servlet Filter that delegates request processing to a Spring-managed Filter bean.
Spring Security uses it to connect the Servlet container with its security infrastructure.
2. FilterChainProxy
FilterChainProxy is a central filter provided by Spring Security.
It receives requests through the delegation mechanism and selects the appropriate security filter chain.
It also provides important infrastructure such as security context cleanup and HTTP firewall integration.
3. SecurityFilterChain
A SecurityFilterChain represents a collection of security filters that should be applied to matching requests.
For example:
One chain can protect REST APIs.
Another chain can protect an admin section.
Another chain can handle browser-based form login.
This allows us to create different security configurations for different parts of our application.
Let's understand their relationship.
                 CLIENT
                    |
                    v
              HTTP REQUEST
                    |
                    v
          SERVLET CONTAINER
                    |
                    v
           DelegatingFilterProxy
                    |
                    v
             FilterChainProxy
                    |
                    v
          Select Matching Chain
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
    SecurityFilterChain 1  SecurityFilterChain 2
          |                   |
          v                   v
     API Security         Browser Security
          |                   |
          +---------+---------+
                    |
                    v
             DispatcherServlet
                    |
                    v
                Controller

An important detail:
When multiple SecurityFilterChain beans exist, FilterChainProxy uses their request matchers and ordering to select the first matching chain.
It does not execute every matching security chain one after another.
Also, SecurityFilterChain itself is not the same thing as FilterChainProxy.
Think of it this way:
FilterChainProxy is the central coordinator.
SecurityFilterChain describes which security filters should run for a particular request.
No.
This is an important thing to remember.
Consider this request:
GET /api/admin/users

Suppose the user is not authenticated.
Spring Security can reject the request before it reaches DispatcherServlet.
Similarly, even if the user is authenticated, they might not have permission to access the endpoint.
The request can still be rejected.
Typical HTTP responses include:
401 Unauthorized: Authentication is required or has failed.
403 Forbidden: The request is understood, but access is denied.
The exact response depends on the configured authentication entry point and access-denied handling.

        Authorization Check

Now we understand why security filters execute before the front controller.
Let's configure them.
Spring Security supports Java-based configuration.
Instead of writing XML configuration, we can create a normal Java configuration class.
This is where @Configuration, @EnableWebSecurity, and SecurityFilterChain come in.
@Configuration does


@Configuration is a Spring annotation used to declare a configuration class.
A configuration class is a place where we define and configure Spring beans.
For example:
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class AppConfig {

    @Bean
    public String applicationName() {

        return "Library Application";
    }
}

What happens here?
The class is marked as a configuration class.
The method annotated with @Bean tells Spring to register the returned object in the ApplicationContext.
So we have a Spring-managed bean named applicationName.
Why do we need this?
Sometimes we want to configure objects that are not discovered through component scanning.
For example:
Security configuration.
Database configuration.
Custom object creation.
Third-party library configuration.
We can define such objects using @Bean methods.
@EnableWebSecurity does


Now let's understand @EnableWebSecurity.
This annotation enables Spring Security's web security support for Servlet-based applications.
In simple words, it activates the infrastructure needed for securing HTTP requests using Spring Security.
Example:
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

}

Why do we use both annotations?
@Configuration tells Spring that this is a configuration class.
@EnableWebSecurity enables the Servlet web security integration.
In a Spring Boot application using the Security starter, much of this infrastructure is already auto-configured.
Therefore, explicitly adding @EnableWebSecurity is common in examples and configuration classes, but it is not always necessary in a Spring Boot application.
Now comes the most important part.
How do we tell Spring Security which endpoints are public and which endpoints require authentication?
We configure a SecurityFilterChain bean.
Let's create a simple configuration for our Library application.
package com.example.library.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.configuration.EnableWebSecurity;

import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(
        HttpSecurity http
    ) throws Exception {

        http
            .authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request

                .requestMatchers("/public/**")
                .permitAll()

                .anyRequest()
                .authenticated()
            )
            .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());

        return http.build();
    }
}

Let's understand what we have written.
1. HttpSecurity
public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(
    HttpSecurity http
)

HttpSecurity is an object used to configure web security.
We use it to configure:
Which requests are allowed.
Which requests require authentication.
Form login.
HTTP Basic authentication.
CSRF protection.
Session management.
Custom security filters.
2. authorizeHttpRequests()
.authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request
    // Authorization rules
)

This allows us to define authorization rules for HTTP requests.
3. requestMatchers()
.requestMatchers("/public/**")
.permitAll()

This tells Spring Security that all endpoints matching /public/** can be accessed without authentication.
For example:
/public/hello
/public/about
/public/contact

All these endpoints are public.
4. anyRequest()
.anyRequest()
.authenticated()

This means every other request requires an authenticated user.
5. formLogin()
.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());

Enables the default form-based login support.
Spring Security can provide a default login page.
6. http.build()
return http.build();

This builds the configured security filter chain.
Spring registers the returned SecurityFilterChain bean and uses it to secure matching requests.
Behind the scenes
             SecurityConfig
                    |
                    v
             HttpSecurity
                    |
                    v
         Configure Security Rules
                    |
                    v
          http.build()
                    |
                    v
          SecurityFilterChain
                    |
                    v
            FilterChainProxy
                    |
                    v
           Incoming HTTP Request

This is how we customize Spring Security using Java configuration.
Let's understand the rules in more detail.
Consider:
.authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request

    .requestMatchers("/users/register", "/users/login")
    .permitAll()

    .requestMatchers("/admin/**")
    .hasRole("ADMIN")

    .anyRequest()
    .authenticated()
)

What does this mean?
1. Registration and login
.requestMatchers("/users/register", "/users/login")
.permitAll()

Anyone can access these endpoints.
This makes sense because users must be able to register and log in before they are authenticated.
2. Admin endpoints
.requestMatchers("/admin/**")
.hasRole("ADMIN")

Only users having the ADMIN role can access these endpoints.
3. Remaining endpoints
.anyRequest()
.authenticated()

All remaining requests require authentication.
One important rule:
The order of authorization rules matters.
Spring Security evaluates the configured matchers in order and applies the first matching rule.
For example, this is wrong:
.authorizeHttpRequests(request -> request

    .anyRequest()
    .authenticated()

    .requestMatchers("/users/login")
    .permitAll()
)

The broad anyRequest() rule must come last.
Otherwise, the later rule cannot be used as intended, and the configuration may fail to build.
You might wonder:
When we define our own SecurityFilterChain bean, does Spring Boot still use its default web security configuration?
In Spring Boot, defining your own SecurityFilterChain causes the default web security configuration to back off.
That means your custom security rules become responsible for protecting the matching requests.
This is important.
Don't assume that Spring Boot will automatically combine every default authorization rule with your custom rules.
You should explicitly define the rules your application needs.
Also, defining a SecurityFilterChain does not automatically provide a user database or custom authentication provider.
Authentication configuration is another part of Spring Security.
We'll explore that in Part 2.
Now let's understand one of the most important security concepts in Spring applications.
CSRF stands for Cross-Site Request Forgery.
You might have seen this line in Spring Security configurations:
.csrf(customizer -> customizer.disable())

Many tutorials include it when creating JWT authentication.
But why?
What is CSRF?
And should we always disable it?
Let's understand the problem first.
Imagine Asha logs into her banking website:
https://bank.example.com

After successful login, the server creates a session and sends a session cookie to her browser.
For example:
Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123

The browser stores this cookie.
Whenever Asha sends another request to the same website, the browser automatically includes the cookie.
Now imagine Asha opens another website created by an attacker:
https://attacker.example.com

The attacker has created a malicious form that sends a request to Asha's banking website.
For example:
<form
    action="https://bank.example.com/transfer"
    method="POST">

    <input name="amount" value="5000">

    <input name="to" value="attacker">

    <button type="submit">
        Click here
    </button>

</form>

Asha clicks the button.
What happens?
Her browser sends the request to the banking website.
Because the browser already has the banking session cookie, it may automatically attach that cookie to the request.
The banking server receives:
POST /transfer

Cookie: JSESSIONID=abc123

amount=5000

to=attacker

The server sees a valid authenticated session.
It might think Asha intentionally initiated this transaction.
But she didn't.
The request was triggered by another website.
This is called a CSRF attack.
Behind the scenes
          ASHA LOGS INTO BANK
                   |
                   v
           Bank Sends Cookie
                   |
                   v
           Browser Stores Cookie
                   |
                   v
       Asha Opens Attacker Website
                   |
                   v
        Attacker Triggers POST
                   |
                   v
          Browser Sends Request
                   |
                   v
        Bank Cookie Is Attached
                   |
                   v
          Bank Receives Request
                   |
                   v
             CSRF ATTACK

The important thing to understand:
The attacker doesn't necessarily need to know Asha's password or session cookie.
The browser automatically attaches the existing cookie.
That's the vulnerability CSRF protection is designed to address.
Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default for Servlet-based applications.
It uses a CSRF token to verify that a state-changing request was intentionally initiated by a trusted application context.
A CSRF token is a unique, unpredictable value associated with the user's request/session context.
For example:
CSRF Token: x7y8z9abc123

When the application renders a form, it includes the token as a hidden field.
Example:
<form action="/transfer" method="POST">

    <input
        type="hidden"
        name="_csrf"
        value="x7y8z9abc123">

    <input name="amount" value="5000">

    <button type="submit">
        Transfer
    </button>

</form>

When the user submits the form, the token is sent along with the request.
Spring Security checks whether the submitted token matches the expected token.
If it matches, the request can continue through the security chain.
If it is missing or invalid, the request is rejected.
Behind the scenes
          User Opens Form
                 |
                 v
       Server Generates CSRF Token
                 |
                 v
          Form Contains Token
                 |
                 v
          User Submits Form
                 |
                 v
         Request Includes Token
                 |
                 v
       Spring Security Validates
                 |
            +----+----+
            |         |
          Valid     Invalid
            |         |
            v         v
        Continue    HTTP 403

Spring Security's default CSRF request matcher protects unsafe HTTP methods.
These include:
POST
PUT
PATCH
DELETE
Safe methods such as GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE are not protected by the default CSRF matcher.
Why?
Because GET requests should be used for retrieving data, not changing application state.
This is where many beginners get confused.
You might see configurations like this:
http
    .csrf(customizer -> customizer.disable());

Why would someone disable CSRF?
Because many REST APIs use bearer tokens.
For example:
GET /api/profile

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

Here, the client explicitly adds the token to the Authorization header.
A browser does not automatically attach an Authorization bearer token from JavaScript's local storage to every cross-site request.
Therefore, this authentication setup generally does not have the same automatic-cookie behaviour that creates the traditional CSRF problem.
For this kind of API, disabling CSRF can be appropriate.
But there is an important exception.
Using JWT does not automatically mean CSRF protection is unnecessary.
Suppose you store your JWT inside an authentication cookie:
Set-Cookie: accessToken=eyJhbGciOi...

The browser automatically sends that cookie with matching requests.
Now the same CSRF concern can exist.
The token format is JWT, but the way the browser sends the credential still matters.
So remember:
JWT in Authorization Header
          |
          v
Explicitly attached by client
          |
          v
Usually no traditional CSRF risk


JWT in Authentication Cookie
          |
          v
Automatically attached by browser
          |
          v
CSRF protection may be required

My recommendation:
Session-based browser authentication: Keep CSRF enabled.
JWT passed explicitly through the Authorization header: Disabling CSRF may be appropriate after reviewing the complete authentication design.
JWT stored in cookies: Keep appropriate CSRF protection.
Don't disable CSRF just because your application uses JWT.
Another common confusion is between CSRF and CORS.
They solve different problems.
CSRF:
Protects a website from unauthorized state-changing requests triggered by another site using the victim's existing authentication context.
CORS:
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a browser mechanism that controls whether JavaScript from one origin can access responses from another origin.
For example:
Frontend:

http://localhost:3000

Backend:

http://localhost:8080

These are different origins because their ports are different.
Your browser may enforce CORS rules when the frontend tries to access the backend.
But CORS is not a replacement for CSRF protection.
A server should configure both according to the application's architecture.

.requestMatchers(

    jwtFilter,
    UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class
)

This registers your custom JWT filter before Spring Security's UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.
The purpose is to inspect the incoming bearer token before the later username/password authentication filter position in the chain.
