Your code is a useful learning example, but there is one architectural point worth discussing.
You currently combine:
.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())

.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())

.sessionManagement(session ->
    session.sessionCreationPolicy(
        SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS
    )
)

.addFilterBefore(
    jwtFilter,
    UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class
)

These are different authentication mechanisms.
Form login: Browser-based username and password authentication.
HTTP Basic: Username and password sent using an HTTP Authorization header.
JWT: Bearer-token-based authentication.
Stateless session policy: Avoids using an HTTP session to persist the security context.
They can coexist in some carefully designed applications, but enabling all of them does not automatically make the application more secure.
For a JWT-only REST API, you would generally configure JWT authentication and avoid enabling form login or HTTP Basic unless you have a specific requirement for them.
For a session-based browser application, you would generally use form login and retain CSRF protection.
We'll refactor your complete configuration after understanding the authentication process and JWT lifecycle.
Let's summarize the important concepts.
Servlet Filter
Use a Servlet Filter when you need to intercept requests or responses at the Servlet container level.
DispatcherServlet
Use it as the entry point for Spring MVC request handling. Security filters normally execute before it.
FilterChainProxy
Spring Security's central filter that delegates requests to the matching security filter chain.
SecurityFilterChain
Use it to define which security filters and HTTP security rules should apply to a group of requests.
@Configuration
Use it to declare Spring configuration classes and bean definitions.
@EnableWebSecurity
Use it to explicitly enable Servlet-based Spring Security configuration when appropriate.
CSRF protection
Keep it enabled for session and cookie-based browser authentication.
Disable it only when the application's authentication design makes CSRF protection unnecessary.
What should be my default approach?
For most Spring Boot applications, start with one clearly defined SecurityFilterChain.
Explicitly define:
Public endpoints.
Protected endpoints.
Authentication mechanisms.
CSRF policy.
Session policy.
Add multiple security chains only when different parts of the application genuinely need different security behaviour.
1. Thinking DispatcherServlet is the first component to receive every request
Servlet filters execute before the target Servlet.
Understand the Servlet lifecycle before debugging security issues.
2. Confusing FilterChainProxy with SecurityFilterChain
FilterChainProxy selects and executes a matching SecurityFilterChain.
One is the coordinator, while the other represents the configured security filters for matching requests.
3. Putting anyRequest() before specific matchers
Authorization rules are evaluated in order.
Always place broad catch-all rules such as anyRequest() after your specific matchers.
4. Assuming @EnableWebSecurity creates your complete authentication system
It enables web security infrastructure.
You still need to configure authentication, authorization, and the appropriate security filters.
5. Disabling CSRF whenever you use JWT
JWT format alone does not determine CSRF risk.
Consider whether credentials are automatically attached by the browser, particularly when using cookies.
6. Enabling every authentication mechanism without understanding the architecture
Form login, HTTP Basic, sessions, and JWT serve different use cases.
Choose the mechanisms your application actually needs.
Spring Security provides authentication, authorization, and protection against common attacks.
Authentication verifies who the user is.
Authorization determines what the user can access.
Servlet Filters intercept requests before they reach the target Servlet.
DispatcherServlet is Spring MVC's front controller.
Spring Security uses DelegatingFilterProxy to integrate with the Servlet container.
FilterChainProxy selects the appropriate SecurityFilterChain.
SecurityFilterChain contains the security filters for matching requests.
@Configuration declares configuration classes.
@Bean registers objects in the Spring container.
@EnableWebSecurity enables Servlet-based web security infrastructure.
HttpSecurity configures HTTP security behaviour.
authorizeHttpRequests() defines request authorization rules.
requestMatchers() identifies request patterns.
permitAll() allows public access.
authenticated() requires an authenticated user.
hasRole() restricts access based on roles.
CSRF stands for Cross-Site Request Forgery.
Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default.
Cookie-based authentication needs careful CSRF protection.
JWT authentication through an explicit Authorization header has different CSRF characteristics from JWT authentication stored in cookies.
CORS and CSRF solve different security problems.
Practice idea:
Create a simple Spring Boot application with these endpoints:
GET  /public/hello
GET  /api/profile
GET  /admin/dashboard

Configure Spring Security so that:
/public/** is accessible without authentication.
/api/** requires authentication.
/admin/** requires the ADMIN role.
Use a custom SecurityFilterChain bean.
Run the application and observe what happens when you access each endpoint.
Bonus experiment:
Create a custom Servlet Filter that logs:
Before request processing
After request processing

Register it and observe where it executes relative to DispatcherServlet.
Then add Spring Security and understand how its filters are integrated into the request lifecycle.
Try sending a POST request without a CSRF token and observe the response.
If this helped, or if you spotted something I should fix, tell me in the comments. I'm still learning too.

articles.title: 7 Best Shadow AI Detection Tools
articles.description:
Shadow AI rarely looks dramatic. On a normal Tuesday it looks like this:
A designer pastes a customer spreadsheet into a personal ChatGPT tab to clean it up.
A developer adds an MCP server to Claude Code with their own API key, so the coding agent can query a staging database.
Someone in finance signs up for an AI meeting notetaker with their work Google account, and it now joins every call on their calendar.
None of these people are trying to cause a problem. They're trying to get work done faster, and the approved tools either don't exist yet or take too long to get access to.
The usual first reaction is to block AI domains. That tends to push the same work onto personal phones and laptops, where you can see even less. So most security teams end up with a different goal: know what AI is being used, by whom, with what data, and then move the useful parts onto an approved path.
That first step is what shadow AI detection tools do. In this article I'll cover what shadow AI actually is, why it's worth caring about, the seven tools I'd look at, and how to roll detection out without blocking useful work.

Shadow AI is any AI tool, model or agent used for work without IT or security knowing about it or approving it. It's the AI version of shadow IT, with one big difference: with most SaaS apps the risk is the account, but with AI the risk is also whatever you type, paste or upload into it. And with agents, it's whatever the AI can do on your behalf.
In practice it shows up in five main forms:
Chat apps on personal accounts. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and similar tools, used from a personal login on a work laptop.
AI features inside approved apps. The SaaS tool you already pay for ships an AI assistant, and it gets switched on without a review.
AI apps connected through OAuth. Notetakers, email assistants and writing tools that get read access to calendars, inboxes or Drive with one click.
Coding agents, CLIs and MCP servers. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor and similar tools running with personal API keys and MCP servers nobody reviewed.
Scripts that call model APIs directly. An internal tool or notebook hitting a provider API with a key that lives in someone's .env file.
The first two are what most people picture. The last three are where a lot of shadow AI detection tools go blind, so keep them in mind as you read the list.

The classic example is Samsung. In 2023, engineers pasted internal source code into ChatGPT, one asked it to check database code, another fed it a meeting recording for minutes. Samsung's response was to ban generative AI tools for staff entirely.
It hasn't gone away since. IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach research found that workers using unapproved AI tools figured in 43% of security incidents, more than double the year before. About half of those incidents ended in data loss or compromise, and nearly seven in ten breached organizations had no governance policies covering AI or spotting unsanctioned use.
The risks break down into four buckets:
Data leaving the company. Customer data, source code and contracts end up in prompts and uploads on accounts you don't control.
Access you never granted. An OAuth app or MCP server can read a mailbox or query a database long after the person who connected it forgot about it.
No audit trail. When a customer or auditor asks where their data went, you can't answer.
Spend you can't see. Personal API keys and individual subscriptions get expensed, and nobody has a total.
None of this means AI use is the problem. The problem is AI use you can't see.

Every shadow AI detection tool in this list sees AI use from one or two vantage points, and each vantage point has blind spots. That matters more than any feature list.



Where it looks
What it catches
What it misses




Network (SSE / secure web gateway)
Traffic to known AI domains from managed devices, including uploads and prompts if traffic is inspected
Devices that aren't routed through it, and AI apps it doesn't recognize


SaaS and identity (email, OAuth, CASB)
Sign-ups, OAuth grants and app logins tied to work accounts
Anything done with a personal account


Browser
What users type, paste and upload into AI sites
Desktop apps, CLIs and coding agents


Endpoint
Desktop AI apps, coding agents, MCP configs and data moving on the device
Unmanaged and personal devices


AI gateway
Every model and MCP call that goes through it, with the user, key and cost
Traffic that never goes through it



No single layer catches everything. Most teams combine a discovery layer (to find what's out there) with a governed path (to give people an approved way to use AI).
I chose tools that cover different layers, so you can see the trade-offs side by side instead of seven variations of the same approach. Everything about each tool comes from its own product pages and docs, checked on 24 November 2026. I didn't run them in a lab, so treat the details as what each vendor says it does, and confirm in a trial.
The list isn't a ranking. The right pick depends on which layer you're missing.
Layer: AI gateway, plus endpoint through Bifrost Edge
Bifrost brings coding agents, MCP servers and desktop AI apps under one AI gateway. Bifrost Edge, an agent for macOS, Windows and Linux, routes AI traffic from each machine through that gateway, so you can see which apps and MCP servers are in use, by whom, and with which models. The gateway is also the approved path: teams get their own keys, budgets and logs, instead of personal accounts nobody can see.
Key features:
Virtual keys per team or app that limit which providers and models it can use, with budgets and rate limits on top.
Edge covers the apps on its supported list: Claude Desktop, ChatGPT desktop, Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, and ChatGPT and Claude on the web.
An inventory of MCP servers configured in Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Antigravity, OpenCode, Codex and Cursor, with allow or deny per server.
Enterprise audit logs of administrative changes, plus request logs that record who called which model under which key. Guardrails for secrets and PII, and SSO.
Native Splunk and Datadog integrations, plus log export to S3 or GCS.

Best for: Engineering-heavy teams whose biggest blind spot is coding agents, MCP servers and API keys, and who want detection and the approved path in one place.
Limitations: Edge only covers the apps on its supported list. It won't find an AI notetaker someone connected through Google OAuth, or AI features inside other SaaS apps.
Pro tip: Hand out virtual keys before you roll out Edge. If developers already have a sanctioned key with a sensible budget, routing their tools through the gateway feels like an upgrade, not a crackdown.
Layer: Network (security service edge)
Netskope sees AI use the way it sees all cloud traffic: inline, from devices routed through its security service edge. If you already send traffic through it, AI discovery is mostly a matter of turning it on.
Key features:
A Cloud Confidence Index that, per Netskope, covers 370+ generative AI apps among 82,000+ SaaS apps.
Instance awareness that tells a corporate ChatGPT workspace apart from a personal one, so you can allow one and restrict the other.
Action-level controls, like stopping uploads or downloads inside an AI app instead of blocking the whole app.
Coaching messages that point users to the approved tool.
Real-time DLP on prompts and responses.

Best for: Organizations that already route traffic through an SSE, or plan to.
Limitations: It only sees traffic that goes through Netskope, so unmanaged devices are out of view. It's a full security platform, which is a lot if all you want is an AI inventory. The page doesn't say how it handles CLIs, coding agents or MCP servers.
Pro tip: Use instance awareness to allow the company ChatGPT workspace and coach on the personal one. Blocking ChatGPT outright just sends people to their phones.
Layer: SaaS / CASB, with endpoint signals
If you're already on Microsoft 365 and Defender, there's a good chance you're paying for AI discovery without using it. Defender for Cloud Apps treats AI apps as a category in its cloud app catalog and lets you act on them like any other app.
Key features:
A Generative AI category with more than a thousand AI apps.
A risk assessment for each app across 90+ factors.
Sanction or unsanction apps, and set policies that unsanction new AI apps automatically based on risk score or number of users.
Prompt-level visibility when paired with Purview DSPM for AI.

Best for: Teams already on Microsoft 365 and Defender, who want AI discovery without another vendor.
Limitations: You see apps, not prompts, unless you also set up Purview, which needs devices onboarded to it. Coverage depends on onboarded devices and traffic logs, and the useful parts are spread across several Microsoft products and licenses.
Pro tip: Watch the discovered list for a few weeks before you turn on automatic unsanctioning. You'll learn which AI apps teams actually depend on, and avoid breaking someone's workflow on day one.
Layer: SaaS and identity
Nudge takes a different route from everything else here. Instead of watching traffic, it reads the paper trail every new tool leaves behind in your work inbox.
Key features:
Read-only connection to Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 that scans for sign-up, billing, password-reset and MFA emails.
Finds AI tools nobody put on a list, including ones from months ago.
API connections to core SaaS apps that show which AI tools were granted access to company data through OAuth.
A browser extension for real-time monitoring.

Best for: Finding AI sign-ups and OAuth grants on work accounts, like the AI notetaker connected to someone's calendar.
Limitations: Nudge's own write-up says email discovery can't see AI used with personal accounts, and API coverage is limited to supported apps. It sees that a tool is in use, not what people type into it, unless the browser extension is installed.
Pro tip: Review the OAuth grants first. An AI app with read access to Drive or a calendar is a bigger risk than one somebody signed up for and never used.
Layer: Browser and endpoint
Harmonic started as a browser extension focused on what people put into AI tools. In May 2026 it added an endpoint agent, which pushed it past the browser and into desktop apps and coding agents.
Key features:
Coverage of 1,000+ AI apps with prompt-level controls.
An endpoint agent for desktop AI apps, IDEs, coding agents and direct API calls from scripts on managed machines, plus an MCP gateway.
Small language models on the endpoint that classify sensitive data in under 200 ms.
Coach, warn, block or redact before a prompt is sent.
Restrict personal accounts while leaving approved tools open.

Best for: Security teams whose main worry is sensitive data in prompts, who want to coach users rather than block them.
Limitations: It only covers managed devices it's deployed to. Its focus is data protection, not model access, budgets or cost.
Pro tip: Start in coach or warn mode. A message that explains why a prompt was flagged teaches people faster than a silent block, and it gives you real data before you tighten anything.
Layer: Endpoint and data
Cyberhaven comes at shadow AI from the data side. Its question isn't only which AI tool is in use, but where the data going into it came from.
Key features:
An endpoint inventory of AI tools as they appear: generative AI apps, IDE and CLI coding assistants, agent frameworks and MCP servers.
A risk score for each tool.
Usage sorted into sanctioned, unsanctioned, tolerated or restricted.
Data lineage that traces where data came from before it reached an AI tool, so you know whether that paste came from a customer database or a public doc.
Block, warn or redact, plus allow-lists for MCP servers.

Best for: Teams that need to investigate what data reached which AI tool, not just which tools are in use.
Limitations: It's a full data security platform with an endpoint agent, so rollout is bigger than a browser extension. It doesn't cover unmanaged devices.
Pro tip: Use the tolerated category. Not every tool needs a yes or no on day one, and "fine for now, but watched" is a useful middle ground.
Layer: Browser (with SaaS DLP)
Nightfall is a DLP vendor, and its shadow AI coverage sits exactly where data leaves: the prompt box, the upload dialog and the clipboard.
Key features:
A browser plugin that watches prompts, uploads and clipboard pastes into AI apps.
Visibility into which users or groups try to share which types of data with which AI app.
Block an upload, or redact only the sensitive part of a prompt and let the rest through.
Messages that show users why something was flagged.
Clipboard monitoring on Mac and Windows.

Best for: Teams that already think in DLP terms and want to stop sensitive data reaching AI sites without blocking the sites.
Limitations: The page focuses on browser AI apps. It doesn't describe coverage for desktop apps, coding agents or MCP, and it's built for data protection more than for building an AI inventory.
Pro tip: Lean on redaction over blocking for the common cases. People keep working, and the sensitive bit never leaves.



Tool
Where it looks
Sees prompts?
Coding agents and MCP
Main action




Bifrost
AI gateway + endpoint (Edge)
Yes, for routed traffic
Yes, on its supported list
Route, allow or deny, budget, log


Netskope
Network (SSE)
Yes, with inline inspection
Not described
Allow, restrict actions, coach, DLP


Defender for Cloud Apps
SaaS / CASB
With Purview DSPM for AI
Not described
Sanction or unsanction apps


Nudge Security
Email, OAuth, browser
With the browser extension
Not described
Inventory, OAuth review, nudge users


Harmonic Security
Browser + endpoint
Yes
Yes
Coach, warn, block, redact


Cyberhaven
Endpoint + data lineage
Yes
Yes
Block, warn, redact, allow-list MCP


Nightfall
Browser + SaaS DLP
Yes
Not described
Block, redact, coach



"Not described" means the product pages I checked don't cover it. It doesn't mean the tool can't do it, so ask in a demo.

The best shadow AI detection tool for you is the one that covers the blind spot that worries you most.
"I don't know which AI tools people signed up for." Start with SaaS and identity discovery: Nudge Security, or Defender for Cloud Apps if you're a Microsoft shop.
"I'm worried about what people paste into AI." Look at the prompt layer: Harmonic, Nightfall or Cyberhaven.
"We already run an SSE." Turn on its AI controls first. Netskope is one example, and Zscaler and Palo Alto offer similar modules.
"Our developers run coding agents and MCP servers with their own keys." Look at the endpoint and gateway layer: Bifrost, Harmonic or Cyberhaven.
Then pair detection with an approved path. Finding 40 AI tools in use only helps if people have somewhere sanctioned to go next. That's usually a company workspace for chat tools, and an AI gateway with per-team keys and budgets for developers and internal apps. Without it, detection just turns into a longer block list, and the cycle starts again.

Buying a tool is the easy part. Here's the order I'd do it in, so detection actually changes behavior instead of just producing a scary report.
1. Get a free first picture. If you're a small team on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, start with what you already have: review third-party OAuth grants in your admin console, check which AI domains show up in DNS or firewall logs, and ask people what they use. A short, no-blame survey often surfaces more than you'd expect.
2. Pick the layer that matches your biggest gap. Use the "How to Choose" list above. Most teams need one discovery layer to start, not three.
3. Watch before you block. Run in monitor or coach mode for a few weeks. You'll learn which tools teams genuinely rely on, and you won't break someone's workflow on day one.
4. Publish the approved path. Before you restrict anything, make sure there's a sanctioned option: a company workspace for chat tools, approved keys for developers, and a short list of reviewed AI apps. Tell people where it is.
5. Tighten gradually. Move from coach to warn to block for the cases that really matter, like customer data, source code and credentials. Leave everything else on coaching.
6. Review on a schedule. New AI tools show up every week. Put a monthly review of the inventory, OAuth grants and MCP servers on the calendar, and update the approved list as you go.
A dedicated tool earns its cost when the list grows faster than you can review it by hand, or when a customer or auditor asks you to prove where their data went.
Shadow AI isn't a sign that people are careless. It's a sign that AI is useful and the approved path hasn't caught up yet. The shadow AI detection tools in this list all help, but they help in different places:
Know your layers. Network, SaaS, browser, endpoint and gateway each see a different slice.
Find before you fix. An inventory beats a block list you wrote from guesses.
Coach before you block. People change habits faster when they understand why.
Give people somewhere to go. Detection without an approved path just restarts the cycle.
Keep reviewing. The list of AI tools in use will look different next quarter.
Pick the layer you're most blind in, trial one tool there, and see what it finds.

articles.title: MAGI-2 (480B) vs Seedance 2.5: Field Notes on 30s 1080p Audio-Video Sync & 20-Asset Prompting
articles.description:
I put together three video briefs I can score frame by frame: a product orbit, a skateboard landing, and a two-person dialogue. Each has a visible or audible event that can fail even when the rest of the clip looks good. These are benchmark prompts and inspection notes. I have no matched set of renders to report, so the model-specific observations below come from release documentation or are questions for the first run.
Sand.ai reports 480 billion total parameters and roughly 28 billion active for its flagship MAGI-2. Active parameters describe the computation selected by the model. The complete checkpoint still has to be stored and its weights made available to the inference process. At two bytes per parameter, 480 billion weights alone would occupy roughly 960 GB before quantization, runtime buffers, or offloading. That's arithmetic for a hypothetical weight representation. It isn't a hardware requirement published by Sand.ai. I designed this protocol for hosted endpoints and would record the exact model variant from each job, especially where an interface lists both MAGI-2 and MAGI-2 Preview. Sand.ai's MAGI-2 release notes
For a paired comparison, I would run each base prompt three times per endpoint, using identical source files where both endpoints accept them. I would record the endpoint, model variant, actual dimensions and duration, asset order, seed if exposed, and whether the provider accepted the request on the first attempt. I'd keep the rejected jobs and the unsuccessful takes in the record. Otherwise a manually selected render could conceal how often a prompt needs a retry.



Setting
MAGI-2 (480B)
Seedance 2.5
Kling 4.0




Single take
Up to 30 s. The planner accepts 4–30 s.
Up to 30 s per ByteDance Seed's release page. Check the endpoint for its minimum.
Up to 30 s per Kuaishou's launch release. Check the endpoint for its minimum.


Audio and 1080p
Joint audio-video generation. Sand.ai reports 1080p output at 25 fps.
Joint audio-video model. Verify that the chosen endpoint offers 1080p and inspect sync separately.
Kuaishou reports simultaneous audio-visual output. Verify 1080p availability on the chosen endpoint.


Multimodal references
Up to 20 total, with ceilings of 10 images, 5 videos, and 5 audio clips.
Reference-based generation and editing. Check the selected route's per-modality caps.
Up to 15 reference assets and up to 10 keyframe inputs in the announced Omni Reference workflow. Check how the endpoint exposes each control.


Script length
20,000 characters in the planner and validator. Confirm provider limits independently.
Confirm the endpoint's character or token limit.
Confirm the endpoint's character or token limit.


What I would test first
Separate identity, camera motion, and Foley references.
A continuous take with an explicit initial and final framing.
Camera blocking with keyframes and a fast-moving subject.



The table compares capabilities and planning limits. To score a 30-second 1080p request, I'd inspect the returned file with ffprobe -v error -show_streams -show_format take.mp4. I would record width, height, frame rate, duration, and whether an audio stream is present. An audio stream establishes the presence of audio. Sync needs a separate check against observable events. If only one route can output 1080p, I'd report the actual sizes and judge fine texture in a separate comparison at a shared resolution.
I would run the short versions first, then extend the dialogue test to 30 seconds. For the extended test, I'd add repeatable contacts around 5, 15, and 25 seconds and compare the three offsets. That separates a roughly constant timing offset from drift that grows over the take.
10 seconds, 16:9, one continuous tabletop shot. A matte cobalt kettle sits on a pale ceramic plinth. Use the front and rear reference stills for the kettle's geometry. Match the camera path of the orbit reference while keeping the kettle's own finish and markings.

00:00–00:02: Hold at tabletop height in front three-quarter view. Show the spout, handle, and vertical seam.
00:02–00:08: Orbit clockwise through 120 degrees at a steady speed. Keep the base fully in frame and maintain the same lighting.
00:08–00:10: Ease to a stop behind the kettle. A hand places a small ceramic cup beside the base at 00:09. Add one ceramic tap at contact, with quiet room tone throughout. No music, cuts, captions, or extra objects.

I'd sample frames near the start, halfway through the turn, and after the stop. I'd score whether the seam, handle attachment points, and spout remain consistent. With MAGI-2, I would test whether separating geometry from camera motion holds up when the motion clip contains a different object. With Seedance 2.5, I would check whether its reference control preserves the orbit's easing and endpoint. Label drift and an extra tap are concrete failure cases for either model. A close match on camera path can coexist with a wrong handle, so those get separate scores.
8 seconds, 16:9, single continuous lateral tracking shot at axle height. An adult skateboarder travels left to right toward a low curb. The reference still defines the rider and board. The motion clip supplies the timing of the crouch, pop, clearance, and landing.

00:00–00:02: Roll on level concrete and lower into a crouch. Keep both feet and all visible wheels in frame.
00:02–00:05: Pop the tail, lift over the curb, and level the deck. Keep the curb under the board and preserve left-to-right travel.
00:05–00:08: Land with both trucks on the raised pavement and roll away. Use continuous wheel noise, one tail pop, and one short landing impact. No slow motion or cutaways.

I would step through the take at the pop, curb clearance, and touchdown. A wheel that crosses the curb edge while still on the ground earns a geometry failure, even if the trick reads at full speed. Sand.ai flags trajectory and continuity artifacts under extreme motion. For MAGI-2 I'd inspect the deck edge and the rider's shoe contact before scoring the overall action. For Seedance 2.5 I'd check whether smooth tracking preserves both feet and the full board when motion peaks. Watch the waveform too. A clean impact sound in the wrong frame can make a convincing landing feel disconnected.
12 seconds, 9:16, two consenting adult performers seated at a quiet café table. A sits screen-left and B screen-right. Use one portrait per speaker. Use the two isolated line readings as timing and delivery references for their corresponding speakers.

00:00–00:02: Establish both faces and a cup on the table. Quiet room tone.
00:02–00:06: Hold on A saying, "Did the print dry?" B listens silently.
00:06–00:10: Reverse to B saying, "Yes, it's packed." A listens silently.
00:10–00:12: Hold on B's reaction. B sets the cup down at 00:11 with one soft tap. Keep room tone continuous across the cut. No music, captions, or overlapping dialogue.

I would count exact lines and speaker swaps, then check the lip closure on the first consonant in “packed” against the waveform. At 25 fps one frame is 40 ms. I'd report offsets in frames and milliseconds, allowing for the cut or mouth visibility to make some cues unscorable. With MAGI-2 I'd look at speaker assignment and whether the cup tap survives a more layered soundscape. With Seedance 2.5 I'd check room-tone continuity and mouth motion across the reverse cut. For both, I'd log any substituted words even when the lips appear in sync.
This is a planner job. The filenames stand for local assets, and the provider adapter supplies upload handles and translates reference labels. Check how the endpoint handles numeric weights before adding them.
{
  "duration_seconds": 30,
  "aspect_ratio": "16:9",
  "audio_tracks": ["Dialogue", "Foley SFX", "Ambient"],
  "script": "[00:00–00:10] Anchor faces to a-front.png and b-front.png. Use wide-blocking.mp4 for movement path only. [00:10–00:20] A asks the question using a-line.wav as the delivery reference. Use a-close.mp4 for framing only. [00:20–00:30] B replies using b-line.wav. Align the cup contact to cup-tap.wav. Keep room-tone.wav continuous. Use chair-slide.wav only during the final reaction.",
  "references": {
    "images": ["a-front.png", "a-profile.png", "a-wardrobe.png", "b-front.png", "b-profile.png", "b-wardrobe.png", "table.png", "cup.png", "room-wide.png", "room-reverse.png"],
    "videos": ["wide-blocking.mp4", "a-close.mp4", "b-reverse.mp4", "cup-insert.mp4", "reaction-hold.mp4"],
    "audio": ["a-line.wav", "b-line.wav", "room-tone.wav", "cup-tap.wav", "chair-slide.wav"]
  }
}

I'd begin with the two frontal portraits, one motion clip, and the two line reads. For the full job I'd assign the remaining files to their individual shots and keep sound references as isolated stems. A reverse angle with different wardrobe is a bad identity reference even if the framing is perfect. When two assets compete, I'd remove one, rerun the same prompt, and judge the affected shot before filling another slot. That's a repeatable way to compare conditioning strength when the interface exposes no weights.
The sample schema and validator are in the GitHub templates. The Hugging Face Prompt Studio offers an interactive way to assemble the same job. magi-2-ai.com is a browser-based MAGI-2 workbench that does not require a local GPU.
Disclosure: magi-2-ai.com is an independent third-party online workbench based on Sand.ai's MAGI-2 model. It is not officially affiliated with Sand.ai. This article was drafted with AI assistance.

articles.title: Kagelin v1.54.0: a keyboard-first focus timer and pickers that survive midnight
How to analyze any Substack newsletter's archive with Python (likes, comments, posting rhythm)
articles.description:
Want to know which posts made a newsletter grow? Every Substack has a public archive, and each post carries its like count, comment count, restacks and word count. Put them in a table and a newsletter's whole history becomes something you can sort.
This walkthrough pulls a full archive into Python. Then it answers three questions you can't easily answer by scrolling:
Which posts got the most likes and comments?
How often does the writer publish, and did the rhythm change?
Do long posts beat short ones?
Disclosure: I built the scraper used below (Substack Scraper on Apify). It costs $0.50 per 1,000 posts, and Apify's free plan includes $5 of credit a month, so everything in this post runs for free. The analysis part works the same on any CSV with these columns.
One row per post, always the same keys:



field
example




title
"Varieties Of Discourseposting"


postDate
2026-11-18T...


likes
220


comments
152


restacks
9


wordCount
1552


isPaid
false


contentText
full text, when includeContent is on



It works with name.substack.com and with custom domains (for example https://www.lennysnewsletter.com). No login is needed: it reads the same public pages a visitor sees, and paid posts return only their free preview.
pip install apify-client pandas
export APIFY_TOKEN=...   # Apify Console > Settings > API & Integrations

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("sumitr_mardy/substack-scraper").call(run_input={
    "newsletters": ["astralcodexten"],
    "maxPostsPerNewsletter": 500,
    "includeContent": False,      # metadata only: faster, and enough for this analysis
})
df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
df = df[df["status"] == "ok"]   # a newsletter that fails returns one free row with another status
df["postDate"] = pd.to_datetime(df["postDate"])
print(len(df), "posts")

To skip code entirely, open the actor page, paste the newsletter URL and press Start. Then download the results as CSV or Excel and continue from pd.read_csv.
Likes reward agreement. Comments reward controversy. Rank on both:
df["engagement"] = df["likes"] + 2 * df["comments"] + 3 * df["restacks"]
top = df.sort_values("engagement", ascending=False)
print(top[["postDate", "title", "likes", "comments", "restacks"]].head(10).to_string(index=False))

The weights are a judgement call. A restack puts the post in front of someone else's audience, so it counts for more than a like. Try weights of your own.
Filter out the recurring threads (Open Thread, Links For, and so on) before ranking. They collect comments every week and push the essays down the list:
essays = df[~df["title"].str.contains(r"Open Thread|Links For|Highlights From", regex=True)]

per_month = df.set_index("postDate").resample("MS").size()
print(per_month.tail(18))

A jump or a drop here usually lines up with something the writer announced, such as a paid tier, a book or a break. Lay the dates over the engagement column to see whether the audience followed.
df["length_bucket"] = pd.cut(df["wordCount"], [0, 500, 1500, 3000, 6000, 100000],
                             labels=["<500", "500-1.5k", "1.5k-3k", "3k-6k", "6k+"])
print(df.groupby("length_bucket", observed=True)[["likes", "comments"]].median())

Use the median, not the mean. One viral post can drag a whole bucket's mean up.
Pass several newsletters in one run. The output carries a newsletter field, so a groupby compares them side by side:
run = client.actor("sumitr_mardy/substack-scraper").call(run_input={
    "newsletters": ["https://www.lennysnewsletter.com", "astralcodexten", "noahpinion"],
    "maxPostsPerNewsletter": 100,
    "sort": "top",
})

With sort: "top" you get each newsletter's most-liked posts first, which is the fastest way to see what has worked in a niche before you write in it.
Set includeContent: true and each row also gets contentText (clean text) and contentHtml. That is enough to:
summarise a competitor's best 20 posts
pull out recurring topics
build a small retrieval index over a newsletter you read
Paid posts only include their free preview.
Actor: https://apify.com/sumitr_mardy/substack-scraper

Examples repo (Python, Node.js, cURL): https://github.com/sumitrmardy/substack-scraper-api



If you try this on a newsletter and the numbers surprise you, I'd like to hear which one.

articles.title: I planted 15 bad pull requests to test my AI code reviewer. Here is what broke.
articles.description:
An AI code reviewer told me "Merge After Fixes."
My tests said the PR was broken.
That gap is why I built CodeGuard AI, a self-hosted pull-request reviewer for Java and Spring Boot. The idea is simple: an AI opinion is not evidence.
Every finding is labeled: verified by rule, rule-based heuristic, AI finding with the code located, or AI inference.
An unverified AI claim cannot score above 60/100, however confident the model sounds.
The merge verdict comes from a policy you configure, not from the model.
With sandbox validation on, it runs the project's tests in Docker on the PR head and the base branch, so a failure is labeled "new in this PR" or "already there."
This post is not a sales pitch. It is about what happened when I stopped adding features and tried to break it.
I wrote 15 pull requests against a small Java project: SQL injection, command injection, path traversal, SSRF, XXE, a broken build, fake tests, and a few pieces of safe code that must not be flagged (a prepared statement, a path guard, a hardened XML parser). Then I ran every one through the real app, with a real AI provider and real Docker.
It found more problems in my own work than months of reading my own code. Here are five.
The policy said Do Not Merge. The AI's summary, written before the policy ran, still said "Safe to Merge." Both were technically correct. Together they were useless.
The fix was a small reconciler: when the final recommendation is stricter than the AI's, the summary gets a line saying so and why.
CodeGuard decision: Do Not Merge. 5 finding(s) meet the blocking policy
(severity >= High, confidence >= 80, VERIFIED, category in [Security, Bug, Team Rule]).
The AI's own summary, written before the policy check and not a verdict: ...

Lesson: when a model and a rule engine both speak, the user needs to know who has the last word.
One rule flags tests that assert a value the test itself stubbed:
PriceService prices = mock(PriceService.class);
when(prices.total(10.0, 2)).thenReturn(20.0);
assertEquals(20.0, prices.total(10.0, 2)); // can never fail

The analyzer first collects fields and locals that are mocks. To avoid counting a mock that is later reassigned to a real object, it used a "shadow" pattern roughly like this:
"\\s*=\\s*(?!(?:Mockito\\.)?mock\\s*\\()"   // assigned to something that is not a mock

Look at = mock(. The greedy \s* can backtrack and give back the space, so the lookahead then sees mock( (with a leading space), which is not mock(, and the negative lookahead passes. The mock was classed as shadowed and dropped. The tautology went unflagged.
The fix is one character:
"\\s*=\\s*+(?!(?:Mockito\\.)?mock\\s*\\()"  // possessive: no backtracking

I only found this because I had planted that exact test and it did not fire. A happy-path demo would never have shown it.
Most of a four-minute review was the sandbox downloading dependencies, because each review starts a fresh docker run --rm. I added an opt-in named volume:
codeguard.validation.dependency-cache-volume=codeguard-deps

which becomes -v codeguard-deps-maven:/root/.m2 for maven: images (and the Gradle equivalent). Typical review time dropped to roughly one to two minutes.
It is opt-in on purpose: a shared cache means code in one PR could influence the dependencies of a later run. That is a trust decision for the person running it, not for me.
A review failed with a generic message. The log showed a 413 from the AI provider: on Groq's free tier, input tokens plus the reserved output tokens count against a per-minute cap. A big diff plus a 4,500-token reservation blew past 8,000.
Two fixes: the real cause now appears in the review message, and the docs explain the limit and the knobs (a smaller input budget, another model, or a paid tier). Errors that name their cause are a feature.
When a PR does not compile, the finding now quotes the compiler output, parsed from Maven's [ERROR] lines: file, line, and the missing symbol.
src/main/java/com/lab/CheckoutService.java:12: cannot find symbol (symbol: variable taxRate)

Fixing five bugs is easy to undo by accident, so I added a frozen benchmark: 73 cases, split into a development set, a held-out set and a set of known gaps. A JUnit test replays the real pipeline (diff parser, deterministic checks, security flow analysis, test-quality rules, ranker, merge policy) with no AI and no Docker, and fails the build if a rule regresses or a compliant case gets blocked.
When I added the new security cases, it immediately caught a false positive of mine: "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM " + TABLE was flagged as SQL concatenation even though only a constant was joined. Fixed the same day, with a test.
The analysis is static and name-based, so it can miss indirect cases.
The benchmark uses planted cases. It proves the rules behave as designed. It does not measure accuracy on real-world code.
AI findings and fixes are advisory.
It is a source-code product you run yourself, not a hosted service.
Plant known-bad cases and known-good ones. False alarms get a tool muted.
Test through the real app at least once. My unit tests passed while the product contradicted itself.
Freeze a benchmark and make the build fail on regression, so improvement cannot quietly undo itself.
Make failures explain themselves.
CodeGuard AI is self-hosted Java 21 and Spring Boot with full source. There is a public preview (README, screenshots, one real module with tests) on GitHub: https://github.com/ISabiTech16/CodeGuard-AI
If you review Java PRs: what would you want an AI reviewer to prove before you trusted it?

articles.title: Building an Async‑First FastAPI Service: Architecture, Patterns, and Production‑Ready Code
articles.description:
Introduction


FastAPI has become the de‑facto framework for building high‑throughput HTTP APIs in Python, thanks to its native async/await support, automatic OpenAPI generation, and type‑driven validation. When you couple FastAPI with modern async libraries—asyncpg for PostgreSQL, aioredis for caching, and httpx for outbound calls—you can construct a service that scales horizontally with minimal thread‑pool overhead.
This article walks through a production‑ready architecture for an asynchronous FastAPI service. We’ll examine each component, illustrate the data flow with an ASCII diagram, and present a fully functional codebase that includes:
Structured dependency injection
Centralized exception handling
Connection pooling for PostgreSQL and Redis
Background tasks for fire‑and‑forget workflows
Graceful startup/shutdown hooks
The goal is to give you a reusable template you can drop into a CI/CD pipeline and ship to Kubernetes, AWS ECS, or any container runtime.
Below is a high‑level ASCII diagram that captures the runtime data path from an external client to the persistent store, including optional side‑cars such as a message broker and a cache layer.
+-----------+      HTTP/2       +----------------+      Async      +-------------------+
|  Client   |  <------------->  |  API Gateway   |  <------------> |   FastAPI App     |
+-----------+   (TLS termination) +----------------+   (uvicorn)   +-------------------+
                                          |                     |
                                          |                     |
                                          |                     |
                                          v                     v
                                 +----------------+    +-------------------+
                                 |  Auth Service  |    |  Rate‑Limiter      |
                                 +----------------+    +-------------------+
                                          |                     |
                                          |                     |
                                          v                     v
                               +----------------+   +-------------------+
                               |   Redis Cache  |   |   PostgreSQL DB   |
                               +----------------+   +-------------------+
                                          |                     |
                                          |                     |
                                          v                     v
                                 +----------------+    +-------------------+
                                 |   Kafka Topic   |   |   Background Jobs |
                                 +----------------+    +-------------------+

Client – Any HTTP/2‑capable consumer (web, mobile, service mesh).
API Gateway – Terminates TLS, performs request routing, and can inject tracing headers.
FastAPI App – The core service, running under uvicorn with the --workers flag to spawn multiple event‑loop processes.
Auth Service / Rate‑Limiter – External micro‑services invoked asynchronously via httpx.
Redis Cache – Short‑lived data (session tokens, query results) accessed via aioredis.
PostgreSQL DB – Main relational store accessed via asyncpg with a connection pool.
Kafka Topic – Event streaming for eventual consistency or analytics.
Background Jobs – Executed via FastAPI’s BackgroundTasks or a dedicated worker (e.g., celery with async broker).
Each arrow represents an asynchronous, non‑blocking I/O operation, ensuring the event loop never stalls on I/O.
fastapi.Depends


FastAPI’s Depends system lets us declare per‑request and application‑lifetime resources. By defining a single get_db_pool coroutine that yields an asyncpg.Pool, we guarantee that every endpoint receives a ready‑to‑use connection without manual acquisition.
A custom ExceptionHandler subclass captures both validation errors and unexpected exceptions, logs them with structured JSON, and returns a sanitized JSON response. This pattern prevents stack traces from leaking to clients while preserving observability.
Both asyncpg and aioredis expose pool objects that internally manage a set of open sockets. Pool size is tuned based on the number of workers and expected concurrency, avoiding the “too many connections” pitfall.
FastAPI’s BackgroundTasks is ideal for fire‑and‑forget actions like publishing a Kafka message after a successful transaction. By delegating to a coroutine that runs after the response is sent, we keep request latency low.
The @app.on_event("startup") and @app.on_event("shutdown") hooks ensure resources are allocated once per process and released cleanly, which is critical for container orchestration platforms that rely on SIGTERM handling.
Below is a minimal yet complete implementation that embodies the patterns described. The code is self‑contained—you can copy it into a repository, run uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4, and start issuing requests.
# main.py
import os
import json
import logging
from typing import AsyncGenerator

import asyncpg
import aioredis
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends, HTTPException, Request, status, BackgroundTasks
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Logging configuration (JSON for log aggregation)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s',
)
logger = logging.getLogger("fastapi-async-service")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration via environment (fallback defaults for demo)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
POSTGRES_DSN = os.getenv("POSTGRES_DSN", "postgresql://user:pass@localhost:5432/appdb")
REDIS_URL = os.getenv("REDIS_URL", "redis://localhost")
KAFKA_ENDPOINT = os.getenv("KAFKA_ENDPOINT", "http://localhost:9092/produce")
AUTH_SERVICE_URL = os.getenv("AUTH_SERVICE_URL", "http://localhost:8001/validate")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pydantic models
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class ItemCreate(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(..., min_length=1, max_length=100)
    description: str | None = Field(None, max_length=500)

class ItemResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str
    description: str | None

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# FastAPI app initialization
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
app = FastAPI(title="Async FastAPI Service", version="1.0.0")

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dependency: PostgreSQL connection pool
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
async def get_pg_pool() -> AsyncGenerator[asyncpg.Pool, None]:
    pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(dsn=POSTGRES_DSN, min_size=5, max_size=20)
    try:
        yield pool
    finally:
        await pool.close()

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dependency: Redis client
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
async def get_redis() -> AsyncGenerator[aioredis.Redis, None]:
    redis = await aioredis.from_url(REDIS_URL)
    try:
        yield redis
    finally:
        await redis.close()

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dependency: HTTPX async client (for auth & external calls)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
async def get_http_client() -> AsyncGenerator[httpx.AsyncClient, None]:
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:
        yield client

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Centralized error handling
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
@app.exception_handler(ValidationError)
async def validation_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: ValidationError):
    logger.warning("Validation error", extra={"path": request.url.path, "errors": exc.errors()})
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=status.HTTP_422_UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY,
        content={"detail": exc.errors()},
    )

@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def generic_exception_handler(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    logger.error("Unhandled exception", exc_info=exc, extra={"path": request.url.path})
    return JSONResponse(
        status_code=status.HTTP_500_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR,
        content={"detail": "Internal server error"},
    )

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helper: Publish event to Kafka (fire‑and‑forget)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
async def publish_event(item_id: int, client: httpx.AsyncClient):
    payload = {"event": "item_created", "item_id": item_id}
    try:
        resp = await client.post(KAFKA_ENDPOINT, json=payload)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        logger.info("Event published", extra=payload)
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error("Failed to publish event", exc_info=e, extra=payload)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Endpoint: Create an item (async DB + cache + background)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
@app.post("/items", response_model=ItemResponse, status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
async def create_item(
    item: ItemCreate,
    background: BackgroundTasks,
    pg_pool: asyncpg.Pool = Depends(get_pg_pool),
    redis: aioredis.Redis = Depends(get_redis),
    http_client: httpx.AsyncClient = Depends(get_http_client),
):
    # 1️⃣ Validate auth token (simulated)
    auth_header = "Bearer dummy-token"
    try:
        auth_resp = await http_client.get(AUTH_SERVICE_URL, headers={"Authorization": auth_header})
        auth_resp.raise_for_status()
    except httpx.HTTPStatusError as e:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Unauthorized") from e

    # 2️⃣ Insert into PostgreSQL
    async with pg_pool.acquire() as conn:
        row = await conn.fetchrow(
            "INSERT INTO items (name, description) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id, name, description",
            item.name,
            item.description,
        )
    if not row:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail="Failed to insert record")

    # 3️⃣ Cache the newly created item (TTL 300s)
    cache_key = f"item:{row['id']}"
    await redis.set(cache_key, json.dumps(dict(row)), ex=300)

    # 4️⃣ Schedule background event publishing
    background.add_task(publish_event, row["id"], http_client)

    return ItemResponse(**row)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Endpoint: Retrieve an item (cache‑first strategy)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
@app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=ItemResponse)
async def get_item(
    item_id: int,
    pg_pool: asyncpg.Pool = Depends(get_pg_pool),
    redis: aioredis.Redis = Depends(get_redis),
):
    cache_key = f"item:{item_id}"
    cached = await redis.get(cache_key)
    if cached:
        logger.info("Cache hit", extra={"item_id": item_id})
        return ItemResponse(**json.loads(cached))

    async with pg_pool.acquire() as conn:
        row = await conn.fetchrow("SELECT id, name, description FROM items WHERE id = $1", item_id)

    if not row:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")

    # Populate cache for next request
    await redis.set(cache_key, json.dumps(dict(row)), ex=300)
    logger.info("Cache miss – fetched from DB", extra={"item_id": item_id})
    return ItemResponse(**row)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Application lifecycle events
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
@app.on_event("startup")
async def on_startup():
    logger.info("Application startup – establishing connection pools")
    # Pools are lazily created on first request; you may eagerly create them here if desired.

@app.on_event("shutdown")
async def on_shutdown():
    logger.info("Application shutdown – cleaning up resources")
    # FastAPI automatically closes dependencies that use `yield`.

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Health check endpoint (useful for orchestrators)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
@app.get("/healthz")
async def health_check():
    return {"status": "ok"}




Concern
Implementation




Typed request/response
Pydantic models (ItemCreate, ItemResponse) enforce schema at runtime and generate OpenAPI docs.


Async DB/Cache

asyncpg.Pool and aioredis provide non‑blocking I/O with connection pooling.


External service calls

httpx.AsyncClient handles auth validation and Kafka publishing without blocking the event loop.


Error handling
Centralized handlers for validation and generic exceptions return consistent JSON payloads and log structured data.


Observability
All major actions emit structured logs (JSON‑compatible) that can be scraped by EL

articles.title: How to Create a Shopify App in 2026 (Shopify CLI Step by Step for Beginners)
articles.description:
How to create a Shopify app in 2026, step by step with Shopify CLI: install, create the app, run it in a real development store and make your first Admin API call. Shopify app development tutorial for beginners — everything shown is real, nothing skipped.
  
  



  
  
  What you'll learn



Install Shopify CLI and check your setup
Create a new app from the official template
Run it with shopify app dev in a dev store
Understand the folder structure
Make your first real Admin API call
How to create a Shopify app in 60 seconds with Shopify CLI — one command, running in a dev store.
▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/njpPG_n1EJQ
Shopify app development: the folders in a new Shopify CLI app and which ones you actually edit.
▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/zAf1DqTH87Q
Shopify app development: make your first real Admin API call from a Shopify CLI app.
▶ 60-second video: https://youtube.com/shorts/6-daprtWDD0
0:00)


This is a real Shopify app, running inside my store's admin, and I built it in this video from an empty folder. If you've been wondering how to create a Shopify app in 2026, this is the exact path, step by step, with every error I hit along the way. It even talks to Shopify.
One click, and it creates a real product through the Admin API. That's the result. Now let's build it from zero.
Everything you'll see is real: real commands, real errors, and a real development store. Nothing is skipped or faked. By the end, you'll have your own app running in your store, and you'll know what every important file does.
This is a Shopify app development tutorial for beginners, so we start with what you need. First, Node. Type node dash v, and you should see a version number.
Mine says twenty six. Second, the Shopify CLI. Shopify version prints five point one.
The CLI is Shopify's command line tool. It creates apps, runs them locally, connects them to your store, and later deploys them. If you don't have it, one npm install command adds it, and the official docs show it for every system.
And third, a development store, a free test store from your Shopify account, where you can try everything without touching real customers. You also need a Shopify account that can create apps. In 2026 that's done through the Dev Dashboard, and the CLI logs you in the first time you run it.
1:35)


Now the main command. Shopify app init creates a new app from Shopify's official template. I add a name, the React Router template, JavaScript, and my organization ID so it skips the account menu.
Without those flags, the CLI simply asks you. The React Router template is what Shopify recommends for new apps right now. It gives you a full web app with login, a database, and the admin design system already set up.
The organization is the account that owns the app. If you work for clients, pick your own, so the app doesn't end up in a client's account. It downloads the template and installs everything with npm.
This takes a couple of minutes, so let's skip ahead. And here's my first real error. App name cannot contain Shopify.
Shopify doesn't let app names include its own brand name. I called it my shopify app, so that's on me. Same command, new name: my store helper.
Creating the app also registers it with Shopify, so it gets its own client ID, like an ID card for your app. Notice it says initializing project with npm. You can switch to yarn or pnpm with the package manager flag.
And there it is. My store helper is ready for you to build. It even prints the next steps: change into the folder, generate extensions later, and run shopify app dev to see it.
3:02)


Before we run it, let's look inside, because most of these files you'll never touch. The app folder is your actual app. Inside, routes holds your pages.
Each file is one screen of your app. App underscore index is the home page. App additional is a second page.
The webhook files are where Shopify sends events. Shopify server.js sets up login and the API connection for you, so you don't write any of that yourself. Then shopify.app.toml.
This is your app's settings file: the name, the client ID, and the scopes. Scopes are permissions. The template asks for write products, which is why it can create products later.
When a store installs your app, the merchant approves exactly these scopes. Ask only for what you really need, because merchants and Shopify's review both check it. Now the home page file.
Two parts matter. The loader runs when the page opens and checks the merchant is logged in with authenticate admin. If you know React, think of the loader as getting data before the page shows, and the action as handling a form submit.
And the action runs when you click the button. It calls admin.graphql with a productCreate mutation. That's your Admin API call.
One more thing: the template now ships with agent files for AI coding tools. We'll use that in the next episode.
4:35)


Time to run it. Change into the folder, then shopify app dev, with my store. This command starts a local server, connects it to Shopify, and installs the app on the store you name.
It reads the toml file and shows what it will use: my organization, my app, and my development store. It also says it will update the URLs. While you develop, the CLI points your app at your computer automatically, so you never edit those by hand.
And if you ever connect the wrong store or app, the hint at the bottom matters: add dash dash reset to choose again. And then, error number two. Could not start Cloudflare tunnel.
A timeout. The CLI creates a tunnel so Shopify can reach the app on your computer. Sometimes that network call just times out.
The message gives two options: run the command again, or use localhost. I tried localhost first. Same command, plus dash dash use localhost.
Read this note carefully: localhost doesn't work with features where Shopify calls your app, like webhooks. It also needs a local certificate, so I say yes, and it uses mkcert to make one. Windows asks once to trust that certificate.
That's normal for local development. And error number three. The template subscribes to productUpdate events, and Shopify can't deliver those to localhost.
That's exactly what the note warned about. So localhost is out for this template. Back to option one: run the plain command again.
This time the tunnel connects. Ready, watching for changes in your app. Keep this terminal open while you work.
If you close it, the app in your admin stops loading. You get two shortcuts: P opens the app preview, G opens GraphiQL to test Admin API queries. GraphiQL is a playground where you can try any Admin API query against your store before you put it in your code.
My advice: if the tunnel fails, just run it again before changing anything else. It usually works the second time.
6:43)


Now open the preview link. It goes straight into the Shopify admin of my development store. Because it's a development store and we used the store flag, the app installs itself.
There it is in the sidebar. On a real merchant's store, they would see an install screen with your scopes and approve it first. This is the home page from that app underscore index file.
Let's press generate a product. That button runs the action we looked at. The app sends a productCreate mutation to the Admin API.
And the real response comes back as JSON: an orange snowboard, its ID, handle, status, and variant. Shopify even shows a product created message at the top. This product now really exists in my store.
Edit product opens it in the admin, so you can see it's a normal product, created by your app. That's the whole loop: page, button, API call, real data. Every Shopify app works this way.
Want to read orders instead? Change the query. Want to update prices?
Use a different mutation. The pattern stays the same.
7:52)


Last step: make it yours. I search for the page title in the home page file and change it to my store helper. Then the first card: my first Shopify app is running.
Save. The dev server is still running and watching for changes. This is the workflow from now on: change code, save, and check the admin.
You'll do this hundreds of times. Back in the admin, the new title and heading are already there. No restart, no redeploy.
8:21)


Before the recap, the three mistakes that cost me time today, so they don't cost you. One: putting Shopify in your app name. The CLI refuses it after the install, so you lose a couple of minutes.
Two: panicking when the tunnel times out. It's usually a temporary network problem. Run the command again first.
Three: using localhost with an app that has webhooks. The template has them, so localhost fails. Use the tunnel, or a tunnel URL of your own.
8:59)


So, how to create a Shopify app: Node and the Shopify CLI, app init with a name that doesn't include Shopify, then shopify app dev on your development store. If the tunnel times out, run it again. And if you use localhost, remember webhooks won't work.
You now have a real app that talks to the Admin API, and that's the base for every feature we build in this series. Your app is still a development app. Nobody else can install it until you deploy it and choose how to distribute it, which we'll cover later in the series.
Ideas to practise right now: change the button text, show the shop's name on the home page, or list your five newest products. Next episode, I build a real feature in this same app with an AI coding agent, step by step, and show what it gets right and wrong. If you're building a Shopify app and want help, I'm a Shopify developer, and the link to work with me is in the description.
See you in the next one.
📖 The full written tutorial with every episode: https://www.wixob.com/how-to-create-a-shopify-app-tutorial/
https://www.wixob.com/shopify-app-development-2026/
https://www.youtube.com/@fayyaz-ahmed-shopify-developer?sub_confirmation=1
Questions about the Shopify GraphQL Admin API? Ask in the comments — I answer every one.

articles.description:

 Information
アジャイルFAQ 連載インデックスはこちらから🫱 アジャイルFAQ
前の記事 👈 【アジャイルFAQ 第15回】POが多忙でチームに来ません
質問
#
 リファクタリングや基盤改善のPBIをバックログに積んでいますが、機能開発に押されて常に後回しです。POに掛け合っても「それ、動いてるんでしょ？」の一言で終わります。開発者としては日に日にコードが触りにくくなっているのを感じています。どう説得すればいいのでしょうか？
回答
#
 この質問は、たいてい次の三つの疑問を束ねたものです。
POは技術を分かっていないから、負債の深刻さが伝わらないのではないか
「動いてるんでしょ？」に、どう反論すればいいのか
そもそも品質の話を、なぜPOに承認してもらわなければならないのか
 耳の痛い話から始めますが、伝わらないのはPOが技術を分かっていないからではなく、負債の影響をPOの言語——価値、スピード、リスク——に翻訳できていないからです。
品質は交渉して獲得するものではなく、日々の開発に織り込むものだからです。

「技術的負債もバックログに積んで、POに優先順位をつけてもらいなさい」という指導に、反論したくなりませんでしたか？
#
 「技術的負債の返済もPBIにしてバックログに積み、POが価値で優先順位をつける」。研修の模範解答ですが、開発者の側からはこう言い返したくなります。
顧客に見える機能と、見えない基盤改善を同じ土俵で比べたら、機能が優先されるのが当たり前ではないか
POが「価値」を判断すると言うが、コードの内部品質の価値をPOが判断できるのか
結局、機能開発の合間にこっそり直すしかないのではないか
 結論を先に書くと、「機能 vs 負債」という土俵に上がった時点で負けている。POが判断できるのは内部品質ではなく、その品質が将来のスピードとリスクに何をもたらすか。そして「こっそり直す」は最悪の選択で、代わりに「堂々と織り込む」。
 この連載のパターンに準じて（読者の皆さんも慣れたでしょう？）、まず負債がどんな扱われ方をしがちかに目を向けてから、解説に戻ります。
技術的負債のアンチパターン
#
 負債に悩むチームには、いくつかのアンチパターンがあります。自分のチームのバックログの下のほうを、思い出しながら読んでください。
その１：万年最下位型——いちばんよくある型です。「リファクタリングPBI」をバックログに積み、機能と並べる。POの目には、片方は「顧客に見える価値」、もう片方は「顧客に見えない何か」と映り、ゼロサムの比較で見えないものが見えるものに勝てる道理がありません。質問者が毎回負けているのが、この勝負です。
その２：美意識訴求型——「コードが汚い」「設計が美しくない」「気持ち悪い」という言葉で訴える型です。開発者が痛みを毎日体感しているのは事実ですが、体感が数字と因果になっていないので、POには趣味の話に聞こえます。訴えるほど、開発者の我儘という印象が強まります。
その３：隠れ返済型——機能開発のPBIの中に、こっそり大きめの作り直しを紛れ込ませる型です。短期的には通りますが、発覚すれば信頼を失い、以後の翻訳がすべて疑われます。見積りが跳ね上がる理由を説明できなくなり、負債の話そのものがタブーになります。
その４：大返済待ち型——日々の開発で品質を犠牲にし、「いつか返済専用のスプリントを取ってまとめて直す」と考えている型です。犠牲が日常で返済が例外である以上、負債は単調増加します。まとめての返済は承認のハードルが高く、承認されても「その間、機能開発が止まる」ため、次はもっと承認されにくくなる。待っている返済の日は、来ません。

「機能 vs 負債」の土俵はどこから来るのか
#
 四つの型に通底しているのは、一つの発想です。品質は、機能と引き換えに獲得するものだという前提です。品質が機能との引き換えなら、同じ土俵で競わせるしかなく（万年最下位）、競り負けるのは訴え方が弱いからで（美意識訴求）、正面から通らないなら裏で取り（隠れ返済）、まとめて取れる日を待つ（大返済待ち）ことになります。四つの型は、この前提から導かれる戦い方の一覧です。
 その前提を外して、三つの疑問を読み直します。
 まず、見える機能と見えない改善を同じ土俵で比べたら勝てない、という点。その通りです。だからこの土俵に上がる回数を減らします。負債の大半は、返済専用のPBIではなく、日々の機能開発の中で少しずつ返すものです。土俵に上げるのは、影響範囲の大きい急所だけに絞る。それなら、勝てる勝負に持ち込めます。
 次に、POが内部品質の価値を判断できるのか、という点。判断できません。判断してもらうのはそこではありません。「動いてるんでしょ？」は、POの立場からは正当な問いです。負債の返済は投資であり、投資には根拠が要る。POが適切な判断を下すために必要とする情報とは、「この改修が半年前は3日だったのに今は8日かかっている」「この領域は直近5回中3回で本番不具合が出ている」「このまま行くと来期の△△機能は見積りが倍になる」という、スピードとリスクと将来の予測です。
 そして、こっそり直すしかないのではないか、という点。逆です。こっそり直す代わりに、堂々と織り込みます。「触ったところは、来たときより少しきれいにして帰る」を、個人の隠れ作業ではなく、完成の定義に明文化したチームの公式な基準にする。
専門職としての仕事の品質基準はPOの承認事項ではありません。隠れ返済型との違いは、何をやっているかが開示されていることです。
 「品質は機能と引き換え」という発想は、どこで刷り込まれるのか。技術的負債は、影響が遅れて、しかも別の場所に現れるからです。今日品質を削ったことで引き起こされる損失は、数ヶ月後の別の機能の遅れとして現れ、どの帳簿にも「あの時の借金の利子」という項目で記録されているわけではありません。第13回のPO不在の損失と同じで、因果が見えない損失は、意思決定から自然に漏れ続けます。第2回で見た「早い、安い」の期待——続くコスト削減のプレッシャー——がこれに重なると、テスト自動化やリファクタリングのような「新しい技術への投資」は真っ先に削られる側に回り、負債の積み上がるスピードだけが上がっていきます（テスト自動化がその典型であることは、末尾のおまけで掘ります）。誰も怠けてはいません。因果が見えないだけです。
 そこで、本来の技術的負債はどう扱うものか。経験主義の三段に当てはめると、次の形になります。
透明性——負債の影響が、開発者の体感ではなく、改修のリードタイム・変更失敗率・見積りの偏りという数字で見えていること。
検査——その数字を将来の予測に変え、どの負債が急所かを見極めること。
適応——急所は投資として意思決定に載せ、それ以外は日々の開発に織り込む。返済の効果が出たら、数字で報告する。
 ここに照らすと、美意識訴求型が何を欠いているかが見えてきます。透明性が体感止まりで、検査（どこが急所か）も適応（何を織り込み、何を投資に載せるか）も始まっていない。「品質を交渉して獲得する」から「翻訳して投資に載せ、残りは織り込む」へ。土俵そのものを変えます。
処方
#
 以下は道具の一覧で、全部やる必要はありません。ただし、「ボーイスカウトルールを掲げました」で終わるなら、隠れ返済に名前が付いただけです。試したあとは、改修のリードタイムが縮んだか、POとの会話が「動いてるんでしょ？」から「その予測の根拠は？」に変わったかで、効き目を判定してください。
まず、改修リードタイムと変更失敗率を記録する
改修リードタイムの伸び: 「◯◯周辺の改修は、着手から届くまでが半年前は3日だったものが今は8日かかっています。この傾向が続くと、来期予定の△△機能は見積りが倍になります」
変更失敗率: 「この領域の改修は、直近5回中3回で本番不具合が出ています」
見積りの偏り: 「プランニングで、この画面に触るPBIだけ毎回見積りが跳ね上がっています。理由はこの構造です」
 これらは今日から記録できます。数スプリント分たまると、感覚が数字と因果関係に変わります。
POの言語——正確には、予算を握る人の言語——に翻訳する
交渉ではなく共同の投資判断に変わります。
大きな返済は、投資対効果で絞って提案する
日常に織り込む——ボーイスカウトルール
それでも大規模返済が必要なら、隠さず意思決定に載せる

なぜこの質問は30年繰り返されるのか
#
 損失の因果が見えにくいという構造は、前提の節で見たとおりです。それに加えて、開発者の側も、世代を問わず同じ罠にはまります。痛みを感覚のまま訴え、美意識の問題として退けられ、諦めて黙り、負債はさらに積もる。この連鎖を断てるのは、感覚を数字と因果に翻訳する地道な記録だけです。翻訳の習慣は、どんなリファクタリング技術よりも先に身につける価値があります。
改修のリードタイムが記録されていて、
返済の効果が数字で報告され、
完成の定義に品質作業が明文化されているかどうか。
 この三つが、このチームが負債を交渉ではなく投資として扱えているかを測る計器になります。
おまけ：なぜ日本では、テスト自動化が一般化しないのか
#
 第11回で、テストを手作業で回し続けるチームの「テスト先送り型」を見ました。現場でこの話をすると、「自動化が大事なのは分かっている。でも、うちでは通らない」という声がよく返ってきます。なぜ通らないのか。筆者なりの見立てを、少し歴史をさかのぼって書いておきます。
 日本では長いあいだ、業界を問わず「コスト削減」がマネジメントの最重要キーワードでした。システム開発も例外ではありません。そしてコストを下げる方法として、テスト自動化には、構造的に不利な点が一つありました。投資が先で、効果が後だということです。テストコードを書き、実行の仕組みを整え、保守できる形にするまでには、まとまった手間がかかります。その手間が回収されるのは、同じテストを何十回、何百回と回したあとです。稟議の時点では、出ていくお金ははっきりしているのに、返ってくるお金は「将来の見込み」でしかありません。
 一方、同じ時期に、もっと分かりやすい解決策がありました。単価の低い人手で、テストを回すことです。オフショアをはじめとする低コストな体制に手作業のテストを移せば、テストの量はそのままで、人件費の単価だけが下がる。キャッシュアウトはその月から減り、効果は次の四半期の数字に出ます。自動化が「投資して、何年かけて回収する」話だったのに対し、こちらは「今期すぐ効く」話でした。
 どちらを選ぶかと問われれば、多くの組織が後者を選んだのは、当時の評価の物差しの上では合理的な判断でした。第2回で、コスト削減の制約のもとでは、体制の編成が単価優先になり、モノづくりの能力への投資が省かれると書きました。テスト自動化は、その「省かれる側」の代表選手だったのです。こうして、「テストは人手で回すもの」という前提が、何年も、何世代も引き継がれてきました。その時々の合理的な選択が、同じ方向に積み重なっただけです。
 しかし、この前提は、いまの速さには耐えられません。手作業のテストのコストは、リリースの回数に比例して増えます。年に2回リリースしていた時代なら、そのたびに人手で回帰テストをしても回りました。2週間ごとにリリースするなら、同じ回帰テストを年に26回回すことになります。単価をいくら下げても、回数が10倍を超えれば、総額は追いつきません。しかも人手のテストには、依頼して、結果が返ってくるまでの待ち時間があり、それがそのままリードタイムに乗ります。第11回で、テストがスプリントに収まらず、リリース間際に積み上がる姿を見ました。単価を下げる解決策は、スプリントという速さの前では、解決策ではなくボトルネックになるのです。
 だから、テスト自動化の議論は、「コスト削減」の土俵から降ろす必要があります。自動化は、テストを安くするための投資ではなく、速く、何度でも確かめられるようにするための投資です。この回の処方で、負債を「将来の予測」に翻訳する話をしました。テスト自動化も同じで、処方で挙げた二つの数字を、単価ではなく回数と待ち時間の言葉で語ってください。そうすれば、議論は「いくら安くなるか」から「どれだけ速く届けられるか」に変わります。
 そして、この前提はいま、別の方向からも崩れつつあります。生成AIが、テストコードを書けるようになったことです。テスト自動化の最大の壁だった「投資が先」の部分——テストを書き起こす手間——は、大きく縮みました。コスト削減の物差しで測っても、自動化が負けにくくなっている。長年見送られてきた投資に、ようやく追い風が吹いている、と言ってよいと思います。

前の記事 👈 【アジャイルFAQ 第14回】スクラムマスターは何をする人？ 暇そうに見えます（そして、AIはSMを置き換えるか、というおまけ）
質問
#
 スクラムでは「自己組織化（あるいは自己管理）されたチーム」が理想と聞きますが、うちの実態は、タスクの割り振りも技術的な判断も、ベテランのリーダーが全部決めています。ただリーダー本人もやることが多すぎて疲弊気味、これではメンバーが育たないという自覚もあるようです。だからといって「自己組織化しろ」と号令をかけて何かが変わるとも思えません。
回答
#
 相談を分解すると、三つの疑問に分かれます（※なんでいつも３つなんだと思ってるでしょ？好きなんです、”３”という数字が）。
リーダーが決めるのは、リーダーが手放さないからなのか
「任せる」と言っても、任せたら失敗する。それでも任せるべきなのか
そもそも自己組織化とは、リーダーがいなくなることなのか
 リーダーが決め続ける状態は、怠慢や権力欲の産物ではなく（と信じたい）、合理的な悪循環の産物です。
リーダーが決めると速くて正確

「チームに任せなさい」——その言葉、現場で使えると思えましたか？
#
 「チームは自己管理する」「リーダーは指示するのではなく、チームに任せる」。研修でそう聞いたとき、リーダーの側にはこんな反論が浮かんだのではないでしょうか。
任せて失敗したら、責任を取るのはリーダーだ。それで任せろと言われても
締め切りが近いのに、判断の練習に付き合っている余裕はない
メンバーの側も、決めたがっていない。任せることが親切とは限らないのでは
 リーダーの立場なら、誰でも一度はそう考えます。しかし、「任せる」とはメンバーへの投資であり、なんであれ投資には元手が要るという認識を持つことが重要です。責任はリーダーに残るからこそ、失敗の被害を小さくする仕組みづくりが先にあるべきです。締め切りの近さは、任せる範囲を段階で刻む理由になっても、永久に任せない理由にはならない。そしてメンバーが決めたがらないのは、決めた経験がないから。
リーダー依存のアンチパターン
#
 リーダーが全部決めるチームには、いくつかのアンチパターンがあります。リーダーご本人にも、メンバーの側にも、覚えがあるはずです。
その１：善意の独裁型——最も多く、最も気づきにくい型です。リーダーが誰よりも速く正確に判断できるので、決める。悪意はなく、むしろチームを守っている自覚があります。締め切りが近いほどこの正しさは増しているようにみえ、「今回は急ぎだから」という理由で任せる機会が見送られます。そしてこの見送りは１回ではすみません。ほぼ毎回です。冒頭の質問にあるチームも、おそらくこの型だと思われます。
その２：号令型——「今日から自己組織化でいく。自分たちで決めてくれ」と、ある日突然すべてを手放す型です。決めた経験のないメンバーは判断できず、判断しても失敗し、数週間後にリーダーが「やっぱり自分がやる」と戻す。この揺り戻しが「うちには自己組織化は無理だ」という結論を組織に残します。
その３：先に答える型——会議でリーダーが最初に意見を言う型です。リーダー本人は「意見を出しただけ」のつもりですが、その瞬間に他の案は死にます。メンバーは決めていないのではなく、決める前にリーダーの答えが出てしまっているのです。独裁のつもりがまったくないリーダーほど、この型に気づきません。

二択の思い込み
#
 三つの型は別々の問題に見えますが、出どころは同じです。**「委譲とは、任せるか任せないかの二択だ」**という前提です。二択しかないなら、任せられないうちは全部決め（善意の独裁）、任せると決めたら全部手放し（号令）、意見を言うだけなら任せたことになる（先に答える）。三つの型は、この二択の中で選べる答えの全部です。
 アジャイルの世界では、「二択」のような思い込みをほどいていくことが大事です。さて、三つの疑問に戻りましょう。
 まず、責任はリーダーに残るのに任せろと言われても、という点。その通りです。だからこそ、任せる前に、失敗しても被害が小さい構造を作るのです。リーダーが決めるのは、短期的には常に正しいのです。判断は速く、精度は高く、手戻りは少ない(そんな人にリーダーになってほしい)。一方、メンバーに任せることは、短期的には常にコストです。時間がかかり、ミスが出て、結局リーダーがレビューで拾うことになる…
「任せる」とは、短期の損失と引き換えに長期の能力を買う投資です。そして投資には元手が要ります。失敗を吸収できる余地、待てる時間、そして「失敗は学習の一部」という合意。これらがないチームでは、任せる投資は毎回見送られ、悪循環が固定します。
これらの元手を先に作る、というのが答えです。
 次に、締め切りが近いのに練習に付き合う余裕はない、という点。余裕がないのは事実です。ただし、余裕がないのは「全部を任せる」と思っているからではありませんか？決定すべき対象を分解すれば、締め切りに響かない小さな判断から任せ始められます。ライブラリの選定は任せられなくても、レビューの合格判断は任せられるかもしれない。任せる範囲を段階で刻めば、締め切りの近さは「今はここまで」の理由にはなっても、「ずっと任せない」の理由にはなりません。
 そして、メンバーが決めたがっていない、という点。決めた経験がなければ、決めたがらないのは当然です。判断の機会がずっとリーダーの発言に食われてきたチームで、「決めてくれ」と言われて手が挙がるほうが不思議です。決めたがらないのは性格ではなく、そのチームの歴史であり、歴史は小さな成功で書き換わります。
 最後に、なぜ「二択」としか思えなくなるのか。「優秀な個人が中心となって判断を下す」体制が、小さな成功の必然的な副産物だからです。立ち上げ期のチームは、頼れる個人の即断で速く走る。その成功体験がリーダーへの依存を深めますが、やがてチームが大きくなったころ、その依存は成長の足かせになっています。このとき組織が知っているのは「リーダーが決める」という一つの形だけで、その反対は「決めない」しか思い浮かびません。誰も間違ったことをしていません。段階があることを、誰も見せてくれなかっただけです。
 ここで本来の自己組織化はどう進むものか。透明性・検査・適応に沿って並べ直すと、こうです。
透明性——チームで日々発生する「決めごと」が一覧になっていて、それぞれをいま誰がどのレベルで決めているかが見えていること。
検査——任せた判断がどうなったかを、責めずに振り返ること。失敗の被害は許容範囲だったか、次はレベルを上げられるか。
適応——決定事項ごとに委譲のレベルを一段ずつ動かすこと。うまくいけば上げ、失敗が大きければ一段戻す。
 この三段に重ねると、号令型がどこで失敗するかが分かります。決めごとの一覧（透明性）がないまま、すべてを一度に最高レベルへ動かし、失敗を検査せずに元へ戻している。「任せるか任せないか」ではなく「決めごとごとに、レベルを刻んで動かす」——委譲の設計とは、この置き換えのことです。この転換が、以下の処方の出発点です。
処方
#
 委譲の枠組みは、以下に挙げるもののほかにもいろいろあります。ただ、「レベルを決めました」だけなら、号令型の看板が変わっただけです。試したあとは、リーダー以外が決めた決定事項が増えたか、リーダーの疲弊が減ったかで確かめます。
まず、決定事項の棚卸しをする
委譲のレベルを7段階で合意する
指示する（リーダーが決めて伝える）
説得する（決めた理由を説明する）
相談する（意見を聞いてからリーダーが決める）
合意する（全員で決める）
助言する（リーダーは助言し、メンバーが決める）
尋ねる（メンバーが決めた後で聞く）
委任する（完全に任せる）
 棚卸しした決定事項ごとに、「今はレベルいくつか」「次の四半期でいくつまで動かすか」をリーダーとメンバーで合意します。「タスク割り振りは今3、次は5へ」のように段階を刻むことで、「全部任せて崩壊」という揺り戻しの典型パターンを避けられます。
リーダーの新しい仕事は「最後に話す」こと
失敗のコストを技術で下げる
委譲のスピードは、実は技術的な安全網の整備のスピードで決まります。

なぜこの質問は30年繰り返されるのか
#
 小さな成功がリーダーへの依存を深めていく——このパターンは、業種も時代も問わず再演されます。リーダー本人が疲弊しているというのは、実は好機です。悪循環の維持コストを一番払っているのはリーダー自身であり、「このままでは自分が持たない」という実感は、どんな正論よりも強い変化の動機になります。
 自己組織化とは、リーダーが不要になることではありません。リーダーの仕事が「決めること」から「決められるチームを作ること」へ移行することです。そしてこの移行は、権限を手放す側の勇気と、引き受ける側の背伸びが、段階を刻んで噛み合ったときにだけ進みます。その背中を押すのは、号令ではなく、安全網の設計なのです。
次回: 「技術的負債の返済をPOが優先してくれません（そして、なぜ日本ではテスト自動化が広がらないのか、というおまけ）」
 -->

articles.title: AI時代のソフトウェアエンジニアリング
articles.description:
AIの時代
#
「あなたの開発現場では、誰がコードを実装し、テストしていますか」
「主にAIが実装しテストしている」と答える現場も少なくないと思います。
「AIの導入によって実装や単体テストの負荷が大幅に減るため、人はより上流の工程に時間を使えるようになる」とよく語られています。
こうした現状に対して、「AIはハルシネーションを起こすから、品質を確保するために人のレビューが不可欠だ」という論調があります。
今、多くのソフトウェアエンジニアが同じ疑問を抱えていると思います。
「我々の仕事は、近い将来なくなるのではないだろうか」

ソフトウェアエンジニアリングの必要性
#
この問い向き合うために、一度原点に立ち返って「ソフトウェアエンジニアとはどういう存在なのか」を考えてみましょう。
ソフトウェアエンジニアとはソフトウェアエンジニアリングを実践する人を指します。
エンジニアリングの必要性を説く際、「趣味のプログラミング」と「仕事のソフトウェア開発」の違いがよく引き合いに出されます。
「趣味のプログラミング」とは、自分が使うためだけに作成したスクリプトなどです。
一方、「仕事のソフトウェア開発」は趣味のものとはまったく異なる次元の品質が求められます。
「責任」 が伴うからです。
その責任を果たし、高い品質を確保するための有効な方法論や具体的な手法が、ソフトウェアエンジニアリングには詰まっています。
AIによってソフトウェアエンジニアリングは不要になるのか
#
近い未来において、AIが人間よりもはるかに高品質でバグの少ないソフトウェアを開発できるようになったとしましょう。
「AIは開発した製品に対する責任を負うことができない」 という厳然たる事実です。
OpenAIやAnthropicなど、AIを開発している組織は、そのAI自体に対する責任を負います。
一方で、外部のAIを使って製品を開発する組織は、自ら開発したわけではないAIそのものに対して責任を負うことはできません。
製品に対する責任とは、障害や事故が起きた際に損害を金銭で補償することだけを指すのではありません。
説明責任を果たすことは、論理的で確かな再発防止策を講じるための土台です。
「AIが自動で設計し実装したので、なぜ壊れたのかわかりません」
そんな言い訳を、社会が容易に許容するとは到底思えません。
ソフトウェアエンジニアリングを見直そう
#
「製品に対する責任」の観点から捉えると、AIに作業を丸投げして中身を把握しないまま進めるソフトウェア開発は、どれだけ高度な機能を実装したとしても「趣味のプログラミング」と大差ありません。
ソフトウェアエンジニアが胸を張り、製品に対する責任を持った「仕事のソフトウェア開発」を行うためには、これまで以上にソフトウェアエンジニアリングが重要になります。
「ソフトウェアエンジニアリング」 です。
実装やテスト、文書作成といった、これまで膨大な手間と時間がかかっていた個々の作業をAIが強力にサポートしてくれるようになった今、私たちは大きな分岐点に立っています。

※本記事の内容は執筆者個人の見解であり、所属する組織・団体の公式見解を示すものではありません。
